div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

DOCTOR: "Now, Johnny, pat out your tongue, and let me see it." Johnny: "Well, I'd rather not. I've been walloped often enough for making faces at you behind your back." THE following appears in a small provincial paper: "The bridegroom's present to the bride was a handsome diamond brooch, besides many other beautiful things in cut-glass." "No, my son, it is not always polite to tell a man what you think of him. It is safer to tell it to somebody else, and is just as effective in most instances." FINISHING TOITCHES.—Snob : "I should like you to paint a few additional wrinkles on my fore- head." Artist: "Why ?" Snob: "To give a more thotighttu expression to the face." NOT TO RE TRUSTED. —Judge : "You were alone in committing the robbery?" Delinquent: "Yes, your worship; you see, when you've got a mate you never know whether he is honest or not." TOPER'S LOGIC.—" Am I to have another glass, or not? My head says •No ' ; my stomach says • Yea.' But my head is the more sensible of the two, and the more sensible party always gives in. Ergo, I'll have another!' 'MAMMA, dear,' said Janet, "at what time in the day was I born !'"‘ At 2 o clod{ in the morning." "And what time was I born?" asked Jack. "Not until 8 o'clock." "Ah !" cried Janet," "my birthday's longer than yours." BARBER: You're getting frightfully bald sir." Customer (savagely) : "Well, I don't see how that concerns you. Barber: "Excuse me, air, but it does. You soon won't have any hair left to cut, and then I shall lose a customer. Ma: "Did you say, Jimmy, that Uncle 'Joe took you to the circus to-day ?" Jimmy: "Yes." Ma: "Well, now, tell me: what was the most surprising thing you saw there ?" Jimmy : "Our cook coming in with the butchers's man." . "I THINK I will take a holiday the next three -weeks," rernarked the secretary and treasurer of a private company to the chairman thereof. ." But you returned from one only two weeks ago." "True; that was my holiday as secretary; I wish to go now as treasurer." WHIPPED CREAM.—" Oh! the charming little dear !" exclaimed 3 geleeman addressing a- lady acquaintance, who was taking a walk with her young hopeful, aged eight. "Is he not ?" said the lady. " Besides, he is very good; in fact, he may be said to be the cream of little boys." "That's why I am whipped so often !" interposed the young urchin, pouting his lips. A STEE.N INJIINCTION.—Judge : "As it has been clearly shown that you are not identical with the person charged with the robbery, the Court declares that you are acquitted. There has been an unfortunate mistake, but be careful for the future, mind! Next time you won't get off so easily." THE HEAD Boss.—Father "Now, Fritzchen, wouldn't you like to be a captain and order people aboule like uncle does ?" Fritzchen (ruminating): "Oh, no. I think I know what I should like." lather: " Well ?" Fritzchen: "I'd rather be mamma, and make you and uncle and everybody do as I wanted them." MANAGER ; "I am greatly disappointed in your acting, sir. You have completely ruined my new play by your cold and wooden performance in the love scenes." Leading Man (angrily) : "Then why in thunder do you have a leading lady who eats onions ?" Itarerm and defendant in an action-at-law have been compared to :wo men ducking their heads in a bucket., a.id ach other to remain longest under water. , A SMALL damsel of twelve; who disliked boys, -wrote an essay upon them, in which she said: "If [had my way, half the boys in the world would be girls and the other half would be dolls." YOUNG LADY (to young man) : "I See by the newspapers that monkeys are dying of influenza." Young Man (thoughtlessly) : "Yes, and it came mighty nigh killing me." • .

FATHER "What makes you so extravagant with my money ?" Son: "Because I didn't think you would like to spend it yourself after working so hard for it." IT MAKES A DIFFERENCE. —" HOW much did you say this was "Three-and-six." "That's a big price, isn't it?' "Oh, no, I assure you; the drugs are very costly." "But I am a druggist myself." "Oh, you are? Well—of course—four- pence ! " FRIS,,NER "Yes, your Worship, it is true that I was intoxicatPd last night; but I can explain all if your honour will give me a little time," His Worship: "Ten days." Miss ETHEL (confidentially) : "Do you know, Clara, that .1 had two offer of marriage last week?' Miss Clara (with enthusiasm) : "Oh, I am delighted, dear ! , Then the report is really true that your uncle left you his money ?" AN UNKIND HUSBAND.—Mrs. Jenks: "Do you know, I always look best in calicoes ?" Mrs. Thorpe: "Who told you so ?" Mrs. Jenks: "My husband." COMMENDABLE DECEPTION. Mrs. Grymes : " Why did you.tell Johnny that it would make his moustache grow to near a piece of court-plaster on his lip ?" Grymes : "He can't whistle while testing the matter." "I LINE to see a man think a goo i deal of his home," said old Mrs. Jason "but when he stays out all night to brag about how happy a home he has, I think he is carrying his affection a little too far." AN ASTUTE MAN.—" How does Tankins manage to keep up his extravagant mode of living ?" "Ho :has credit." "How did he get it ?" By pre- tending to be worried almost to death over the income-tax." " %Veil," said Jack, " what% the use of being born before it's time to get up?" - .

- - THAT JEWEL OF A GIRL. —Mrs. Barkington from the depths of the pantry) : " Delila' what have you done with that salad I made yesterday ?" Della (the new girl) : "Sure, mum, I threw it out; it had turned sour." BEGIN AT HOME. Mrs. Suffrage: "It's

woman's highest mis-don to correct the crying -evils of the time." Mr. Suffrage (mildly) : "Then hadn't you better spank hose twins and put them to bed before they yell tile roof off?" " YE% sir, 'every heart Icnoweth its own bitter- ness.' There's G---- who just passed us; did you notice his melancholy look ?". "I did. Has he had some great grief ? ' "He has. He bought on the instalment plan a handsome present for a lady to whom ho was engaged. She jilted him a week ago, and he hs still two instalments to pay on the present. 'lf that isn't a great grief I don't knew what is!" - A NEIGHBOURLY HINT. —Mrs. Suburb: "Why in the world don't you grease that lawn-mower of yours?' Neighbour's 'Hired Man "The missus told sue not to till you had your pianer tuned." Too LATE !—The other day the Bohemian, on receiving some money from a rich uncle took it into his head o square otf some of his most pressing debts. He first called at his tailor's and heard that the poor man had just died. His widow, all in tears, desired to know the visitor's errand. "I have come to pay my bill," he simply replied. "Au l" sobbed out the widow, "if my poor husband had only lived till this morning, the shock might have bronght him round." COULDN'T ADVISE HEIL —She threw herself into a chair, and wept miserably. "I don't know"— She wrung her hands in desperation. "—whether to go back to m.mma or k-k-kill myself." The man with the large neck put his feet on the table, and smiled. "My dear," he observed, "I really would not like to advise you on so close a question of preference." SomEnoov ETSE.—Kathleen had been put out to service, and Mrs. Berry liked the rosy face of the young Irish girl. One day Kathleen was sent on an errand to town. She was longer than usual, and ',qrs. Berry stood in the porch as she came through the field. Kathleen was happy, and Mrs. Berry observed : " Why, Kathleen happy face to-day! You look as if what a rosy, the dew had kissed you." Kathleen dropped her eyes and. murmured: "Indade, mum, but that wasn't his name." "You are accused of having committed forgeries all over the country under the names of Scholz, Miller, Meyers, etc., and none of these names is yours by right," said the judge to the prisoner. Prisoner: "Why, judge, you do not suppose that I would allow toy own honest name to be used in .connection with such swindling transactions, do you?" Nearly every man, woman, and child in Egypt isa srin,ker of ciarettes, and a pipe is hardly ever seen ;n the month of a nalve.

div.head: '"CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: '"CAPITAL" CHAT.

I hear that Mr. Labouchere is to second the reso- lution of whicb Mr. A. C. Morton has given notice in regard to the allowance to the Duke of Coburg. A great deal of interest is felt on the subject below the Ministerial gangway,and the Radicals will issue a special whip in support of the motion. The Duke's presence in London will add piquancy :to the de- bate. _

The little Queen of the Netherlands—for she is very little considering she is fifteen years of age— is in no way pretty, but her manners are most courtly. It is ridiculous to wed her name already with Prince Alfred of Coburg, for one can see quite plainly that she is still brought up in the nursery, and has not the slightest inclination to look at any- one as a possible suitor. Her delight in London is profound, but at the same time juvenile. She is not to be presented at any of our drawing-rooms, and, to tell the truth, does not look like being pre- pared for society for another four years at least.

If the two sections of the labour world in London cannot agree upon a common day for celebrating the May labour festival, they should at least agree, in the interests of labour; not to abuse each other. Sunday afternoon's spectacle on Clapham Common was not an edifying one; but Mr. John Burns, hav- ing been born and developed amid tbe .conflicts of labour, never avoids a battle. The party which he was trying te form in antagonism to Mr. Heir Hardie's Independent Labour party has not taken organised shape but as a series of separate units it is very powerful, and its vote will be cast in sup- port of the Ministerial candidates at the general election. The split goes deeper than the eight hours question, for the Socialist party are as strongly in fifvour of an eight hours' day as the party of Mr. Burns; but the Socialist section wishes to keep ;n line with the Continental labour movement, whereas the Trades' Council, and Mr. Burns with them, narrow their issue to a demon- stration in favour of the eight bours' day alone. From the side of industry generally, Mr. Burns's proposal has the recommendation in its favour, that it is ft proposal for a Sunday demonstration on May-day, which would bring work in London generally to a stop on Wednesday. It is also like opening the labour guns on a particular citadel.

The brewers have now formally decided on the attitude which they will adopt towards the tied- house agitation 1 hey will not attempt to oppose or reply to the agitation, which is, no doubt, wise on their part. They will,however,seek to convince the publicans that it is purel/y a party manoeuvre and designed only to stir up had blood between the wholesale and retail branches of the trade.

It is confidently expected that the Government will seek an early, opportunity to amend the laws relating to. building societies, and particularly to render accountants more completely responsible for their certificates. One member of the 'Cabinet at least is, as I have reason to know, in favour of the establishment of a State inspectorship, after the American fashion; and as his influence on such questions counts for a good deal, it is not impro- bable that something of that kind may be at- tempted. It would be sure to command the ap- proval of the great majority of the Government ' following. As to directors, a proposal. has been made by a leading legal member of the House that directors, when proved by public examination to have been guilty of great negligence in the case of one or two companies, shall be "suspended " for a period of years from joining any other board. Thi.; would undoubtedly mean a great reform, as, al- though a bankrupt whose discharge is suspended May trade in another name or through another person, a person could not very well be a director with an alias.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer's announcement that the Government intend to bring in the One Man One Vote Bill on Tuesday caused quite a sens- ation in the House, and especially on the Opposi- tion benches. Of course their decision is suscep- tible of a very simple interpretation. It has been their plan throughout to lay the whole of their measures before the House at the earliest possible opportunity, and Tuesday's sitting offered a chance which is not likely to recur, when the House goes into Committee on the important measures which have been read a second time. At the same time the announcement, it must be admitted, was en- tirely unlooked for. The prevailing impression in the House was that the One Man One Vote Bill would be'the last of the Government measures taken in band, and that it would be a portion of the busi- ness of the autumn session. In all the circum- stance*it is not to be wondered at. that. the rumours of an early dissolution have revived, and that the action of the Government is interpreted in some quarters as one of the preparations for the event. 1 am told that the Unionist leaders—or some of them, at all events—are strongly disposed to put this serious construction on the introduction of the Bill, and possibly we may hear something of their views on the subject in the debate on the first reading.

The business of the Divorce Court is in great ar- rear, and all who have anything to clO with it are loud in their complaints at the accumulation of work. Sir Francis Jenne is very much more de- liberate in his proceedings than was Sir James Han- nen who was in the .habit of clearing the list for the day with extraordinary rapidlty,and of getting through one, and often two, supplementary lists besides. Sir Francis is one of the most industrious and plodding of judges. It is a common thing for him to it in court till half-past six and half-past seven o'clock, to. the disgust of counsel. clerks. jurors. and witnesses. Suitors from remote parts of the island are often kept hanging about for a week betore receiving any assurance as to when their case will COl2lB on.

The amount paid last year to the unemployed members by the ik at alga mated Sncipt v of Carpenters and Joiners was the largest. in its historv. It was £41,085, or an average of £1 04. Bd. on the trltal membership. Payments for )naintaining " trade privileges," strikes, lock-outs, &c., were £9,346.

It is candidly admitted by the Anti-ParnelP`rs that the continued imposition of the extra duty on spirits will be a source of embarrassment to them and of possible danger to the Government, and as matters at present stand there is no prospect that the party can be brought. absolUtely into line in support. of the continuation of the larger duty. The defections may not be many, but when added to the Parnellites they will form a force that must be reckoned with. The situation has,lunderstand, en2aged the anxious consideration of the party, and will again if it comes to a question of a critical division. At present there are no more then five Anti-Parnellites who are personally pledged to oppose the reimpositi -I of the duty, but there are others who are anxious to escape the odium of sup- porting it.

A scheme iP, I learn, being considersd by the PoPtmaster General for the purnose of affording vet further advantages to depositors in the Post-office Savings, Bank. If it should comp into operation it will prove a nearer approach to State banking than anything yet attempted. It will thus prob- ably create a good deal of opposition in the banking world.

The contest at Walworth, where a vacancy has been caused by the death of Mr. Saunders, will be particularly interesting. It is in this constituency that the Social Democrats have been conrentretinz their efforts for the last twelve months. Their candidate, Mr. George Lansburv. was a former member of the London Liberal and Radical Union, and it was he who first introduced that body to sceept the eight hours resolution. Ile is very well known in Walworth from hi close association with the municipal life of the district. He is, I believe, both a vestryman and a guardian. and he has been prominent in inducing those bodies to follow the labour policy of the London County Council. Several attempts have been made to bring about an understanding between- this gentleman and Mr. Colquhoun Read, the accepted Liberal candidate, but they have failed. The Tories are coneequently anticipating that they will secure the seat.

There is no doubt that the Opposition mean to fight the One Man One Vote Bill by every means in their power. They make no secret (4 the fact that its passing would have a very serious effect on their chances at the general election, especially perhaps in London. The London Unionists nro at all events preparing to give the bill a dotermined opposition and I see.that one of them has already put down notion for its rejection 11.4 was only justbehind Mr. Maclure in doing so.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 4. 1895. LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 4. 1895. LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, Blouses, as I told you before, have come to stay, and nearly all of them are pretty. Changeati petunia of every imaginable shade and combination is first favourite as regards colour, and heliotrope holds its own in gowns. In hats, the tints at first strike one ascrude, but the eye is soon accus- tomed even to the violent contrast of—to use the old-fashioned names—violet and magenta combined on a peen straw I Some of the Parisian hats are veritable bouquets of mammoth poppies (chiefly in petunia shades). heartsease, or hydrangea, some- times all combined. Enormous breadth and com- ps -ative flatness are the distinguishing features of • the latest creations I' A typical one, absolute triumph of tho milliner's art, but " somewhat startling to English ideas, con- sisted of a small shape with two enormous black satin bows about the middle of the crown, sue on each side. In front of them, on one side, a hydrangea, quite the natural Biz% and on the other a poppy in reddish petunia, forming a lovely harmony with the tints of the hydrangea, in front of tLese a steel buckle over a folded piece of the blAck setin ribbon, the ribbon bEing about eight inches wide. At the back, nestling on each side uf the crown behind the satin bows, were °hoax of remade chiffon ; quite at the hack, turning up Vie brim, were 'bout a dozsn gardenia-shaped flowers, ranging in hue from pinkish-mauve to de..pest petunia. J.ckeis have not changed. They are made, as you know, in light materials, with exoeedingly wide revere, and sleeves bigger than ever. They are nearly all tailor-made. Six huge buttons, in two row,, are, I need hardly remind you, the usual number.

A pretty afternoon dress may be made of fancy crepon in a shade of cornflower blue with black fancy silk trimmings combined with bead gimp. The skirt should be trimmed at the foot with two cross-cut bands of orgpon, headed with gimp. The bodice may fasten either back or front. It is trimmed with a vandyked yoke of silk, bordered with jot. The tinder-arm seams of material are joined up independently of the lining to give a baggy effect. A shaped silk belt completes the waist. The stock collar is of silk, and the gigot sleeves are made to match, with a silk cuff. You would require about seven yards of ciepon, one and a quar,er yards of silk, and nine and a quarter yards of gimp. Just) one more—and this a very stylish one! It Is of black fancy crepon, and the trimmings are of black satin ribbon caught with jet ornaments.

The most salient point, cam sorry to say, about the majority of the pats and bonnets of the day-- especially the former—ls the intense gaudiness of their colouring. There is not much to be said against the snapes in vogue, although decided eccentrioitias are to be feunci if search be made for them, but the brilliant greens, the magenta reds, the dazzling purples and blues,, mixed as they often are in kaleidoscopic confusion,, are, to say the least of it, rather overpowering to persons whose tastes lean towards the quiet. Green straw hats promise to be very popular, and a moderately subdued specimen Is of very rough straw, and bai a fairly high, rather pointed crown and wide brim, which is edged with a mane of black chin. Three black ostrich tips stand high at the sides to show two small bunches of brown and gold poly- anthus beneath. In another hat of much the same shape, the crown only is of green straw, the brim being composed of kilted black chiffon, and the trimming consisting of two monster bows of chine ribbon that has a blurred pattern in pink on a faint biscuit-tinted ground, one bow being placed at each side of the crown,

Some of the prettiest toques have orowns of open jet-work, with brims of closely massed flowers, and they are very wide, measuring in many cases more from side to side than from back to front, A stylish model has the crown composed of violet leaves, arta the brim of purple violets, with bows of white lac, and sprays of very pale pink roses at the side, while a third has a polyanthus crown, a black chiffon hrim, and metallic bluish-green wings in front. Black straw hats are being largely worn, and a pretty one of this material had large protruding cream lace butterfly wings. Yours lovingly. JENNIE
Miss Ellen Terry loves canaries. The Empress Eugenie always carries a pet beOgehog with her in a little basket.

President Cleveland has made a pet of a solemn old owl, who perches on his shoulder while he writes or thinks out his speeches. The Empress Dowager of Russia has a jointure of one hundred thousand pounds per annum, and a palace in St. Petersburg, a country place, and the Villa Livadia, where the Czar died, for life, all the establishments to be kept up by the State, quite independent of her in- come. _ _

A breach of promise action' legally must be brought within six years from the time of the breach ; but prac- tically, if it is not brought much sooner than that the lady of blighted affections has but a poor chance of com- pensation. Some years ago a nunkber ofvrecise experitnents were made, when it was ascertained that £lOO worth of sovereigns lost £3 93. 8.4. d of their value in 100 years of use ' • similarly £lOO worth of half-crowns lost £l3 119.8 Bd.

It is believed that there are traces in the animal kingdom of the law that fixes the extreme duration of life at five times that of growth. The latter period in man may be said to average twenty-one years ; hence the full span of a perfec,rty hea!thy man's life should range from one hundred to one hundred and five years. How many people know what a "size "is ? Every- thing from ready-made clothing to gloves is made in sizes, but few know the 'measurement of them. In coats a size is one inch ; a size in underwear is two inches; in a sock, an inch •, in a collar, half an inch ; in shoes, one-sixth of an inch ;in treuiers, one inch ; in gloves, a quarter of an inch ; and in hats, one-eighth.

Royal Extravagance. The German Empress seldom wears silks or satin cost- ing less than ten pounds a yard. The materials for her derni-tiolet cost on an average four to five pounds per yard ; house and carriage costumes from three to four pounds. The latter require, in addition, an immense outlay of " extras," bits of decoration trimmings, &c. The Empress wears a Court dress only once, or, if it be of extremely great value, twice ; but before she wears it a second time its decorations are entirely changed. A Royal wedding calls for eight or nine State full-dress toilets.

Swallowed Halfpennies. A death is reported from (Thorley of a young woman who, eight years ago, swallowed a halfpenny, but had suffered no inconvenience from it. Death was caused by sudden sickness, and the consequent rupture of a blood vesFel. She vomited a green corroded halfpenny. A similar case was that of a boy, three years old, who,on November 12th, 1874. swallowed a bronze halfpenny. Occasionally he had difficulties of swallowing, which he had to overcome by stretching his neck to oneside, and changing his position, but otherwise he had no pain or Inconvenience. On September 21st, 1882, the halfpenny was brought up unexpectedly, and without effort or vomitmg, the boy having swallowed it just thirteen years and ten months previously. He has since been entirely free from symptoms. The halfpenny was very thin and light, and gave the impression that it might have been gradually dissolved,had it not been so happily got rid of. It weight was 57 grains, that of a new bronza halfpenny being 88 grains.

Matrimony in China. The ways of matrimonial negotiations are certainly curious. In China, when a man wishes a certain girl to be his wife, his father writes to her father as follows "On my knees I beg you not to despise this cold and common request, but listen to the words of the matri- monial agent, and give your honourable daughter to my slave of a son, so that the pair, bound in silken threads, may have the greatest joy. In the beautiful spring-time I shall offer wedding presents and give a couple of geese, and let us hope for long and continued fortune. I look forward through endless generations to the fulfilment of genuine love. May they sing of plenty and have every joy. On my knees I beg you to consider my proposal favourably, and throw the mirror-like glance of your eyes on these liner." To this the father of the prospec- tive bride replies that he will " attend to the portion of his poor, poverty-stricken daughter, that she:might not be without bed-clothes, cotton clothing, hair-pins, and earrings. Therefore, it was to be hoped that the couple would have constant fortune."

div.head: LORD CHIEF JUSTICE.
div.p: THE LORD CHIEF JUSTICE.

It was often said, when the famous advocate was pro- moted first to a Lord Justiceship of Appeal and then to be Lord Chief Justice, that he was bound tin be a failure as a judge. The reason when examined was,says a writer in " Cassell's Family Magazine," quite inadequate. It was that it is impissible for a man who has been a brils• liant advocate to be a success as a judge. Lord Russell of Killowen has disappointed his critics in the most pleasing manner. He will rank high in the list, not only of great advocates, but great judges. Ido not say that all lawyers will re- gard him with affection. He has a way of suggesting arrangements and hastening settle- ments in cases which might be prolonged, and be cor- respondingly expensive, which touches the solicitors' pockets. Thrn be has also a way with barristers. Some of the gentlemen practising in his court have already come to dread the tap of the cedar pencil with which he enforces order in his court, the pencil which has effec- tively taken the place of the snuff-box he formerly uti- Bsed. A counsel is badgering a witness—an art,in which, by the way, if report is to be credited, the Lord Chief Justice was himself not inexpert. Comes the warning tap : " Mr. Snooks, I think you are going too far." " I am sorry you should think so, my lud—" " Well, Ido think so," and counsel is wise not to pursue the matter further. Above all, there is the same kindly Sir Charles Russell regarding the court from the Bench, the Sir Charles who used, when tired of the debate in the House of Commons, to slip away to the workiag-men's club in Elackney,and join in a hand at whist till recalled to Westminster. lam told he still keeps a keen eye on the interests of all who come in contact with him in any official or semi-official capacity. It used to be that the press representatives in the courts were not regarded with esteem, and affection was not to be suggested. So far as Lord Russell can,he has changed that in his court; and lam told by Mr. Collins, one of the °lcier •La w Courts reporters, that he has personally seen to the im- provement of the press accommodation, and had it labelled in brass as reserved for the use of the news- paper men. Even still the Lord Chief Justice makes the delivery of a judgment rather a pleasing thing to listen to, and not by any means a circumstance to be fled from, as is the case with some judges. But the contrast between Sir Charles Russell the advocate.,and Lord Russell the judge, is marked. I have, as luck has served, heard him in some of his famous cases. I re- member his speech when defending Mrs. Maybrick—a bigger effort than the exposure of the immortal Richard Pigott; and as an instance of forensic eloquence it must rank high, especially as he knew he was fighting with both judge and jury against Wm.—From " Cassell's Family Magazine " for April.

div.head: WE PARTED AT THE ALTAR; ;
div.p: WE PARTED AT THE ALTAR; ;
By LAURA JEAN LIBBEY,
Author of "A Mad Betrothal," "lone," "Parted by Fate," "Floribel's Lover," etc., etc.
CHAPTER XXIII.

THE MISSING HEIRESS. "No, no," repeated Doris, vehemently, "I can- not accept any favour from a stranger's hands. It would not be right." Fate decreed that it should be otherwise, how- ever ; for at that moment, overcome by the pain of the swollen ankle, Doris suddenly fell backward against the cushions in a deep swoon. Mr. Lancaster immediately gave the order to No. West Twenty-third-street. This was a fashionable up-town boarding-house, and to the landlady, Mrs. Morgan, Dr. Lancaster's son was well -known. .

_ She was sitting at the window when the coach stopped before her door. She looked with amaze. ment as the door of the vehicle was suddenly flung open, and Mr. Lancaster stepped to the pavement bearing the unconscious figure of a young girl in his aTms. What could it possibly mean? She admitted him herself. _ _ _

In a few brief words, as he laid his unconscious burden upon the sofa, Karl told Mrs. Morgan how he had met the lovely young stranger, and rescued her from being crippled for life—but that the violent fall to the pavement had injured her ankle, however. _

With Mrs. Morgan's assistance, the swollen ankle was soon attended to. It was not as bad as he had at first supposed ; still it would necessitate the fair patient's keeping her room for a fortnight at least. "And you want me 0 keep her here until she is able to be about?" asked Mrs. Morgan, dubiously. "I would do anything in the world for you or your family, Karl, for your father's skill saved my child's life once—l never forget that; but I feel a little reluctant about taking in this stranger. You should have taken her to the hospital." Karl could not bear the thought, somehow. "She is so fair, so fragile and delicate, it seems a pity to send her there." While they had been speaking, Mrs. Morgan had been vigorously applying cold water, to which a few drops of ammonia had been added, to the patient's face' to revive her from her protracted swoon. Her face, hands and hair were bathed and rubbed briskly to start the circulation of blood, when lo! a strange thing happened under the strong action of the ammonia. I. The dark stain commenced to quickly disappear from both face and hair. .

Mrs. Morgan called Karl to her side with a cry of dismay. "Look, Mr.. Lancaster !" she cried. "The girl i 8 disguised! She is fair as a lily—not dark !" Karl's amazement was certainly as great as her own. They looked at each other in silence and dismay. "There is some dark mystery here, depend upon it," declared Mrs. Morgan, emphatically. "No young woman who lives an honest, straight- forword life has anything to conceal. This girl may be a thief, an impostor, or worse. I am sorry I took her in. I shall never know a moment's peace, with watching her night and day, while she is under this roof. She must be taken away." "I cannot bring myself to believe that there is anything wrong about her," declared Karl, impul- sively. "I really cannot." Mrs. Morgan looked at him sharply. "I should say her pretty face has bewitched you, Mr. Lancaster. She little dreamed how near the truth these words were. "As I sad before, out of this house she goes to-morrow, Mr. Karl. lam sorry for her ; but I cannot have her here. She must be taken to the hospital." "I will call to-morrow, then, and see about effecting the change, if you must have it so," said Karl, disappointedly and co'dly. When ice morrow came, Doris could not be moved. Al high fever set in, and her condition was qui'e alarming. In a week's time, however, the fever hal abated, and the danger was past. But in those few days Karl had been a daily visitor at the house. Whole hours he spent at his patient's bedside, skillfully battling with the fatal fever, until at last it was under control. And in those days Karl had learned to love the beautiful stranger with all the ardour of his nature. She was his first and only love—and first love is the sweetest dream of life. At the end of the week, again Mrs. Morgan insisted upon having the lovely young stranger removed. Though weak, Doris was conscious. She had refuse to divulge her name to Mrs. Morgan, say- ing simply, "Call me Doris ; only that. More I cannot tell you. lam very unhappy. No young girl has suffered more than I have in this world, and more unjustly." One day, when Karl called, he found Doris's eyes heavy with unshed tears, and he felt then that Mrs. Morgan must have spoken to Doris about wanting her apartment. "I am going to leave you to-day, Mr. Lancas- ter," she said, holding out a mite of a white hand to him. "You have been very kind to me. I can never repay you for it, save by my most heartfelt gratitude.' "But where are you gong ?" he asked, earnestly. "You are too weak and ill to face the world. What will you do ?" "I do not know," responded Doris, drearly. In a moment handsome, impulsive Karl was beside her. "Let me tell you what to do," he cried, eagerly, "Marry me. I love you. When I first looked upon your face I said to myself : She and no other shall be my bride ill can win her. Our acquaintance has not been long, still, it has been long eit,:tgli for me to know. If I lost you, die would not be worth the living. Yes, I love you with all the deep, earnest affection of a heart that has never throbbed with love for any woman before. Marry me, and let me take you to my father's home, and present you to hint and to my mother as my cherished bride. My life will be devoted to you. You shall never know one wish unfulfilled.' "Stop ! stop I" gasp d Doris, incoherently, as she endeavoured to check the torrent of his im- passioned words. "Do not, I pray you, speak so to me. It can never be. I—l am sorry, for you have been so kind to me. While lam most grate- ful to you, I repeat that I can never, never marry you." The young man started to his feet, dropped the little hand he held, and looked at her. Never had she appeared so fatally lovely to him, as in this moment in which she told him she never could be his. "Tell me," he cried, approaching a step nearer to her, his face paling, "is my causejlopeless ? Do you love any one else !" "Yes," she said, simply, "I love another, and love as hopelessly as you love me. For that reason my heart aches with the Keenest sympathy for you. You must learn to forget me, Mr. Lancaster." "It will be hard ior me," he said gently. "I have learned to love you so well. If you were to ask me for my life at this moment I would give it to you • and if ever you want a friend, remember my words. I will give my life to serve you." "Thank you," she faltered. "If the time should come when I want you, I shall not forget." "You will at least give me your full name?" he said, sadly. "It is cruel to know you only DA Doris." "Then know me as Doris Brandon," she mur- mured. The name had a strangely familiar sound to it, but he was too much perturbed just then to think of it. "If I knew you were going to home and friends I should feel happier," he said. And he never forgot the sad voice in which she replied: "On the whole face of the earth I have neither home nor kindred. I am alone in the world! Alone?" Those were the words which haunted him as he left the house and walked slowly toward his home.

His father was in the library. Karl paused on the threshold as his father called his name. "Still pouring over those papers, father?" he asked, as he drew up a chair to the table. " I have advised you, in my opinion, the only way to find this long-lost heiress, Mits Fielding, is to advertise in all the leading pipers for information concerning her." "Many an adventuress, tempted by so magnifi- cent a fortune, might respond," declared the doctor. "No; I prefer to go *about it in a more methodical way, by tracing Miss Fielding, or Miss Brandon—Miss Doris Brandon, the name she was called there by—from the school she—" In a flash Kt.s,rl Lancaster had sprung to his feet,
"Doris Brandon /" he gasped. " (*mat Heaven! am I Mad, or do I dream ? ' ' In an instant he had se:zed his hat and rustmd from the house.

Dr. Lancaster stared after his son's rapidly vanishing form in the greatest astonishment. "I cannot th nk what is getting over the boy of late," he mused. "Now, why should he start off in that abrupt fashion ?" Meanwhile Karl had hailed a passing cab and sprang into it. "To Number West Twenty-third-street I" he cried. "Be as quick as you can, driver." The man whipped up his horses, and the vehicle fairly flew down the avenue, but to the impatient young man it seemed to fairly creep along. "Doris Brandon !" he cried, hoarsely. "Heaven ! how strange it is that the name did not strike me as the one by which Mr. Hulbert Brandon Field- ing's long-lost heiress was known by while at boarding-school! And her face! Ah ! there could be no mistaking the lovely childish face, framed in its rings of soft golden curls, so like the face of Mr. Brandon's wife, only younger, sweeter, fairer." There remained no doubt in his mind but what Doris was the long-lost heiress for whom his father was searching so diligently. A moment later the coach drew up in front of Mrs. Morgan's boarding-house. In a flash Karl was up the steps and the vigorous peal of the bell brought the landlady her- self to the door. " What ! Is ft you back so soon again, Mr. Lan- caster ?" she said, looking curiously into the flushed, eager, handsome face. "Yes !" he answered, impetuously. "I must see Doris at once, please. Tell her it is a matter of the greatest importance." "You are too late, Mr. Lancaster," she replied. "Doris is gone. She left the house about twenty minutes ago." Gone ! Gone I He could scarcely believe he had heard aright.
CHAPTER XXIV. THE GIPSY GIRL.

SINCE the night of the sad tragedy Frederick Thornton was a changed man. He grew morose and silent, spending his time shut up in the library, or whole hours by the river bank, gazing thoughtfully, and with bitter regret, on the sunlit water, beneath which he believed Doris lay in all her sweet beauty. The discovery of Vivian's true disposition, beneath that mask of smiles had been a severe shock to him; his own soul revolted at the thought of marrying her now. He concluded to leave home for awhile, and seek such solace as a life of travel would bring him and forget, as far as he could, the sweet, fair face Of the lately young bride whom he had won only to lose on their bridal day. One morning, corning down to breakfast a little earlier than usual, ldrs. Thornton saw her son standing, buried in deep thought, by the lace. draped window. "Mother," he called, wheeling suddenly about, "will you see that a few necessary articles are packed up in my valise with as little delay as possible? I am going away for a few months." Mrs. Thornton trembled. This was an unlooked- for procedure. In vain she pleaded, coaxed and argued with her handsome son. He was inexor- able. "I must go away for a time, mother," he said. "Do not oppose me." "But Vivian 1" she said. "Your going will, break her heart." A scornful smile curled his cynical lips. He was just about to reply : "You are mistaken there, mother; she has no heart," but he checked the impetuous words. His mother had scarcely quitted the morning. room ere he saw a small lad approaching the house in a hesitating manner. Frederick drew back the lace curtain, and called to ti.e boy. "I want to see Mr. Frederick Thornton," said the lad. "Can you tell me where I can find him, sir ?" "Here, my boy. I am Frederick Thornton. What can Ido for you r _ _

"1 am to place this letter in your hand, sir, and wait for a reply," he said, touching his cap. "The genth man who gave it to me is pacing up and down the ravine yonder, waiting for the answer." "I will not keep you waiting long," said Fred- erick. He had noticed that the envelope was addressed in Mr. Courtney's writing, and was written in pen- cil. He tore open the envelope, and ran his eyes over the no e it contained, his handsome face turn- ing strangely pale as he read. It was brief, to the point, and read as follows: "Mn. FREDERICK THORNTON—Sir : The an- nouncement of the dissolution of the engagement of marriage which has existed between my daughter Vivian and yourself has just reached me. You have annulled that bond coolly and deliberatty, it seems, without just cause or provocation (as there is no barrier between you and Vivian), ex- posing her to the comment of the whole social world by this outrageous conduct. I, as her father and protector, demand that the marriage shall go on. She must be your wife ere the sun sets, or I shall demand, on your ref uSal to comply with so perfectly reasonable a request, the only satisfaction one gentleman can accord another—a duel. And within the hour in the deep ravine that skirts the cliff down the road, there I await your answer. "COLONEL COURTNEY."

_ Not a muscle of Frederick Thornton's face changed. A stern expression crept into the grave, dark eyes and around his mouth. He knew that the colonel was perfectly well aware of the conditions under which that engagement with Vivian was contracte 1; that, owing to that fatal accident, all memory of a bride waiting for him, or all trace of her presence, had been obliterated completely from his mind. In all truth and honour, be had believed himself free to woo and win the old soldier's daughter. • It was quite true, since Doris's death (as he believed her to be dead), no barrier rose between himself and Vivian save his own inclina- tion. He was too honourable to wed Vivian without love' and love her he did not. He had no heart to offer her. His heart was buried in poor little Doris's grave. He would not be coerced into marrying Vivian. He would be true to poor little Doris's memory while his life lasted. He tore a leaf from his memorandum book and pencilled the following words upon it: "I will be upon the ground at the appointed Uwe.
" FREDERICH THORNTON."
This he hastily folded up and handed to the lad, who quickly disappeared with the fatal mes•

sage. Five—ten—minutes passed. Frederick Thor. ton still stood by the window, motionless, gazing out into the brilliant sunshine; then he turned away with a sigh, and set about making his pre- parations for the coming event. The time was short, but he completed his business arangements, and wrote out the directions for the distribution of his effects. The whole earth looked so peaceful, so smiling, under the light of the summer s sun, that poor Frederick told himself it would be hard, indeed, to leave it. Mrs. Thornton never foriot how pale her hand- some son looked as he came into the room, took her in his arms and kissed her, saying that he was going t., stroll down the road a little way, the morning was so fine. Was it instinct, a forewarning of some dread calamity, that caused his mother to follow him to the porch, refusing to be comforted? "I don t feel right about your going out this morning, Frederick, my son," she sobbed. "Something tells inc I shall never 930 you as I see you now. Something tells me you should not go." "Nonsense, mother, I will come back to you in an hour's time, if my life is spared," he said, with stiff, white lips. Would to Heaven she could have understood how fatally true those words were. He tore himself from her clingine, clasp, and kiss- ing the white hands that would' have held him back from ruin and destru3tion, with swift foot- steps walkel rapidly down the paved walked, and out of the grounds. He stooped a moment on the brow of the lull and looked a, oend him. When that sale sun rose again he might never see ii, or if he lived, his hands would be dyed with a fellow-creature's life-blood. Frederick Thornton shuddered, then a reckless sort of laugh broke from his lips How green the slopir?ef hillside looked, dotted here and there with brilliant wild flowers and spreading beech trees. The river danced in the sunlight beyond and its music &milled like a dirge in his ears. Toward the right of the stream the greensward

WaS dotted hefe and there with gipsy tents; swarthy men and maidens making the air ring with their songs. Quite ap 4rt from the rest, and directly in the path before Frederick, a young girl sat. A tambourine, decked with bright, gay rib- bons, lay on the grass beside her, and her gaudY, picturesque dress, her long dark 'hair, and bright, black, glancing eyes betokened her race. A gay, dashing song broke from her crimson lips, and Frederick Thornton stopped short in the path, his arms folded across his chest, his head drooping upon his bt east, and listened. The gipsy girl raised her eyes suddenlY, and saw the stranger standing in the daisy-studded path. She bounded to her feet with the agility of graceful young gazelle, and courtesied low before him. "Have you come to us to have your fortune told, handsome youth ?" she asked, raising lustrous eyes to his face. I can tell you all the mysteries that lie in the future, and the dark shadows that have gathered in the background of the past." her dark, Although he knew better, Frederick stood for a , moment irresolute. At any other time in life he would have scorned the proffered offer; but neWP when life and death hung in the balance, a fever- . ish unrest possessed him to hear what she fiould tell him. Long and earnestly the gipsy girl gazed into the palm of the white, shapely hand she held ill her own small dusk ones. "You are unhappy in your love," she said, slowly Frederick Thornton laughed a mirthless, reek; less laugh; but a strange, brooding shadow creP; into his eyes, and a flu-h rose to his Pale! lian-; some face, which told the crafty maiden that he- shaft had struck home, as it usually did. •" Do you see a long life or a speedy death for me?" he questioned, curiously. liPg And although he spoke carelessly, his whitened perceptibly. "Death," she said, in a whisper. "Let it come—l have courted. it," rettirr:ecive. Frederick, impatiently. "I have nothing t° for, any how.' Vic Although he spoke bravely, he could realise hard it was to die in the spring-time of youth bid farewell to the green earth and fair, sai,illoll7, heavens; to he rushed all unprepared—where 'gal could hear no more. div.head: RAIL NVAY TIME TA BLE.
div.p: RAIL NVAY TIME TA BLE.
FROM WARRINUTON TO
MR. LESTER B A.RRETT AT WA RRINGTON.

The Warrington Shop Assistants' Association, judged wisely in deciding to engage Mr. L-ster Barrett for Monday evening at the Co-operative Hall,Sankey-street. Early on Monday morning the promoter's of the enter- tainment received from Mr. Barrett the following tele! gram : "Leave Manchester in good form 5.30 to-day." This, of course, set all doubts at rest as to the possibility et Mr. Barrett not being able to appear, and the town was very soon flooded with handbills announcing the certainty of hie advent. At the time for commencing the programme the Hall was crowded and Mr. James Batchelder, the eminent pianist and composer, led off with an overture entitled " Pianoforte," which he per- formed with his usual succ?.ss. Following this Mr. Bar- rett, who was received with an enthusiastic burst of applause, rendered at intervals :—Humorous song," By the sad sea waves ;" character song, He couldn't take the two. of us ;" patter sketch, " A disappointed Author," with song, " My Sister's Serenaders ;" charac- ter song, " That was enough for me "; new sketch, " Spring cleaning •," new song, " I didn't know till afterwards." Mr. Batchelder gave another pianoforte solo entitledi" Men of Hariech," which he played with many enhancing variations. Miss Marie Smith sang" A woodland serenade," and " The Holy City," the latter being encored. Miss Smith has a beautiful voice and she I did more than justice to the above mentioned songs. This concluded the first half of the evening's "menu" and after the lapse of a short interval the following items were given :—Mr.B ..tcholder in another pianoforte selection entitled " Selected," Mr. Barrett in the songs "Stammering Sweetiv•ar,s," and "My Fire-. side Castle," while Miss Marie Smith gave " Killarney "and " Dear Heart," both of which were very sweet renditions; the former received on enthusias- tic encore and it is no exaggeration to say. that "Kil- larney," was hardly ever heard to better advantage in the Co-operative Hall. All the items enumerated and taken part in by Mr. Barrett, were without exception accorded laughter and applause wholesale. Indeed.of " hilarity" there was no end and the pcpular comedian scored a huge success. In the character songs his get-up was particularly appropriate and added not a little to the vocal part of the entertainment. In addition to his songs Mr. Barrett had an abundant repertoire of buns and jokes which he was continually " cracking off " to the great enjoyment of his audience. The chief piece was however, the entertainer's new seaside sketch "Says Mr. Brown to Me," or " Papa's left at Home," in which Mr. Barrett makes his appearance arrayed in feminine costume of fashionable cut, which represents him rather destitute of figure,though he is not 18 stone as be alleges the fabulous Mrs. Brown to be. The sketch in question is full of Americanisms,jokes, and amusing contretemps, ' and was undoubtedly the piece of the :evening, which was brought to a dose by Mr. Barrett renderiog " Some dance the lancers," at the same time introducing what the others danced With laughable effect. Taken all round it is some time since Warringtonians had such an opportunity of indulging in uncontrolled merriment and they certainly, on this occasion, made no secret in " throwing off the yoke."

div.head: EXTENSION OF THE MERSEY WHITE
div.p: EXTENSION OF THE MERSEY WHITE
LEAD WORKS.
THE MANUFACTURE OF WHITE LEAD.

' The business at the Mersey White Lead Works, Sankey, has been very prospbrous, and from time to time the premises have had to be extended. The largest extension which has yet taken place has been made recently, and consists of seven large corroding chambers, new becks, and new grinding machinery. This will give an increased output of 1,500 tons of white lead per annum and will, of course, find work for a considerable number of fresh hands. This is good news when we hear so much about other works going short time, or even closing altogether. Al visit to the works, of which Mr. George Thompson is the manager, is very inter- esting and instructive. The process of converting the " blue" lead into white lead occupies a considerable time—about three months, and consequently there is always a large quantity of lead either in the pig or in the the transitory state or finished. The pig or blue lead is first melted and run into long flat strips of a convenient size. These strips are then taken to the corroding chambers, which are large buildings, some of them capable of holding upwards of 18 or 19 tons of lead. The modes operandi is as follows number of earthen pots about the size of ordinary jars are laid on the floor, and each pot is filled with dilute acetic acid. Over these are placed the strips of lead above mentioned, and these in turn are covered with the bark which is the"well known waste pr.)- duct of tanyards. This in turn is covered with boards which thus form a fresh loon Another row of pots is then placed on these boards,and the lead. &c., placed above, and thus the chambers are at length tilled with the pots and lead and bark. These chambers are then kept at a temperature of about 150 degrees for three months, when the lead strips are completely metamorphosised into white lead. The lead has been acted upon by the acetic acid, which thus forms an acetate, and this in turn is acted upon by the bark which has de- composed, and the carbonate formed. The strips of white lead are then taken to the grinding house, where they are ultimately ground to a fine powder. The pigment is kept damp, in fact, wet through, the whole of the time this goes on, in order that there may be no dust. The finished article is then packed in boxes damp, ready for transit. A large number of men are employed at the Mersey White Lead Works, and although this is regarded by some as a rather dangerous employment ,such are the sanitary arrangements that there is no sickness whatever other than what might occur in ether places of business. There is absolutely no lead poisoning. There is a lavatory in which are two baths, and the men are required to bath at least once a week and as much oftener as they please. There is also a washing basin in every room. The men by this means are enabled to remove all trace of the deleterious white lead powder, and thus suffer no ill-effects from it. There is no doubt but that the business is a very prosperous one, and this is a matter for congrathlation to the district.

div.head: FORGETCS OUTFIT.
div.p: A FORGETCS OUTFIT.

SINGULAR DISCOVERY BY THE POLICE. The London police have in custody a mah named Meodal Howard on a charge of having in his possession engraved plates and other material for the manufacture of American, French and German bank notes, railway bonds and eon pons. After his arrest his hence was searched, and the police found printing machines, photographic apparatus and chemicals, forged nates,and in fact everything necessary for the production of forged " securities " on an extensive scale. The prisoner,who was described on thn charge sheet as " a scientific investigator," and who when arrested said lie was " an experimentalist," was on Tuesday remanded for a week. He had in his possession a passport showing that he is an American citizen.

, more successful issue, if they could only put their hearts into it. It would be a very great pity if they could net get anyone to " court " them,and that the division went by default, 4nd they allowed Mr. Legh to have a walk over. (Hear, hear.) Although they had been defeated in the past they still had hope for the future. With regard to the education question,he said that he was sure that the Board of Management in connection with Penketh schools would be very pleased if certain of the inhabit- ants of Penketh were nominated by a public meeting or other means to act with the Board of Management. He was glad that upon the subject of payment of members, the caneidate had spoken with no uncertain sound. Until the people could get men to represent them from themselves, and dependent to some extent upon them- selves, he did not think that the subjects upon which they were specially interested,would have that force and support in Parliament that it was necessary for them to have. There was no doubt that the land interest and the capitalist interest—the latter was probablf the strong- er—were over represented. It was only when the workers themselves were more directly represented that they could expect that the questions they were specially in- terested in to make progress. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in moving the vote of thanks to Mr. Moon and of expressing their great obligation to him and also Mr. Rawlins for coming to speak at that meeting.

Mr. ROGUES seconded the motion. The Camaraax, in putting the motion to the meeting, hoped that the young men present would not be afraid of being called Radicals, as a Radical meant a reformer. The Tories believed in standing still, and letting well alone. There , was, however, no letting well alone- They must either be progressive or retrogressive. The young men should try to be progressive,and they should always remember that they had the welfare and respon- sibility not only of glorious little England, but also of the gre3t empire over which she ruled. He hoped that everyone present would be imbued with the spirit of true Liberalism, and that they would endeavour to make the Newton division in accord with their princi- ples. ( Appla use.) The motion was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously. Mr. Moon, in response, said that he would like to join issue with Mr. Parker when he said that it required a plucky' matt to accept an invitation to contest Newton. He thought the tone adopted in the Newton division was a mistaken one. If he were sup- ported by the party unanitndusly be had practically 4,000 voters supporting him, and he did not think it re- quired much pluck for any man to champion a cause which was so well supported as that. At the meetings he had had the honour of attending, ke had been delighted with the earnestness and the enthusiasm of those attending them. •He thought it most encouraging that in a place like Penketh, there should be such a large gathering on such a beautiful evening as it was, when there were so many ways of spending it muck more pleasantly. He was convinced that if the Liberals of the Newton division would put their shoulders to the wheel there would be a different tale to tell than in the past. Hitherto, as Mr. Rawlins had said, there had been reasons for defeat, but he was certain that if everyone would feel his responsibility, they would be able to win Newton for the Liberal cause. (Applause.) He believed it possible to win Newton, but he would not contest the division unless he had the hearty and enthusiastic sup- port of every Liberal. (Applause.) He concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Aitken for taking the chair that night, and he hoped that when the time came, Mr. Aitken would perfarm more important duties.
Mr. RAwLms seconded the motion. He said that hoped that the Club, with Mr. Aitken at its head as President would do good work for Liberalism. _ .

The motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. Aitken in reply said that he believed they had got a body of as good, steady-going Liberals in connection with that club as could be found anywhere. At the last election they polled every man they expected. He hoped that at the next election, they would be equally unanimous,and that they would be more successful in the aggregate. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING A.T P.ENKETEL
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING A.T P.ENKETEL
ADDRESS BY MR. J. MOON.

A meeting of Liberals was held at the Penketh Liberal Club on Monday evening, for the purpose of choosing members to attend the Liberal 300 of the Newton Parliamentary division, which will shortly be held. There was a good attendance and the chair was occupied by Mr. J. B. Aitken, and there were also present Messrs. J. Moon, G. W. Rawlins, C. E. Parker, Longshaw, Hughes, White, Cros3, etc. The following members were appointed members of ' the executive, Messrs. J. B. Aitken, R. Greenhalgh, A. White, W. Longshaw, F. Hughes H. Wilkinson and L. Humphries, and Messrs. Longshaw and Aitken were appointed members of the executive committee. After this preliminary business bad been completed, Mr. J. Moon, of Liverpool, who will be recommended as a suitable candidate for the Newton division at the forth- coming meeting of the Liberal 300, addressed the meet- ing. He was received with applause, and said that he considered it a great honour to be invited to visit the various polling districts of the Newton division. He should feel it a great honour of course to contest the seat, but he should be sorry to undertake the task of becoming their candidate unless he had behind him the hearty and enthusiastic support of the Liberal party, and that Rapport they could not give unless they were acquainted .with their candidate. Having made up their minds on the subject, he hoped they would throw themselves into the work with enthusiasm and energy, and try to win the seat. The question whether it would be won largely depended upon themselves. He would not have been present if he had not been a strong be- liever in the present Government and îü the programme the Government were trying to carry out. That pro- gramme was being proceeded with to the best of their ability, and he believed that the prospect of carrying many of the measures which had been introduced was brighter than ever. (Applause.) It had been thought that the House of Lords would throw some of them out—he referred to the Irish Land Bill, the Welsh Disestabliehment Bill, the Local Veto Bill, and let them hope the Registration Bill, which was still to be introduced, might be included. But suppos- ing they did throw them all out, what then? Remember it was the same body which opposed the ballot, the Reform Bill of 1832, Catholic Emancipation, National Education, and which rejected the provision in Lord Palmerston's Mines Bill of 1880 for allowing pit children' the same facilities for education as the children of the I factory. It was said they would throw out the Bills now before Parliament, but what if they did? Well, if they did, and Nswton still returned a Conservative to endorse that action, so much the worse for the cause of progress and social advancement. As long as constituencies like Newton supported the Conservative party, so long would that wing of the Conservative party, the House of Lords, continue to thwart and retard the measures of the Liberal party. (Applause.) The work of the Liberal party was to educate the voters to their political creed; that was the only remedy for the present state of things. It was useless to discuss im- practicable measures, and it would he far better for them to make their voice heard, a united voice—and not voices in sections, as he was afraid they were inclined to do. If they spoke witn a united voice they would be irresistible. (Applause.) He had every confidence that the Liberal party were not losing ground. They had had rebuffs and re-actions, and he should be glad to make the Conservatives a present of Oxford if they would only make the Liberal party a present of Newton. (Laughter and applause.) He was in thorough sympathy with the Local Veto Bill,lbelieving that the drink traffic ought to be placed in the hands of the peo-' pie themselves. If the people wanted more public-houses let them have them,but if they did not want them there was no reason why they should be forced upon them. At the last general election the brewers devoted £lOO,OOO to assist the Conservative party, and, therefore, it was not surprising that the Conservatives were slow to dis- connect themselves from the brewers. ' Then there was the question of one man one vote. It was a pity the Li betel party had not placed that measure in the front rank, because so long as they had duplicate voters it was quite impossible to tell what the feeling of the country was. At Newton they had a Conservative majority of several hundreds, and yet he had been given to understand that there were over 1,000 out voters ; so that at present they were in this position : that a constituency having a majority on one side might be swamped once or twice over by outside and faggot voters. That was a question which Liberals would been to keep in the front rank, and which would do more than anything else to enable the democracy to express their wishes with no uncertain voice. (Applause.) Lord Rosebery said recently that politics was net a game in which the pawns were to be knocked down by the castles and the Knights, but was an ennobling effort on the part of men to make the con- ditions of life better. That was the view he (Mr. Moon) took of politics, and it could only be done when the masses of the country were considered as well as the better classes. If he accepted the candidature of the division he trusted the party would not be thrown off the scent by red herrings across their path. Hs hoped they would not be turned aside by every little difference of view that might be brought forward. No two men were alike, and whilst he was in total . yeleathy with the Liberal party he had views, and those views he liked to follow to the best of his ability without regard to con- sequences either war. (Applause.) Mr. rOWNALL asked what were Mr. Moon's ideas about compensation for the brewers and publicans. Mr. Moor: replied that with reference to compenaation, he had no conscientious objection to it, so lone, as it came from the right quarter. If they decreased the number of licenses, they increased tha value of the licenses which were left, and therefore he thought the question should be left to the publicans themselves. In dealing with that question, he would mention that a short time ago he saw in a Manchester paper that in Manchester, there 3,000 licensed houses. and 2.960 of these houses were brewers' houses, thus only leaving eo owned by private individuals. So far as the ratepayer were concerned he was certainly opposed to any com- pensation coming from them. (Applause.) Another gentleman asked Mr. Moon what his views were with reference to the eight -hours for miners. _

Mr. WHITE said that he did not-cinit.C-ae-e with Mr. Moon when he said they should net fight in sections. He considered that when in the case of Ireland eight- tenths of the people were in favour of Home Rule, they should grant Ireland Home Rule, and when in the case of Wales, nine-tenths of the people were in favour of the disestahlishment of the Church, the should have that granted them. He hoped also that Mr. Moon was in favour of eight hours, and the payment of members.

Mr. MOON' said that Mr. White should have understood him to have meant small sections. He was certainly of opinion that disstablishment of the Church in Wales should he granted. and also Home Rule for Ireland. He would also vote for payment. of members. With regard to the Miners Eight Hours' Bill, last week he met the onlliers at Haydock who were particularly interested in the matter, and he was told at that meeting that his an- swer 7ave satisfaction, and it was to the effeet ,thitt he was in sympathy with the movement for reducing the number of hours of work. With regard to the mines the question was a technical and complicated one, and one upon which the miners were not unanimous. He therefor. preferred to keep an open mind on the sub- ject until he got further information. His attitude was therefore one of neutrality, but it was one of friendly neutrality. (Applause.) _ . _ . .

- , Another questiOn was askod.whether Mr. Moon would place voluntary and board schools on an equal footing with rAgard to the benefits they received from the Educational Department. Mr. AITKEN Said that they did receive equal benefits already.
Mr. Moon vas then asked whether he wag in favour of voluntary schoolq. receiving aid.frons the local rates.

Mr. MOON replied that he would have no objection, provided that they would allow the local ratepayers to he represented on the Board of Management. (Applause.) Mr. LONGSITAW thought this was a satisfactory ex- planation. Ile thoughtithat no aid should he given un- less representation were also allowed. With regard to the Eight Hours' Bill, he thought it ought to he sup- ported. He thought their candidate should rally the miners of that division to the standard of the Eight Flours-question. He thought that it would have a great deal of influence in securing his return. (Applause.) He would, however, have great pleasure in supporting Mr. Moon a,nd doing all he could to secure his election. (Applause.) Ile honed he would be a little more definite upon the Eight Hours' question. . Mr. (1. W. RAWLINS after briefly referring to tiva Eight Hours question in which he showed that the miners were not unanimous with regard to details of the measure, said that he hoped a cordial invitation would be given to Mr. Moon by the 300, to contest the Newton division. The division required efficient organi- sation and thorough registration, and to obtain this, it was intended to have a theroughlY efficient and experi- enced registration agent permanently employed for that purpose. It was also absolutely essential that all the polling districts should he so organised that every man would know what he was expected to do when the day of election came. He knew the Newton division well, and he kmew there was ample material for winning R great victory for Liberalism if only they were well organised. :(Apolause.) The Liberal party had failed in the Newton division for want of erganisation. They were also under another disadvantage,. Ritherto they had had what were called "carpet baggers." This time, however, they had not got a "carpet bagger." They had a Lancashire man, and one who would not leave them directly after the election was over. Mr. Moon was rather in love with the Newton division. He wished o carryi Present, a little flirtation with it ati he hoped would be consolidated (enr) for_ whee h into a much more lasting sort of arrangement, and perhaps a suitable political marriage would be arranged, 'and that they would live happily ever afterwards. (Laughter.) Tie hoped that when the rieht time came, a unanimous invitation would he given to Mr. Moon to contest the division. (A ppla use. ) Mr. C. Ti. PARSER proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Moon for his address that night. He could only say that Mr. Moon was, really a very plucky man, and they all admired plucky men. They had been somewhat dis- heartened in the past, hut there were certain features mentioned by Mr. Rawlins which made them hope for a

The Assrsratgt CLERK reported that the balance in tnA and ne the treasurer in favour of the Union was R 3,870 184. 7d.—Mr. HICKMAN asked whether it was usual to have such a large balance in hand.—The CLERK replied that it was not, but the greater part of it might be spent before the next meeting.— Me CHAIRMAN said that sometimes they had ta draw on the treasurer. The estimates were more favourable than usual this year.
SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.
This committee reported that they had elected .Mr. Davies, chairman, and Mr. G Pilling, vice-choirman.— The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Devirs. seconded by Mr. PILLING.
ROUSE COMNITTEE.-THE PROPOSED NEW INFIRDERRY.

At a meeting of the House Committee, the master was requested to take the chah pro. tem. when Mr. Knowles proposed, and Mr. Halton seconded that Mr. S. Davies be elected for the ensuing year. An amendment was moved by Mr. Hickman, seconded by Father Moore,that Mr. J. Clarke be elected chairman. On the amendment being put, it was carried by a majority of one. Mr. Clarke then, took the chair and Mr. Thompson proposed and Mr. Billinge seconded that Mr. A. J. Jolloy,be elected vice-chairman. This was carried. It was decided that the firewood offered by Mr. Denham be accepted at 14s. 6d. per ton, delivered at the Workhouse within one month, as the committee considered it much the best sample submitted. At a subsequent meeting it was recommended for the puiposes of carrying out the minute of the commitee under date February Ist, and unanimously approved and adopted by the Board that a new Workhouse Infirmary was desirable, and a commit- tee of eight guardians be appointed to act as an Infirm- ary Committee, with power to take any action thereon, and that such committee be requested to report their proceedings at an early special meeting of this committee. The Beard at the meeting on Wednesday appointed the Rev. J. Fl. Riddette, Messrs. I. W. Knowles, G. Thomp- son. Pilling, A. Jolley, J. Clarke, W. Boughton, and A.J. Jolley.—The minutes of the committee were carried on the motion of Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, secOnded by Mr. MALKIN.

div.head: AFTERNOON TEA.
div.p: AFTERNOON TEA.

"I think singing is a gift and not a thing you can learn," said Molly, as she tried to insert a blunt chisel into a tin of condensed milk. "Now there's the girl next door to us, she thinks she can sing, but—"

Here Azulab's voice made itself heard, "It is a grand idea. You call at a house, and ask how many members of the family attend a place of worship." "lo they tell you, I would'nt,' muttered Pierre, critically examining a mole on her face, with the aid of a minute piece of looking glass. Azulati who had Salvation Army tendencies, drank her tea in silence, the very picture of patience. There were twenty girls in my room, at Harding and Co.'s and nearly all were drinking tea on that genial spiing afternoon. Overhead a complicated arrangement of wheels and leather bands, revolved and shot swiftly onward, to the accompaniment of a low droning thunder. To be heard across the room, we bad to shout, Shakspeare's ideal woman's voice, if a girl happened to possess it, was sighed farewell to as an impractieal possession. A soft breeze railed my hair as I leaned against the open *win- dow, idly counting the' chimneys within my' view. There were twenty-eight, all smoking steadily. I scanned them with a searching eye. No, I could not accuse one of the whole two dozen and a quar- ter, with my own half hearted attention to business. Beyond the chimneys rose a huge building, with the staring label, ':Smith's Furniture Repository." I had a strong dislike to Smith although I never met him, and I hated his ugly and depressing ' re- pository ' with a thoroughness and heartiness I seldom threw into my work, according to the plain opinion, frequently volunteered by the other girls. They earned more money than I did, for they were bright, practical and alert, waist I was given to dreaming at inconvenient hours of the working ay. "Freda, Freda," shouted Pierre, "It is your turn to make tea." With a sigh I turned from the window, and held out my hand for the teapot, a large one holding about ten cup fulls. In the yard half a dozen stalwart young packers, their shirt sleeves rolled up to the elbows, were endeavouring to force a heavily loaded truck through a narrow passage. Ginger was with them directing and assisting, Ginger was an apprentice of nineteen and was supposed to be qualifying for the position of a master in the near future. After business hours he was well worth seeing in his perfectly fitting clothes, jewelled •breastpin and rings, and flower in his buttonhole, but Just now he was minus collar and coat, and his youthful brow was bedewed with perspiration. "Oh Freda, do move on," exclaimed two or three girls behind me, "Stop pushing," I said menacing the nearest with my tea pot, "the road's blocked." By dint of strenuous exertions the truck was forced through the gap, and I darted after it, cast- ing an apprehensive glance at the high wall of bales still shaking with the concussion. A flight of stone steps and I was in the stoke hole. The stoker was absent from his domain,and I cautiously opened the iron door of the furnace end peeped in. I loved to watch the tremendous imprisoned fire. The crowd of girls was so great I could not get near the hot water tap, so I wandered into a mysterious underground cavern, illuminated with a single gas jet, and filled with old iron,and ancient machines. Nobody seemed to know what they were or why they were there. My theory, that they were relics of medieval instruments of torture was accepted without question by my confiding companions. Returning with my teapot filled to the brim with boiling water, I found Ginger sitting on a bale. "It did me good to see you work," I said admiringly, "I did'ut know you could do it." "What did you think I was here for," be demanded with a look of pain, for I had spilled, but quite by accident, some hot tea over his foot. "Oh to look pretty and to impress callers, " I hazarded. " Bah, get upstairts," said the disgusted Ginger, and I "got." The oily wheels of the machine glistening in the blazing sun, seemed more distasteful than ever after the fresh outside air. I closed my eyes, and suffered my cup to stand unheeded before me. "A penny for your thoughts, Freda," said Molly. I opened my eyes unwillingly. "I was wishing for something." Always wishing and wanting ; you will never be happy while you are so discontented." "Give me a cure for discontent," I asked, picking the loose fluff and bits of cotton, off her dress, but the reply fell flat, because I knew it beforehand. "Give your attention to your work, and then you can't think of other things." And Molly returned to her machine, a noisy object, with a spiteful trick of flicking oil into your eyes, when you were least expecting such an attention. Tea was over, and we returned to work. The air was cooler, but the time seemed leaden winged. Yet we were working our hardest. The close of the afternoon is the busiest time of the day. A distabt half-stifled warning, then a tremendous shriek of escaping steam. It was six o'clock. Oh the blessed ,relief from the noise of the machinery. • Our tongues wagged incessantly. We said nothing worth listen- to, but it was so pleasant to hear one's self speak without bawling. "Has anybody noticed,' said Kittums (short for Katherine), " that a young man meets Molly every night." Molly who was leisurely buttoning her walking boots, looked up with a startled expression. This was nutg to %Warns. "You the steady girl of the room," she continued severely. "If it was Freda noiv.—" But you see it Isn't Freda," I said cheerfully. "I should be ashamed of such conduct," said Pierre loftily, (How that girl got her name we never knew; we generally called her Psars Soap). "There's Molly keeping company, and Kittums follows them about; I think." But Molly, flushed to the _temples vanished from the room.

"Didn't she open her eves," chuckled Kittums. "She never thought I saw her goings on. Are you going to be another hour faking yourself up, Freddie?" "You leave me alone," I returned, not pausing in the vigorous brushing I was besto wing upon my dress and jacket, but looking sourly at Kittums for Molly was my chum. "What are you going to do," said she in alarm edging away from me." Let me live a little longer,Freda,'Pears' Soap owes me sixpence." "You're always throwing that in my face," said Pierre tranquilly. " Yes, and I shall be throwing something else if you dont pay up." "Oh take it and be quiet," and Pierre flung a sixpence across the table. Kittums pocketed it 'With alacrity. "After this, the deluge as Scripture I says," she remarked -as we filed down the stairs. FRFCDA. GREY. • THE EAST LEEDS ELECTION.

div.head: GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY.
div.p: GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY.

The polling for the election of a member of Parliament to succeed Mr. Gene (Liberal) took place at East Leeds on Tuesday, the candidates being Mr. Leuty (Liberal), and Mr. Power (Conservative). The Irish party mus- tered strongly for Mr. Leuty, the Liberal candidate, while the Anti-Vetoists gave their support to Mr. Danvers Powers. The most sanguine of Mr. Powers' workers, however, did not hope for victory, but they expected to see the Liberal majority of 800 considerably reduced. The result was declared as follows :
Mr. F. R. Leuty (L) 3,999 Mr. J.,Danvers Powers (C) g.868 -- Liberal Majority

The result of the poll was wa great surprise to the Con- servatives,but among the Liberals it created the greatest enthusiasm. A Ikrge crowd assembled outside the Town Hall,and cheered lustily when the figures were exhibited. Mr. Leuty moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor for acting as returning officer, and Mr. Power seconded. Mr. Lemy subsequently spoke... _
