div.head: 13/PERIAL PARLIAMENT
div.p: 13/PERIAL PARLIAMENT
MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday, Mr. CAMPBELL- BANNERiIAN,repIying to a question put by Mr. A. MORTON, said he had no doubt that when a vacancy occured in the office of Commander-in-Chief of the Army the Gov- ernment of the day would take into consideration the recommendations of the Harrington Commission. Answering a question about the British occupation of Corinto, Sir E. GREY said the foreign population and the natives remained on friendly terms, but the officials bad removed from the town. Sir W. HARCOURT moved his resolution giving _during the remainder of the session priority to Government business on Tuesdays and at morning sittings to be held on Fridays. Mr. BETON- limaa moved an amendment declining to give any addi- tional facilities for the discussion of Government business. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN spoke i &opposition to the Government motion. Ile said that he and his friends declined to help the Government to further waste time in dealing with bills which were not wanted and which would not pass. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL supported the motion. Mr. LABOUCHERE, replying to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. said the Government were going to use the time to pass the Welsh Disestablishment Bill, of which be always thought Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was in favoux. Mr. BALFOUR said he regarded the whole of the proceedings of the present session as an elaborate practical joke. They were not there for work, and it was abstird to give the Govern- ment the time they asked for. On a division Sir W. HARCOURT'S motion was carried by 252 to 230. On a vote for contract work for shipbuilding and re- pairs Mr. FORWOOD moved a reduction to the extent of the cost of the Bellville boilers for new cruisers. The Admiralty were, he said, taking a leap in the dark. A long discussion of a technical character followed, at the close of which Mr. ROBERTSON defended the conduct of the Admiralty in acting upon the advice of the experts. The amendment was withdrawn and the vote agreed to, and the House resumed. . .

The second reading of the Government's Fisheries Acts Amendment Bill was opposed by Mr. Ma,clure, and the second reading Of Mr. Johnston's Sale of Intoxicating Liquors to Children Bill by Mr. Bromley-Daienport,and, it being, past midnight, the motions had subsequently to stand over.

div.head: TUESDAY.-ONE MAN ONE VOTE.
div.p: TUESDAY.-ONE MAN ONE VOTE.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening Mr. SRAW-LEFEVRE asked leave to introduce a bill to prohibit plural voting at Parliamentary elections and to provide for taking the polls at a Parliamentary election on one day. He said the Government desired to deal with these two subjects before touching upon registration. As to the day for the elections, the only question: was whether a day in the week should be fixed by the Government of the day or whether they should ask Par- liament to settle it, and they had decided that Parlia- ment should determine the day, and that it should be Saturday. The Government proposed to prohibit persons who had more than one qualification for different con- stituencies from voting more than onae at a general election or within the year until the next registration. What the bill proposed to do was to apply to Parliamen- tary elections the same principle which had been laid down in the case of local elections. Sir J. GORST said he thought the day of election of the bill—Saturday—might well be deferred till the Committee stage. H the prin- ciple of this bill was to be adopted there must be equal electoral areas. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said if they were going to do away with plural voting it seemed almost surplusage to have a one day election, and, indeed, such a proposal was open to very grave objections. The bill was a mere attempt to doctor the electorate in favour of the Government; it was a party bill and nothing else, and the Opposition could not let it pass without the most exhaustive examination. Sir G. TREVELYAN spoke of support of the bill,and Mr. GosowEN against it. After a protracted discussion leave was given to bring in the bill, and it was read the first time. The second reading was provisionally fixed for Wednesday. Mr. BRYCE moved the second reading of the Concilia- tion (Trade Disputes) Bill, but the debate had to be ad- journed at midnight. WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday Mr. T. H. Horace; moved the second reading of the Corrupt and Illegal Practices Prevention Act (1883) Amendment Bill. He explained that the chief purpose of the measure was to make the uttering of false statements affecting the personal character and conduct of candidates at Parlia- mentary elections an illegal practice punishable by a finO net exceeding £lOO, to be recovered by summary pro- ceeding, and incapacity to be registered as an elector in the constituency where the statement was made for five years. If the offence was committed by a candidate or his agent the seat would be vacated,but if by any other person the seat would not be vacated unless it could be shown that the election of the sitting member was pro- cured or materially assisted by the circulation of the slanderous statement. Sir F. MINER, who seconded the motion, said no candidate or agent ought to go fishing about in the dustbins of scandal to find , out something about his opponent. Dr. FARQUHARSON thought the Bill ought to extend to newspapers, because under the editorial " we " many statements were made by the Tory press about members opposed to their views which if made in a room would lead to uncomfortable physical consequences. Mr;Houtrousz thought one of the greatest dangers of the present system was the practice of flooding a constituency with irresponsible outsiders, who went from village to village making speeches here and there at election times. Mr. W. ALLAN said he would substitute three months' hard lab our for the fine of £lOO, and would take out the clause which acquitted a slanderer if he could prove he believed the slander he uttered. The ATTORNEY GENERAL said he was strongly in favour of the principle of the Bill. He sin- cerely hoped that newspapers would be included among the persons who could make false statements. The newspapers of this country were very honourably con- ducted in the main, but there were exceptions, and on both sides dirty and cowardly work had been done in the way of making aspersions en gentlemen of whom the newspapers knew nothing except that they differed from them in politics. The Bill was read a second time and afterwards referred to the Standing Committees on Law. _ _
Mr. Macnowa moOed the second reading of the Parlia- mentary Franchise (Women) Bill but the measure was talked out by Mr. Labnuchere.

div.head: WRECK OF THE ELBE.
div.p: THE WRECK OF THE ELBE.

At the Town Hall. Lowestoft, the inquiry into the circumstances attending the Elbe disaster was yesumed on Wednesdr.y and concluded. The jury fotind that there was gross negligence on the part of the mate and look-out man of the Crathie, the vessel which collided with the Elbe; but, owing to the absence of evidence from the Elbe, they were of opinion there was not suffi- cient proof that the Crathie was solely to blame for the collision. No blame was attached to the captain of the Crathie.

div.head: OSCAR WILDE CASE.
div.p: THE OSCAR WILDE CASE.
AN ABORTIVE TRIAL.

The trial of Oscar Wilde and Alfred Taylor was re- Burned at the Old Bailey on Wednesday. The jury,after nearly four hours' consultation, announced that they could not agree upon the principal issues. By the judge's direction tlpw returned a verdict of not guilty on the conspiraoy af.counts, and also upon those in re- ference to the witneqses Atkins and Mayor, and they were discharged from giving a verdict on the other -counts. It was stated that the case would have to be tried again. Application for bail on behalf of both of the prisoners was made and refused.

COMPLAINTS FROM WESTON. Mr. James Collier, clerk to the Weston Parish Council', wrote stating that at a meeting of the above council a presentment was ordeeed to be forwarded, namPlY, that the time had arrived for immediate steps to be taken by ' them for making a contract or otherwise for the empty- ing of all ashpits and closets in the Weston and Weaver ward, and that the attentibn of the District Council be called to the deplorable state of the roads at Weston • Paint, viz., South-road and Post Office-road. The Council were asked to take the necessary steps to give. effect to this.—Mr. Aaron asked if the Inspector had not power to summon the owners if they neglected to empty the ashpits within reasonable time.—The Inspector replied in the affirmative.—Mr. Aaron continuing, said the matter had been neglected, and he would move that the Inspecter give notice to the owners to attend to the matter, and '' , hey did not do so. they should he sum- moned before • a magistrate.—Mr. Chadwick seconded the motion.—Dr. Adams said it was a chronic condition with regard to these premises. He had repeatedly visited them and found them in a disgraceful condition. Some steps should be taken at once.—Mr. Barter said he thought it would be somewhat degrading if as a District Council they went emptying ashpits for Parish Councils. (Laughter.)—The motion was carried.—Mr. Heywood moved that they reply to the communication that having two more sanitary inspectors they hoped their nuisance inspector would be able to give better at-, tion to the MA ttor.—Mr. Aaron seconded.—The Inspector said he objected to the statement that there had been neglect. The medical efficer referred to one placeeviz. r Pritchard's-sow, but the communication referred to the whole of the township. Some of the privies in Weston Point had been cleansed through his interference. There was a difficulty with the owners as to where to place the material.—Mr. Heywood said he had no intention of charging their Inspec•or.—This motion was carried.— With reference to the roads the Clerk said they were private ones.—Me. Aaron moved that a small commit- tee go over the roads, consisting of Messrs. Derbyshire. Wright, Stokes, Chadwick and Aaron,with the surveyor (Mr. Diggle) and the Clerk —Mr. Chadwick seconded.— Mr. Stokes said the roads in question had not been adopted by the Council. Re wished to know whether they had now any 'increased power.—The Clerk : No- -Mr. Prandrerh : lilt ig a nuisance we have power.— Mr. Stokes said they had been unable to prove in the past that the bad condition of the roads was a nuisance. —The Clerk said the committee would be able to view the made was a Meisel:cp.—The Clerk said the commit- tee would be able to view the roads and call upon the owners to nut them in repair if they found it necessary. If the work was not carried nut the Authority could take the roads over.—After some discuseion the motions was carried.

div.head: EXNIYIINEII,
div.p: THE EXNIYIINEII,
SATURDAY, MAY 4TI, 1895.
THERE have been two or three The Political interesting and important Arena.

incidents in the political• world during the present week. On Tuesday, for in- stance, there was an election in East Leeds which was of more than ordinary significance. The vacancy was caused by the death of Mr. GANE, well-known and active Liberal, who was returned to Parliament in 1892 by a majority of 827. The Unionists seemed to think that there was an ex- cellent opportunity for proving conclusively that the " flowing tide "is in their favour, and con- sequently they brought forward a candidate to oppose the return of Mr. LEIITY, a local gentle- man who had been nominated by the Liberals. But what is the result ? The" flowing tide" has been so little in their favour that their candidate has been beaten by a majority of 1,131, the largest majority ever polled in East Leeds. The majority was,indeed, so large that it surprised not only the Tories who were decisively defeated but even the Liberal themselves who seem to have been almost prepared for a reduction upon the figures of the previous election. There has in con- sequence been a good deal of speculation as to the unexpected proportions which it assumed. Upon this subject there is, of course, a great variety of opinions, but one thing comes out clearly above all else, and that is, that the election was a most significant victory for temperance reform. The Local Veto Bill seems to have been the main rally- ing cry of one side, and the principal object of the attack of the other. The Tories evidently thought that in this large working-class constituency the principles embodied in the Local Veto Bill would be unpopular, and they have acted upon the as- sumption. They have now discovered that they made a serious mistake. Temperance reform is, in spite of all that has been said, not the weakest plank in the Government platform ; it is, in fact, one of the strongest. There is a grow- ing feeling thii,t the provisions of tho Veto Bill are essentially just and calculated to further the welfare of the country ; and the East Leeds election is an unMistakeab:e and effective reproof of those who are disposed to place the money in- terests of a few monopolist brewers before the good of the community as a whole. Another important political incident was the introduction into the House of Commons on Tues- day of what is known as the "One man one vote" Bill. This Bill is intended to abolish plural vot- ing and to provide for the taking of all elections on one day, two reforms which have long been urgently needed. In explainirt the Bill, Mr. SuAw-Larzyna gave some remarkable evidence of the extent to which plural voting is carried on and used to swamp the local majorities of particular constituencies. As he said the system now pre- vailing is a " monstrous blot on our electoral sys- tem." He had,. he said, Known a man who had twenty votes in different parts of the country, and who had at a general election given them all. In other words under the present so-called "free and equal system" one man may have twenty or thirty times the voting power of some other man. There are, it appears, persons who are entitled to vote in all the twenty-three parliamentary dis- tricts in Lancashire, and this privilege of plurality of voting is, it seems,particularly taken advantage of by members of some firms of brewers whose "tied houses" will no doubt give them the neces- sary qualifications. In London ens agent admitted that he had been instrumental in putting on the registers four members of one firm in twenty different districts no that they had no fewer than eighty votes amongst them. Con- trast such a result as this with the fact that hundreds and thousands of persons in every way suitable to use the franchise are prevented from voting at all by absurd restrictions such as the residential qualification ! In the city of London alone there are 19,000 non- resident occupation voters and 9,000 non-resident verymen, and in some of the other Parliamentary

divisions of the metropolis the faggot voters are to be numbered by thousands, thus completely over-riding the resident majorities in those dis- tricts. In view of such glaring anomalies as these it is difficult to understand by what arguments the "One man one vote" Bill is to be opposed. Yet it is already evident that the Bill is to be opposed, bitterly and exhaustively. The Tory party is, in fact, too much dependent in sll parts of the coun- try upon faggot voters for its majorities to allow this Bill to pass without opposition. The opposi- tion will, however, not take the form of an honest and downright defence of plural voting. 111 kinds of side issues will be fastened upon to retard the pro3ress of the measure. The Government will be accused of bringing in a Bill for electioneering purposes and of not dealing at one time and in one session with the whole field of electoral reform. But:the country will have,no difficulty be detecting the worthlessness of these flimsy subterfuges. There can be no electioneering dodgery in deal- ing with a reform which the Liberal Party pledged itself to deal with prior to the last election; that is simply fulfilling a promise honestly made. And as for not dealing with the whole complex question of electoral reform at one time and in one Bill, the attempt would have been hopeless. "dne thing at a time" is a good motto for those who have control of the Parliamentary machine at the pre- sent time.

JuDania by the meeting at Thc Newton Division. Penketh on Monday, Mr. MeoN, the probable Liberal candidate for the Newton Division, is making an excellent impression This impression will be deepened when comparisons are made between his utterances and those of the present member,Mr. T. W. LEGIT, who has also been in the constituency within the last few days. There is certainly this to be said for Mr. LEGH—ho is -a Tory of the Tories and he makes no pretence to be anything else. He is for "standing still." But as Mr. Amcnx,chairrnan of Mr. Moores meeting, very aptly pointed out there can be no standing still in politics. There must be either progression or retrogression. This being the case Mr. LEGH is clearly for retrogression. His speeches are one prolonged negative. Evidently as far as Mr. LEGH is con- cerned this is the best of all possible worlds, and he does not seem to be able to realise the fact that other less fortunately placed individuals—who are after all the great majority—may not be able to see things in the same light. He does not regard his position in Parliament as an opportunity for redressing wrongs or for making life easier for the masses of the people. All his efforts are devoted towards spragging the wheels of progress, and as a consequence his•speeches from beginning to end consist of criticism and disparagement of the pro- posals of others. It is true, of course, that Mr. LEGH is not formidable as a critic, but that is not his fault; he does his best. In all respects Mr. MOON offers a pleasing contrast. His speeches are of the positive and not of the negative order as he gives a hearty support to practically all the reforms which are now identified with the Liberal party. Mr. LEGH professes to think lightly of the prospects, of his opponent, but the re are solid grounds for the belief expressed by Mr. Moon- that with a united and enthusiastic Liberal party, Newton division can be won for the cause of pro- gress. For the artisan, the miner, and the agri- cultural labourer, and indeed for all men who believe that steady progress is the best and safest form of conservatism there can be no attraction in Mr. Limn's sterile political creed.
ENGLAND is in a pre-eminent An Atnerican

View of degree the country of sports and English sport. athletics, and an American writer, Mr. WHITNEY, in a book on " English Sport through American Spectacles," has abun- dantly acknowledged the fact. He has been struck by the unversality of the sporting interests in England—from the duke with his magnificent kennels and stables to the man who " will sing a linnet against a linnet, one in the mouth, an home-and-home race, for a side" in a West- minster slum. And at the samo time he has some useful and interesting comparisons to make be- tween English and American athletes and their , methods. Rugby footballers will perhaps be sur- prised to learn that Americans are credited with a vast •deal more " science " inithis game than the English players. We are told that in this parti- cular department of athletics the Americans have nothing to learn but much to teach. Mr. WHIT - NEY, in fact, declares that in watching some ot the best Rugby clubs he was witnessing an elementary , game. He could trace the rudiments of the game as it is played in the States, but there it has, he claims, been scientifically developed into something superior. Perhaps, this may be partly due to the fact that the youthful American apparently looks . upon football as a much more serious business than does his English cousin. Football is cer- tainly a sufficiently absorbing subject with many, people even here, but the sight familiar to the American of members of a defeated team throwing themselves prostrate on the field, and even going so far as to shed tears in the agony of bitter dis- appointment would, as Mr. WHITNEY truly says, " make Englishmen stare in wonderment." Our vanquished player, however hard they may struggle before the whistle blows,are rarely-so coin- pletely prostrated by an adverse result as seems to be the fashion on the other side of the Atlantic, and they generally retain a vigorous appetite for the subsequent repast. As to cycle racing this American writer has not much that is good to say either for his own country or this. The status of the amateur rider is low in America but it is, he declares, even loWer in England—if that be possible. " Tho manufac- turer's hireling has professionalised the sport from end to end of Great Britain and driven bona fide ameteurs out of active competition; " and he adds to this heavy indictment by declaring that , "bookmakers at games are all too common, andl sharp practices that go even so far as roping, selling races, and running men to order are preva- lent at nearly all the meetings. Outside of the Universities an!' a very few clubs—so few as to be counted on the fingers of one hand—one may say there is no honesty, from an amateur point of view, in athletics in all England." This is, surely, a sweeping condemnation, and we are strongly of opinion that it is a good deal too sweeping. .Mr. WHITNEY has delivered his Verdict upon too little evidence as visitors generally do. A more exter, sive knowledge of English sport would most assuredly have given him a higher opinion of the vast bulk of its votaries. It should be said, how- ever, that he exempts cricket from the scope of his remarks as that game, he considers, is " free from scandal and corruption."

div.p: A SUCCESSFUL MUSIC STUDENT. Miss Soulby, of Grove House, Runcorn, pupil of Miss Clegg, has successfully passed the examination for Seniors, in connection with the Royal Academy, for pianoforte playing. THE SCHOOLS QUESTION AT RUNCORN. On Thursday afternoon an interview between the managers of the Wesleyan Day Schools, Runcorn, and the members of the Runcorn School Board took place Tito business had regard to the purchase by the Board of the Granville-st. Schools, the Education Department having given their consent to the transfer subject to certain alterations being made. A final settlement was not arrived at, but it is expected that negotiations will be successfully completed within the next few days,and thus enable the Board to conduct the schools after the forthcoming examination. RUNCORN BOATING CLUB. On Wednesday evening the first annual dinner in connection with the Runcorn Boating Club was held at Wilson's Hotel, and was fairly well attended. Mr. and Mrs. Dutton prepared an excellent repast, and the room was tastefully decorated. The chair was occupied by Mr. G trle. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts having been offered, Mr. J. A. Smith, jun., submitted the toast of the president and vice-president in eulogistic terms.—Mr. Millington submitted'' Success to ihe Runcorn Boating Club." Mr. A. Abel responded,and then submitted " The town and trade of Runcorn." Other toasts were pro- posed sad duly honoured. The proceedings were en_ livened by songs given at intervals. CONGREGATIONAL "AT HOME" AT RUNCORN. The eighth congregational " At Home " in connection with Bethesda Congregational Church, was held in the Lecture Hall on Wednesday evening. There was a good attndance. The room had been tastefully decorated or the occasion by the f 'Bowing ladies : Miss Lydiate, Miss I Heatherington, Mrs. Royle, Mr. G. Hayes and Mr. B. Outhwaite. Some of the decorations had been kindly Tent by Mr. Steele. The pastor (Rev. J. Simpson) gave a few words of welcome, after which a programme of vocal and instrumental music was proceeded with. Solos were given by Miss Ainsworth, Miss Heatherington,Miss E. Worrall, Mr. Worrall, and Mr. George Lacey. Instru- mental selections were contributed by Mr. B. Cartwright, Mr. C. C. Le Couteur and Mr. Mark. Miss Rogers recited. A dialogue was also given in which the follow- ing took part :—Miss Heatherington, Miss Ainsworth, the Misses Stone, Mr. E. R. Roberts, Mr. Johnson and Masters . Ainsworth and Outhwaithe. The duties of accompanist were satisfactorily fulfilled by Mr. C. C. Le Couteur. During the evening, refreshments were handed round, and this department was in charge of Miss Lydiate, Mrs. Boyle and Mrs. Powell, who were assisted by several young ladies. FEARED Loss OF A RUNCORN BOUND STEAMER AND ALL ' HANDS.—It is feared that the Liverpool steamer Marie has been lost with all hands. The Marie, which is owned I by the Marie Steamship Company, of London, Messrs. W. Esplln and Co. being the managing owners, is an iron three-Masted steamer ot 520 gross tonage, and was built at Danzig, in 1863. She left St. Valory on the 21st Apr:l for Runcorn, with a cargo of flints, and since then a boat has been picked up with the name Marie on it. Six bodies have also been picked up, and the greatest I fears are entertained that the Marie has foundered with all hands. The following is a list of the crew as far as can be ascertained when the vessel left St. Valery :—M. Cowper, master, Liverpool ; S. Walker, chief officer, Magee Island, Ireland ; James West, chief engineer, Bootle ; John Riley, second engineer, Garston ; Thomas Wilson, Liverpool ; Edward Price, Garston ; and Joseph Davies, Widnes, sailors ; and William Williams, Liver- pool, and Frank Keefe, Liverpool, firemen. It is known that several others were on board, but their names have not been aseertained. FIRE BRIGADE PRACTICE. • • • •

On Thursday evening the Runcorn Fire Brigade and also the brigade of the Bridgewater Undertaking at Run- corn turned out for practice. The fire buzzers were blown and there was a general question as to where the conflagration was. It was found that it consisted merely of a few blocks of timber which had been pur- posely set on fire at the docks for a test practice. The dock brigade directed their attention to this, whilst the Runcorn brigade played upon the Co-operative build- ings in Church-st.

Acting on instructions from Mr.'Brunner,M.P., a copy of the proposed trust deed of the above-mentioned build- ing has been forwarded by Mr. William Handley to the various trades societies, friendly societies and other or- ganisations of a public character in the town. The communication accompanying the deed states it is Mr. Brunner's earnest hope that as full use as possible may be made of the premises, and the deed is forwarded to the organisations mentioned with a view to the receiving of any suggestions in furtherance of the object for which the premises are intended.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

There is nothing for Runcornians to be enthusias- tic about in the report of the Urban Council's deputation to Dir. Brock, the chairman of the United:Alkali Company. There is scarcely a bright line from beginning to end, and prospects of increased activity at the Runcorn works are dashed to the ground until brisker times in the chemical market. The Alkali Cmapatiy, according to Mr. Brock's version, have been the saviours of trade in Runcorn. He told the deputation that "If the Syndicate had not been formed the loss of trade at Runcorn would have been greater than it is at present." Such a statement must surely be conjectural. Runcorn people, after the bitter experience of the past winter, are of the firm opinion that the chemical trade at Runcorn could not have been much worse, and that such a state of things was never experienced when the works were under private ownership. With regard to the future, Mr. Brock said the Runcorn Soap and Alkali and the Weston works are to go on much as at present, which means that these two works now almost at a standstill, are to remain so.

At Camden works, it was contended that more work was now carried on than when the works were taken over by the company. This may be true,but it must then have been at a very low ebb, for the number of men now employed at these works can- not be called large, and does not in any w,ay com- pensate for the marked diminution in the number of hands engaged at the other works in the town belonging to the company. As regards the Old Quay works—which by the way, the Manchester Ship Canal Co. have cause to remember—the com- mencement of a new industry is promised either at or near to the works. The present industry carried on there, it would appear is to be stopped until a revival of trade, and as some compensation for this loss a new industry is promised. It was not stated what the new industry is to be, and there is some doubt as to whether it will prove as bene- ficial to the town as the old one.

The memorial of the Council which has already been printed, is to be brought before the direc- tors of the United Alkali Company at their meet- ing in May, but from the tenor of Mr. Brock's remarks it may be presumed that he has expressed their intentions as far as Runcorn is concerned. Any further extension of labour in the town on their part, it would seem, depends upon increased activity in the chemical trade itself. At any rate we shall know what the Company's intentions are within a fortnight, and it will then be time to discuss what steps must be taken in the town. Reports regarding the chemical industry are now much more hopeful than has been the case for months past, but whether the revival of trade, if there be a revival, will result in busier times for Runcorn remains to be seen.

The Non-conformist ministers of Runcorn have signed a petition in favour of the Local Veto Bill, and this will be submitted to the House of Com- mons by the member for the division, Mr. J. T. Brunner, MP. The memorialists state that they believe in the placing of the control of the liquor traffic in the hands of the people. They consider it just and equitable, and it is demanded in the in- terests of religion and good government. It vc ill tend, they think, to increase sobriety in the habits of the people by placing the resonsibility of their well-being in their own hands. It is well to have an expression of opinion on the subject from the pastors of various churches in the town, especially as it is not often they speak on topics which have any political colour. The Government will require all the support they can obtain for the passing of the measure in view of the fact that the majority on the second reading of the bill has been anticipated to be no more than two.

The agreement between the Manchester Ship Canal Company and the Runcorn Urban Council has at last been adopted and received the seal of the Council. Many will now look forward to an ire- mediate commencement of operations, inasmuch as the agreement stipulates that the work is to be carried out within a few months This should find employment for many who have been unable to obtain it in the town. That the accommodation to be provided for the berthage of vessels on the Ship Canal at Runcorn will prove beneficial to the town is beyond doubt, and it is to be ardently hoped that the sentiments expressed at the Council meeting yesterday, as to its being the beginning of brighter and more pros- perous times for Runcorn, may prove to be true.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURI)AY, MAY 4 1895 RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL. 1 RUNCORN COUNCIL AND THE ALKALI COMPANY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURI)AY, MAY 4 1895 RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL. 1 RUNCORN COUNCIL AND THE ALKALI COMPANY,

At the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Thurday morning, the monthly meeting of the Council was held. Mr. E. unison, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present—Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Tayler, J.P., C.C., J. Pritchard, F. Wiswall, H. J. Grice, W. Collier, G. H. Kirkham, J. W. Lightburn, G. Hewitt, T. Dean, D. Bisbrown, M. Sweetman, Mr. F. A. Lak3 (law clerk), Mr. E. Marshall (secretdry), and Mr. M. Barker (sur- veyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. McDougall, in his report, stated that the number of deaths registered during, the past month amounted to 16. One was an inquest case, and of the remaining 15 deaths, 4 were due to bronchitis, 2 to pneumonia, 2 to convulsions, and 1 each to congenital disease, diarrhcea, inflammation of lining membrane of brain, phthisis, diphtheria, puerpural convulsions, and apoplexy. The 16 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 10.00, and exclusive of the inquest case of 9.04 of the estimated population. Yneteen deaths were registered in the corresponding month of last year. The births registered numbered 66 during the month.—Dr. Gastaldi asked what was the estimated population.—Mr. McDougall ; 19,00 D at the present time.— Die report was considered highly satisfactory.
REPORT OF THE DEPUTATION TO MR. BROCK.

The adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Urban Coun- cil was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Monday evening. Mr. E. Imison, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present .—Rey. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., J. Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, G.H. Kirkham, D. Bisbrown, M. Sweetman, W. Collier, H. J. Grice, J. Wilson, F. Wiswall, T. Dean, R. H. Posnett,G. Hewitt, Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), Mr. E. Marshall (secretary), and Mr. M. Barker (surveyor). Mr. Speakman said the deputation which was ap- pointed by the Council re the rumoured closing of the chemical works, in accordance with instructions, waited upon Mr.Brock,chairman of the directors of the United Alkali Company. He could say that they were very well received, but as they could not get a reply to the memorial of the Council until after May 17th, whatever discussion might take place with regard to a suhject of such vast importance it was to the interests of the town that whatever was done should be done in committee. They were all keenly interested in the subject, and he was sure the Council would not like to do or say anything in one way or another until they had re- ceived a reply to the memcrial. The report which the committee had drawn up would be communicated to the papers if the Council so desired. He thought it would be desirable to that the public might know where they were; I but any discussion arising, so long as they had not got a formal reply, would be unwise. He, thereforeonoved that the Council go into committee.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the proposition. He knew that their memorial touched upon very tender ground, and they wished to make some little effort to convey to Mr. Brock the idea that in no way they wished t. 4 dictate to them,or charge them with anything which was inequitable, but that unfortunate word crept in. He could assure them it was not the way to approach people to obtain concessions by saying anything that would lead to an element which would destroy the good feeling which ought to exist in those negotiations. He thought the public should know the result of the deputation's visit without any statement made in the discussion.—The proposition was carried unanimously,and the Council then went into committee. —After a long discussion, the following report was unanimously adopted in open council on the motion of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Lightburn, and supported by Dr. Gastaldi : " A deputation from the Runcorn District Council, eon- sisting of Messrs. P. Speakman, J. Pritchard and J. W. Lightburn, preseeted a memorial from the above Coun- cil to the directors of the United Alkali Company through the Chairman, J. Brock, Esq., at the Company's Office, Liverpool, on Wednesday afternoon, the 26th inst.—Mr. Brock after perusing the memorial said he would have pleasure in presenting it to the directors of the Company who met on the 17th of the next month. He said the first object of the directors was to promote the interests of the shareholders .without regard to locality, and impressed on the deputation that Runcorn did not suffer in the least degree by not being repre- sented on the Board of Directors and that if the chemi- cal syndicate had not been formed, the loss of trade at Runcorn would have been greater than it is at present. After reviewing the condition of the chemical trade generally he referred to the local works, stating, as his opinion that in the immediate future, and if trade did not improve, the Runcorn Soap and Alkali and the Wes- ton works would go on much as at present; that the Camden (Elazlehurst's) works were doing more now than when purchased by the Company and that a greater development there was confidently expected. He stated that it was contemplated to start a new industry at the Old Quay, and a survey was now being made to deter- mine whether the old works should be so utilised or whether they should build entirely new ones en the ad- jacent land belonging to the United Alkali Company, Mr. Brock further stated that in no case would the works be dismantled but the machinery and plant generally would be kept in good condition to be ready to meet immediately any demand arising from increased trade, adding that the trade outlook was now brighter but prices were still low. The deputation stated that the Council did not pretend to offer suggestions as to the conducting of the Company's trade ; that it struggled through the terrible distress of the winter as best it could; that it had been requisitioned to convene a public meeting on the subject; so that the Council could not be charged with acting precipitately or without cause. The deputation further urged that the object of the memorial and deputation was to earnestly plead for an extension of labour at Runcorn and to respectfully re- quest the directors of the Company to forward their decision as early as possible as failing increased trade at the works some effort must at once be made to find additional employment and so relieve distressed work- men and almost bankrupt shopkeepers. After cordially thanking Mr. Brock for his great courtesy, the deputa- tion withdrew." RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, the fort- nightly weekly meeting of this Board was held under the presidency of Mr. J. Knowles. In addition to the members of the Rural Council being present, there were Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mesrrs. S. Taylor. J.P., C.C.. T. Handley, J.P., A. R. Norman, S. Yarwood and Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and Mr. Cunnah (Workhouse master).

COST OF MAINTENANCE °PPM:PER LUNATICS. Mr. Alex Elornby, clerk to the County Asylum, Ches- ter, wrote intimating that the rate of maintenance of pauper lunatics in the asylum for the quarter ending 30th June next, was fixed at 61. sd. per head.

div.head: HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

The Committee recommended that the application of Mr. J. Sefton to have the time for the completion of the contract for the making of private streets in Duke's Field extended by three month a on account of the severe wiLter be granted ; that the sum of two guineas be paid to Mr. W. Littler, tor expenses incurred by him in con- sequence of the blocking of the main street in Bentinck- st. ; that the tender of Messrs. J. Brundrit and Co. ,Run- corn, for the supply of 2,000 tons of broken stone, be accepted ; that the tender of Mr. J. Horsefield,Runcorn, for the supply of 50 tons of limestone chippings, be ac- cepted • that the tender of Mr. William Moore, Runcorn, for the 'Private Street Works to be done in Speakman. ii., Handley-st.,Grove-st Hope-st., Unnamed-st., off Hope-st., Clarence-st., Greek-st., Penketh-lane, and Spring-st. be accepted ; that the plan of Mr. Thomas Handleyd.P.,for the erectionof a house and outbuildings in Weston-road, be approved, subject to the house being put back to a fine shown by the Surveyor on the plan. Mr. Wiswall moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. D. Bisbrovrn in seconding the proposition said that with reference to the £2 2. to be paid to Mr. Littler, some of the members might not know that it was on account of the blocking of the main sewer which caused Mr. Littler some considerable amount of trouble and expense. As it was no fault of his own the Committee felt that he should receive some recompense. With reference to the pronosed street making, it would entail an expenditure of £1,900 and would find work for a number of men.— Mr. Dean took exception to the extension of time pro- posed to be given to the contractor for the making of private streets in Duke's Field. The work had already been go,ng on for seven months, and he thought that was an unreasonable time and a positive nuisance to the residents. If they extended the time it would have taken almost twelve months for work which should have been done in four.—Mr. Taylor explained that the cause of the delay was owing to the severe winter, and the great difficulty the contractor had experienced in getting the material for the streets.—The Law Clerk said that unless the Council extended the time tile contrac- tor wAs under a penalty.—The minutes were ultimately carried, Mr. Dean voting against.

div.head: WEAVER TRUST DEPUTATION.
div.p: THE WEAVER TRUST DEPUTATION.

Dr. Gastaldi moved the adoption of the miautes of the Parliamentory and General Purposes Committee. The Committee reported that the following statement had been submittod by the Chairman of the committee on behalf of Mr. Pritchard and himself with regard to their efforts to obtain the :representation of Runcorn on the new River Weaver Trust.—The sub-committee had met Mr. Brunner as to the representation of this Council of the River Weaver Trust. Mr. Brunner was gnite agree- able so far as he was concerned that Runcorn should be represented. It was agreed that a deputation shonld attend in London to see what could be done. The Chair- man with Mr. Pritchard saw the persons interested in London on Monday the Bth instant. They promised that if Winslow] was only given one representative instead of two, as was proposed,they would mention that Runcorn wanted a representative on the Trust. It had been agreed that the Cheshire County Council should have 12 representatives. The Trust would be constituted as follows: 12 representatives of the Cheshire County Coun- cil, 10 trustees, 14 traders, 1 for Winsford, 1 for North- wich. Manchester, Liverpool, Birkenhead, Stockport, and North Staffordshire had been represented by Counsel at great cost and had been all strack out. No other town except Winsford and Northwich would be repre- sented except through the 12 County Councillors who would represent the County as a whole." The committee also recommended that the expenses of the deputation amounting to £8 17s. be paid.—Mr. Lightburn', se- conded the adoption of th minutes.—Mr.Collier moved an amendment for the rejection of the recommendation as to paying the expenses of the deputation. He said that the deputation was appointed to meet Mr. Brunner at Runcorn with regard to the Weaver Trust, but no ex- pense was ts be incurred. It was irregular and without precedent for a committee to take upon themselves to go to London without the sanction. of the Council.—Mr. Dean seconded the amendment.—Mr. Wiswall said the instructions to the deputation was not to incur any IParliamentary expenses.—Mr. Taylor said there were four appointed to meet Mr. Brunner. On the following Saturday aftern )on they met him, and he told them that if any good was to he done they must be in London by Monday morning. That being the case,they thought they surely might take it upon themselves to appoint two to go to London. If they had succeeded in getting a representative on the Weaver Trust not a word would have been said. He thought it was rather too fine to object.—Mr. Grice said the business was sprung on the committee and he thought they acted very wisely in sending two members to London. If they refuted to pay the deputation their expenses they would place them- selves in a very contemptible position.—Mr. Bisbrown said he could not support the amendment although he was inclined to think they spent too much on deputa- Nene. —Mr. Hewitt fully endoped what had been said by Mr. Taylor. It was the only course open for the deputa- tion to go to London.—Mr. Lightburn said the amend- ment was of a far reaching character. It would mean that the town would suffer if a committee had not time to call a meeting of the Council to sanctionexpenditure. —On the amendment being put to the vote, four voted in support of it, and the rest of the Council against.— The minutes of the committee were then passed.

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMISSION.
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMISSION.

It was recommended by this committee that the tenders of Messrs. John Heywood and Sons, Manchester, for contracts for the furnishing of the Technieal Insti- tute, be accepted, in the place of Messrs. W. Farrell and Sons, withdrawn.—Mr. Wiswall moved the adoption of the minute, and said that as Messrs. Farrell and Sons had withdrawn their contract the committee recon- sidered the matter and unanimously agreed to let the contract as now proposed.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion, and the minute was passed.
THE UPPER MERSEY NAVIGATION COMMITTEE.

Mr. Grice moved "That Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., be ap- pointed to represent this Council on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission for the ensuin,, three year.i, and that the seal of the Council be affixed to the deed of appointment."—The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi seconded the proposition which was .carried.—Mr. Grice suggested that Mr. Taylor should present them with a report occa- sionally.—Mr. Taylor said nothing ot importance had arisen of interest to the town. , When anything did he would acquaint the Council with it.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AGREEMENT.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AGREEMENT.

Mr. Pritchard moved that the agreement between the Council and the Manchester Ship Canal Company be adopted and that the seal of the Council be affixed there- to. He was sure they all regretted the delay that had arisen, but this was owing to one or two matters which required to be arranged. The agreement was in accord- ance with the propositions of the Council. It was very important that this work should be proceeded with as early as possible. He was sure the Runcorn people were looking forward to the contracts being let. The time when timber ships would arrive would be soon upon them and they wished them to be discharged in the neighbourhood.—Mr. Bisbrown seconded the motion.— The work, he said, would be commenced at once, and would find employment for many in making the coal and salt tips, lay-bys,and wharves. A great deal of the success of the negotiations was due to their officials,Mr. Lake and Mr. Marshall, who deserved credit for the way they had handled the matter.—Mr. Lightburn did not think he ever had greater pleasure in supporting any proposition brought before the Council than the present one. He felt they had passed through a crisis which could not be properly appreciated without they contem- plated what would have happened if a different conclu- sion had been arrived at. He believed the undertaking to be the beginning of brighter days in Runcorn. It, his opinion they would have the old Runcorn docks swept ' away and better ones substituted for them.—The motion was carried. THE COMPOSITION OF THE WEAVER TRUST. Mr. Bisbrown said that as the County Council would probably be appointing representatives on the Weaver Trust it was within the range of probability that Run- corn would have one or two gentlemen on the trust to represent the trade interests. He thought they could leave it safely in the hands of their two County Council representatives.—The'Cliairman said the Weaver Trust was merely a Bill, it had not become an Act. They ought not to discuss the matter until it was settled.— Mr. Taylor said it was rather premature to raise the question as the Bill had not passed the Flc•use of Com- mons. When the question came before the Council he had no doubt but that Mr.Speakman and himself would be alive to the interests of Runcorn.—Mr. Pritchard said he believed the interests of Runcorn had suffered as they had not taken the matter in hand before. If Runcorn interests had been looked after a little earlier they would have had a representative an the trust by Act of Parliament. •
NOTICE OF MOTION.

Mr. Hewitt gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that Mr. Taylor give the Council some in- formation respecting the rates charged for lights and buoyage by the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission, as there was a grievance that a higher rate WAS charged for Runcorn than for ships going up to Manchester. This concluded the tusiness.

div.head: RATING OF MACHINERY.
div.p: THE RATING OF MACHINERY.

A printed circular letter from the Central As.ociation of Agriculture was received, asking the Council to pass a petition against the exemption of rating machinery.— Mr. Mclntyre moved that a petition against the bill he passed.—Mr. Baxter stated that land was very heavily rated at the present time, and out of proportion to that on machinery. He seconded the motion.—Mr. Stokes supported, and the motion was carried. .

THE COST OF NORLEY PARISH COI7NCIL EaCTION. Mr. William Dutton' clerk of Norley Parish Council, wrote stating that when the bill from the Rural District Council was brought forward, for the amount of £23 is. 3d., expenses of the recent Parish Council elec- tion at Norley, before payment was ordered to be made, he was requested to write to the District Council asking if some deduction could not be made. He forwarded the. following resolution which was passed " Resolved that in the opinion of the Council the charges are excessive and the Clerk be instructed to get them revised." The Clerk said the hill had been made out according to scale, and had been laid before a committee of the Council.

div.head: STANDING ORDERS.
div.p: THE STANDING ORDERS.

Mr. Heywood moved the ad-oP-t-i-On. of the Standing Orders —Mr. Wright seconded.—A discussion toz,k plAce as to the desirability of having the meeting of the Board of Guardians prior to the meeting of the Rural Council and it was ultimately decided that the Board of Guardians meet at 1230, and the Rural Council at two p.m.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER FOR WESTON.
div.p: THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER FOR WESTON.

On the recommendation of the School Attendance Committee, Mr. W. 13. Brimelow, of Church-street, Run- corn,was appointed school attendance officer for Weston at a salary of £l5 per annum, in accordance with the suggestion of the Weston School Attendance Committee.

div.head: TREAT TO THE CHILDREN OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: THE TREAT TO THE CHILDREN OF THE HOUSE.

It was decided on the recommendation of the House Cemmittee that the thanks of OM Board be conveyed to Mr. W. Shaw, of the Mersey. Mission to Seamen. Run- corn branch, for his kindness in inviting the children of the house to attend the concert at Runcorn given by boys from the training ship "Indefatigable," and also to Mrs. Canon Weed and Mrs. F. R. Norman for providing the children with tea. THE APPOINTMENTS OF NURSE AND ASSISTANT MATRON. Mr. Handley submitted the minutes of the special Rouse Committee who recommended that the question of appointing an assistant matron be left over for six months, and the question of appointing an additional nurse be deferred for a fortnight. These recommenda- tions were approved of. This concluded the business.
P.S.A. AT T II- -E.- Y.M.C.A.

At the usual meeting of the above in the Y.M.C.A. Lecture-room on Sunday, Mr. J. C. Harrington oc- cupied the chair for the first time, and judging from the neat little speech he made at the com- mencement it is not likely to be his last appearance. Mr. Roylance, of Moore, was the speaker, and he gave greet satisfaction by an address both humor_ nus and earnest. Miss Kent sang "The Star of Bethlehem," and Mr. Travis, jun., acted as accom- panist. There was a good attendance.

RABIES AT LOWER WHITLEY. On Saturday morning, Mr. John Bate, jun., a veterinary surgeon, went to Mrs. Joynson's Grim- ditch Mill, Lower Whitley, for the purpose of attending a cow. Wljilst there he saw a mad mongrel doz. Pie at once borrowed a gun and shot the animal. On making a post-mortem examina- tion of its stomach he found there stones, Pieces of wood, and a quantity of frogs' spawn. The animal was suffering from well developed symptoms of rabies. It is not known whether anyone has been bitten by the dog.

div.head: 0801)811AM.
div.p: PAROCHIAL Comm-rm.—The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Friday evening, in the Town Hall, Frodsham. There were present—Messrs. H. E. Heywood (chairman), J. M. Williams, W. E. Shore, W. Youd, T. Earlam, W. Booth, P. Booth, G. Rogers, F. D. Ringrose, John Barrow, J. Corker, T. A. Rigby, J. Illidge, Farrington (inspector), and Ashton (clerk).—The Inspec- tor reported that he had served notices upon certain owners of property as directed at the last meeting, recommending them to lay OR water to their property from the authority's water main' and that he had only received one reply, namely from Mr. Linaker.—After a long discussion it was decided that the several owners have notice from the Inspector requiring them to do as they had been recommended. Tenders were produced from Messrs. F. W. Spencer and James Hough for water connections to cottages the property of the railway com- pany, and after consideration it was resolved that Mr. Spencer's contract be accepted, the work to be done forthwith.—A letter was read from Mr. Rodgers, of the Railway Inn, calling the committee's attention to the great nuisance of waggons of shoddy, which were occas- ionally left at the Frodsham Station in the siding close to his house.—On the motion of air. Youd, seconded by Mr. Barrow, it was decided that the railway company be required to remove all shoddy waggons away from the station for the week-end.—Mr. Rodgers was directed to take notice af any wilful misuse of water, and to warn anyone found doing so that if they persist in continuing the offence proceedings will be instituted.—Mr. Corker referred to the many discussions which had take place with reference to Mr. Rothwell's window, and to what had really been done. He considered that it was high time to have the matter at once settled.— The Chairman having briefly stated the position of affairs at the present time, Mr. Shore,in accordance with his notice of motion, moved that the Clerk write to Mr. Rothwell requesting him to put back the windows to the boundary line, and to inform him that failing to comply, ' with the Act of Parliament within fourteen days legal proceedings would be taken.—Mr. Earlam seconded the motion.—Mr. Rigby asked whether it would not bias the opinion of the justices, the fact that the committee was so evenly divided on the question ?—The Clerk did not think that this would make any difference.—Mr. Wil- liams, said that it would be a great hardship upon Mr. Rothwell and his. tenant if the windows were put back. This was not a , case of landgrabbing. The existing building was an ornament to the street.—Mr. Youd was sorry the matter had brought in animosity and dissen- sion amongst the members of the committee. Prior to this matter business had been settled amicably by the committee.—Mr. Williams strongly objected to the ex- pression of Mr. Youd.—Mr. Ringrose considered that as the committee were placed in the position of administer- ing justice it would be well before commencing legal proceedings to consider well their true position. In his opinion it would be preferable to allow the matter to settle quietly.—The Chairman then put the proposition to the meeting, when six voted in favour thereof and six against. The Chairman, after some reflection, said that the best course would be fur the matter if disputed to be settled bythe magistrates, and gave his casting rote in favour of Mr. Shore's motion.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
MANCHESTER AND THE MEAT. TRADE.
SAILING OF THE FIRST STEAMER FROM AUSTRALIA.

It is now Nearly a year (says the " Mancliestel Guar- dian "1 since it was announced that all arrangements •had been completed for steamers of the Gulf line to in- reigurate direct sailing between Manchester and the Austrdian Colonies. We understand that a vessel was actually advertised to load for Manchester,but owing to the c tttle lairages and the cold-air stores not being ready in time instructions had to be cabled out to the agents to withdraw the steamer, and the sea- son's trade was lost to the Canal. The cold-air stores are now ready, and are only waiting to be utilised ; while the cattle lairages, it is hoped, will be in a sufficiently forward state to accotnmodate a thousaud head of foreign cattle before the end of the present month should nothing unforeseen occur to delay the work. It is therefore gratifying to learn that the first steamer to bring foreign battle and dead meat to Mac- cheater is sainig this week from Sydney, New... South Wales, for this port direct. The vessel in question is the Gulf liner Gulf of Genoa, a large steamer of 3,448 tons register, owned by the Greenuck Steamship Company, Limited, and trading regularly between the I Clyde Mersey, and Australian ports. The principal I portion of the cargo on the present voyage consists of ' dead meat, but the vessel is also bringicg a large num- ber of cattle which will be discharged at Mode Wheel if the lairages are ready ti receive them on their arrival. Otherwise the cattle will be discharged at Birkenhead, and the remainder of the cargo brought up the canal and warehoused in Corporation cold-air stores. I ANOTHER COLLISION ON THE SHIP CANAL.

On Wednesday another somewhat serious collision occurred on the Shin Canal, between Runcorn and' Latchford. The Dutch steamer Angelo, going to Manchester, and the steamer Manchestria, of Liverpool, proceeding seawards, collided with each other with con- siderable force on reaching the coal wharf of Messrs. Evans, at Acton Grange. The result was that they were both damaged, especially the Angeln, which had a portion of her bulwarks stove in; She was, however, able to proceed to her destination. The Manchestria journeyed to Ellesmere Port for examination. MANCEIESFER CORPORA now AND THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY.

The "Manchester Guardian" of yesterday says :—We understand that the representatives of the Manchester Corporation on the Board of the Ship Canal Company have been in consultation with Mr. Fletcher Moulton, QC., M.P., the legal adviser of the Corporation in Par- liamentary matters, as to the way in which the Corpora- tion can best assist the Canal Company in its present difficulties The whole position of affairs was laid before the learned counsel, who after consideration and exam- ination of the Acts of Parliament will report to the Lord Mayor. A fact which may have s(,me bearing on at least one of the recommendations of Mr. Moulton is the possession by the Corporation of a sum of money paid by the Canal Company, almost sufficient to meet a year's interest (£250,000) on the Corporation loan of £5,000,000. The Corporation pay a trifle over 3 per cent to the lenders of the money. Tne Canal Company have in turn paid the City Treasurer 41 per cent on the instal- ments, and now on the completed sum, advanced to hem.
THE- GLASGOW AND MANCHESTER TRADE.- FIRST TRIP OF A NEW STEAMER.

The new steamer Spaniel, belonging to Messrs. G. and J. Burns, Glasgow, made her first trip up the Man- chester Ship Canal on Thursday, under Most favourable auspices. The steamer is 250 feet long, and 33 feet 6 inch. beam. She is fitted with triple-expansion engines, end on a six hours' trial attained an average speed of 14 knots, with a maximum of 15 knots. She was built specially by Messrs. Inglis, of Glasgow, for Messrs. Burns's trade between Glasgow, Liverpool, and Manchester. There is splendid sleeping accom- modation for ninety cabin passengers. There is alas a handsome dining saloon and smokeroom, with electric lights throughout. Messrs. Burns are now taking the Glasgow and Liverpool trade into their own hands, and with the splendid cabin accommodation provided in this new vessel there is no doubt an 'increasing number of passengers will be induced to travel by the sea route during the summer months. We understand that Messrs. Burns intend to establish a daily service between the Mersey and the Clyde by their steamers sailing to and from Manchester and Liverpool: The Spaniel has also capacity for carrying general cargo. The Spaniel left Glasgow at nine o'clock on Wednesday night, and arrived alongside the Liverpool Landing stage about noon yesterday She had on board a large general, cargo for Manchester, including a considerable consign- ment of hay from Ayrshire and a number of Scotch cattle for the Manchester market.
FOOTBALL .-MARRIED V. SINGLE

On Monday night a match between the married and single players of the Runcorn Football Club took place on the Runcorn ground. The teams were :—Married side: Houghton, back; Cawley, Robinson, Faulkner, and Wainwright, three-quarters; Nickson and Gregory, half-backs; Riley, Jones, Farmer. Taylor, Shaw and Urmson, forwards; single: Jolley, back ; Durrbabin, Myers, Warder, and Gayter, three-quarters; George Robinson and Woodward, half-backs; Langley, Walker, Pendlebury, Williams, Lightfoot, and Stubbs, forwards. The match was a most interesting one, but the •single players quite outmatched the Benedict% winning easily by one goal, two tries to nil.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPS. —The last entertainment of the season was given on Wednesday evening, in the schoolroom, Mr. Looker presiding. A capital programme of recitations, dialogues, and vocal and instrumental music was gone through. Votes of thanks were given to the officers for the very efficient manner in which they have performed their labours during the season.. •

WESLEYAN CHURCH —At the con-clusion of the usual week-night service on Tuesday, the presentation of an intaid writing:desk:to Mr. John Baguley,of the Hallwood, took place. For many years Mr. Baguley has been con- nected with the Halton Wesleyan Church as steward, Sunday school teacher, treasurer of clothing club, Itc., but is now leaving Balton for Newport, Salop. The presentation was made by the Rev. S. Herbert 'rite, on behalf of the many friends who wished to show their appreciation of Mr. Baguley's services, and to mark the love and esteem in which he has been held by them.

SUNDAY SCLIOOL ANNIVERSARY.—On Sunday afternoon and evening Mr. George Hunter, of Leigh, preached in the Sion Chapel, Cherry•laue, Lymm, in celebration of the anniversary of the Sunday school. There werelarge congregations, and the remarks of the speaker were listened to with attention. The offertories were liberal, and are for the benefit of the Sunday school.

On Saturday evening Mr. and Mrs. Rutter, Mer- sey-et.' had gone out, of the. house leaving an oil lamp burning low on the mantel-piece. Shortly , after their departure it was observed through the parlour window that the reservoir of the lamp had burst, and that the burning oil bad communicated with the mantel-piece and had ignited it. On Tuesday evening a deputation, representative of both workmen and employers in the glass trade of St. Helens, Warrington, Birmingham, Leeds, Castleford, Seaham Harbour, Sunderland, South Shields, and other districts, waited on Mr. Asquith, and urged that, under its special and peculiar cir- e.umstances, the glass trade elliould be exempted from the provision of the new Factories Bill which would prohibit the employment of boys under six- teen years of age at nightwork. After an interview of nearly two hours' duration, during which many speakers addressed him, the Home Secretary ad, mitted that the deputation bad made out a case for the exemption of their trade from the provision in question so far as concerned boys between fourteen and sixteen years of age, but said that nothing short of the exceptional conditions they had placed before him would have justified differential treat- ment in their favour. div.head: . . ACCIDRNT TO A BRICK MANUFACTURER.
div.p: . . ACCIDRNT TO A BRICK MANUFACTURER.

Mr. Richard Whiteman, brick manufacturer, visited the yard about noon on Saturday, leaving his pony and tray unattended. Whilst Mr. White- man was away the pony wandered about the yard, and eventually got on to a heap of tiles, when the trap was overturned. Mr. Whiteman together with one of the workmen, named John Bennett, ran to . the pony, and both took hold of it by the head. The ' pony became restive, and reared. Bennett loosed his hold, hut Mr. Whiteman stuck to its head and the pony kicked him severely with its fore feet. causing serious dislocations of the collar bone and shoulder blade. Dr. McCarthy, of Warrington. was summoned, and was quickly in attendance. lie at once set on 6 portion of the dislocation, but the other part required the assistance of three medical men to place it in position. Mr. Whiteman is pro- gressing as favourably as can be expected. - - -

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A DISORDERLY *CHARACTER DISPOSED OF.

On Friday morning at the Warrington Police Court, before Alderman Wright (chairman), Councillor Roberts and Mr. S. Wright, Julia Ann Shields,Pilling's-court,was charged with wilfully breaking a number of glasses and jugs, the property of Thomas Mather, on the 20th April. —Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, said that he appeared to prosecute on behalf of Mr. Thomas Mather, of the Old Crow Inn, whose constant endeavour it had been to keep up the respectability of his house. He had decided not to serve such characters as the prisoner, and for 12 months she had not been served in the house. Instead, she kept coming and breaking windows and jugs, and it was only a fortnight since she was sent to gaol for 14 , days for throwing her clog through the window at one ' o'clock in the morning. On the day complained about the taproom was full of customers,and the prisoner came in about 6 p.m and was put out by Mr. Mather. She however, came back at 9 p.m. sober, and they beard a great smash in thetauroom and found that prisoner had taken off her boot and broken ten glasses, three pint jugs, one quart jug, and two spirit glasses, spilling their contents on the floor. Mrs. Smith came down and prisoner said, "If you lock me up before I have finished I will smash every window in the place." She also called the landlady disgusting names. In consequence the police had to watch the house, and Mr. Browne said he was in- structed to press the case as strongly as he could. He mentioned that the prisoner had on some occasions picked up a man's glass of beer and drunk it before his face because they would not serve her, and he wanted this practice put a stop to. He asked for the full penalty as the woman had been there often before.—Mr. Hunt endorsed everything Mr. Browne had said as to the woman being a nuisance to the Old Crow and the police. She and otberswent and got drunk and Mr. Mather had to rely on the police to enable him to keep the law. The police could not always be going, and the prisoner ought to know that the landlord and landlady were liable to be summoned if they did not take action in a case like that. —Alderman Wright said the defendant's conduct was disgraceful and her character worse, and be would send her to gaol for one month with hard labour. • " TIIE ROAD TO Runs." At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day, before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), and Mr. J. H. Fleming, William Jackson 16 Dial-st., was charged with stealing from a yard off Allen-at., on April 29th, newt. sf scrap iron value fis., the property of John Gandy who carried on business as broker in Allen-st. Mr. Hunt stated that the defendant was the son of Thomas Jackson, land-lord of the " Rose " beerhouse. Dial-st. At ten o'clock on Monday morning, complainant saw five or six cwt. of big scraps of iron in his yard ard also six lbs. of smaller scraps. On Tuesday he noticed that the heap was smaller and the bag of small scrap was gone. He gave in- formation to Detective Monaghan who, in the course of his enquiries, visited Taylor's marine store and Mr. Tay- lor, jun., told him they had bought some scrap iron from a boy whom he gave a description of. In consequence Monaghan went to Jackson's, and Taylor identified the defendant as the lad who had sold him the iron tor 2s. 3d. When charged, he replied "I took it from the Arch and sold it to him," (Taylor). Defendant's father said the lad behaved himself well at home, but he did not know what he did outside.—Mr. Hunt said the boy bad been sent to the "Clio" for not going to school, and his father had employed a solicitor and got him nut.— The Chairman said the lad was on the road to ruin, but as it was his first offence a conviction only would be recorded against him, but the next time he came up he would be seat to a reformatory for five years.

div.head: MINOR CASES. ' _ WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT.
div.p: MINOR CASES. ' _ WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT.

MONDAV.—Before the Mayor (chairman), Aldermen Francomb, Harrison, and Wright, Messrs. F. Monks, and J. W. Hayward. STREET RUFFIANISM : BRUTAL AMU:MT.—Willi= Cunningham, labourer, St. James'-street. was charged with assaulting and beating Joseph Gibson in Butter- market-st. on Saturday night.—Joseph Gibson, the complainant, a respectable looking man, stated that on Saturday night he was going down Buttermarket-st. when he was stopped by four men, the prisoner among them. They set upon him and threw him to the ground and kicked him, and defendant butted him in the face several times with his head. the police then'appeared. —George Hampson said he was coming down Butter- market-street with complainant and stopped behind a short distance to speak to someone. His friend (com- plainant) was knocked down and assaulted by the ruffians.—Edward Bradley also said he was comin,, down Buttermarket-at. at the same time and behind the last witnesaes. He saw Gibson as- saulted, and defendant seize him by the collar and butt complainant in the face with his head. P.C. Evans deposed that he noticed the crowd and saw prisoner knock prosecutor down and butt him.—Con- stable Bell apprehended prisoner while witness went to the assistance a complainant who MS bleeding in the face and very exhausted. The remainder of the men were a gang that the defendant belonged to and were a complete terror.—P.C. Bell corroborated.—During the hearing of the evidence the prisoner Had behaved in a very childish fashion, weeping very dolefully which, however, had no effect on the Bench, and thel Mayor observed that they were determined to put a stopl to that sort, of game, and defendant would have the full penalty and go to gaol for two months. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—TaIneS Clifton, 7 Tilley-sto, was fined Sc. including costs for being drunk and dia- firderly in Brick-st., on the 20th April; Mary Emson, 42 Ashton-at., was charged with the same offence in John-st. on the same date and pleaded not guilty. —Sergeant Cheney stated that on the night of the date in question he had a very violent prisoner in custody in John-at., when the defendant came up and acted in a very disorderly manner, inciting the crowd to rescue the prisoner.—She was fined 2i. 61. including cosr4, as it was her first appearance.—Jane Johnson, 9. Silver-square, was charged with a similar offence in Winwick-st., on the same date. Priaoner,who made her 40th appearance, and had evidently learnt Something, said, "I was not drunk ; hit I'll give in ; there's nowt like pleading guilty." As the case had ex- tenuating circumstances the prisoner was dismissed.— A similar charge was preferred against Katherine Knight, 3, Morris-yard, who had been drunk in Silver- square on the same date. She appeared at tha Court obviously under the influence of drink, and the Maynr said that as she was not sober they would take csre of her until Tuesday night, when she would perhaps be sober. , Colonel Ridgway. AN UNTRUSTWORTHY EMPLOYEIL—John Flannigan was charged, that he being the servant of John Longshaw, stole 18s. 63., his cash, on Friday, the 28th April. Mr. Hunt said that the complainant was a greengrocer in Mill-st, and the defendant was well known in Warring- ton and had been employed about a week prior to the 26th at the rate of ss. a week and board and lodgings. On Friday he was sent out with a load of " greent" to Widnes, and he should have returned the same day, but did not. On Saturday morning complainant went to Widnes and there saw the harness, cart, and a portion of the green-groceries ()Aside the "Castle" beerhouse. There were goods to the value of 18s. 6d. short ; and the horse was afterwards found at the farm of a Mr: Bilshaw. Information was given to Detective Monag- hani who subiequently arrested prisoner, who when charged said, "I only drew 10s. for the stuff and spent it." John Longshaw, the complainant, gave conobora- tive evidence,and stated that the prisoner had been sent. to Frodsham about two months since on a similar er- rand and in that case he kent the money—The magis- trates sent hid.' to. gaol for 14 days' hard labour. BREACH or THE Nam—Samuel Prosser was charged with having, on the 20th of April, committed a breach of the peace by fighting, in hloore.—S rgeant Gosling gave evidence showing that there had been a bit of a scuffle in which thetefendant ts as concerned, and he had struck a man named Taylor.—Defendant pleaded not guilty, and the magistrates ultimately bound him over to keep the peace in a surety of £5. MASTER AND MAN.—Ralph Tickle was charged with having on the 15th of April, in Appleton, assaulted and beaten Albert Green. Defendant pleaded not guilty. Albert Green, the complainant, labourer, and last work- ing for defendant, said that oa the 15:h of April he went to defendant's house and the latter asked him if he had got another job and complainant said "yes." whereupon his late master said the sooner he paid 12s. and the bet- ter,alleging that 6s. was for a pair of breeches and 63.f0r week's notice. Defendant then ordered complainant off the premises, and following him up seized him by the neck and kicked him at the same time, striking him in the face. The defendant, Mr. Tickle, denied assaulting the complainant at all, and said that he only put him nut of the yard by the coat collar. Michael Fleming,who was working close to at the time said that hr neither heard or saw anything in the nature ot an assault.—The Bench decided that the charge was unfounded, and dis- missed the case.

TRANSFER OF A PUBLICHOUSE -9-DENIAND FOR AN APOLOGY.—An application was made by Thomas Forster Nevins for the transfer of his licence of the Dog and Partridge, Paddington to his wife Sarah N'.vins. Mr. Arthur Browne evil() appeared for the husband said that before the transfer was granted, he would like to say that Mr. and Mrs. Nevins had kept the publichouse for some considerable time, but owing to a certain arrange- ment which had been made. Mr. Nevins had decided to leave the house to his wife, who would then be the licensee. On Wednesday in the week previous, Mr. Jenkins appeared for the wife at Warrington County Sessions, and according to a Warrinetnn newspaper he had said that Mr. Nevins had deserted his wife. Ms. Nevins wished him (Mr. Browne) to say that that was absolutely untrue, and before he applied for the trans- fer of the licence, he must ask his friend Mr Jenkins to withdraw the expression that Mr. Nevins had deserted his wife. He (Mr. Browne) had asked one of the reporters who said that it was a perfectly accurate report. He must therefore call upon Mr. Jenkins to withdraw —Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins said that this was an endeavour to drag into court the petty squabbles of Mr. and Mrs. Nevins. He must tell their worships that he never made use of the expression "desertion." He did say that Nevins had left his wife and that wag true. but he never said , that he deserted her.—After some further conversation, the magistrates retired, and on their return, Mr. Jenkins • said the, although he had not used the word "desertion," if it was any consolation to Mr. Nevins, he would withdraw any imputation if any was cast upon him at the court at Warrington.—Mr. Browne expressed himself eatisfied, and Mr. Gillespie said that the bench were glad that thia was so, otherwise they had intended ta adjourn the case. They accordingly granted the transfer. INFRINGEMENT OF THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.— David Mather. Newton, was charged with haying in his possession 21b., jib., and 40z., weights which were unjust, and also certain weights which were unstamped. —lnspector Spencer proved the case.—The defendant said that he had only used the weights on that day, while his other weights were sent to Golhorne to he adjusted. He produced a certificate which proved his assertion, and accordingly the magistrates dismissed the defendant on payment of costs. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A FlORSE.—Joshua Ball, farmer, Croft, and Hamblett Houehtnn, were charged, the for- mer with causing the horse to be worked while in an un- fit state on Anrill7, and the latter with working it.— Inspector Leff said that he visited Mr. Ball's farm on April 17, and saw a black mare at work in the field carting manure. He examined her and found a sore on the near shoulder between si and 4in. long, and from 1 to llj in width. The collar had been cut to ease the wound hut it nevertheless still pressed on the wound. Flooghton who was in charge told witness that the mare had been bad a month previous, and that the wound was caused by a bad fitting collar. He had bathed it wPh salt and hot water.—Serepant Barnes end P.C. Callaghan corroborated.—Mr. J. W. Knowles, who defended, denied that there was any sore. He said that the mare had had a kind of a shake, an enlarged veins, and a lernp had formed near the shoulder. The collar Was made en that it would not irritate the lumn, and it had not done so. The horse was worth from £25 to £3l—Evidence to show that no wound was on the shoulder was given by Joshua Rll. Smile! Hewitt (veterinary surgeon). Lewis Birchall, William Croft, and George Birchall, and the maeistrates decided to dismiss the case, hut said that the inspector was justified in bringing the cause into court.

ALLEGED BRUTAL ASSAULT AT GoLnowni.—James, Navin and Willitincldanatidrwere charged with in- flicting grevious bodily harm . upon Joseph Blundell, at Golborne, on April 13th. Mr: Stuart defended.—The complainant. said that on the date mentioned he went out of his house at 11.10.p.m., and as soon as he got out MacMahon gave him a blow in the jaw. Complainant clord with him and they fell to the ground. While on the ground Navin kicked him on the right snoulder, and caused such injuries that he had been under Dr. Part ever since.—Mary Ana Blundell, the wife of complain- ant, gave corroborative evidence, and in reply to Mr. Stuart, she said that she had the poker but had no chance to use it.—Further evidence was given by Robert Honderwood, P.C. Blundell, and Dr. Part, the latter of whom saying that Blundell's shoulder blade, and also his 11th or floating rib were broken. This could be caused by a kick. In reply to Mr. Stuart, he said that the injuries might also be caused by falling on a stone. —The prisoners were committed to the Liverpool Assizes.
