div.head: YOUR. WATCH GOES TO SLEEP.
div.p: YOUR. WATCH GOES TO SLEEP.

You carry a watch? Hardly a doubt of it; most people do. Watches are cheap nowadays, and a poor man can afford abetter one than a rich man could 100 years ago. Well, sometimes your watch stops. You don't see what ails it on the instant. You give it a shake. It wakes up and ticks along for Ave minutes and then goes to sleep again. What does ail it,anyhow Your watchmaker puts the trouble in three words : Dirty," he says," wants cleaning." Your bodily machinery isn't right. It doesn't stop ; if it did nobody on earth could start it again. But it goes irregularly, sometimes fast, sometirpes slow. A man, speaking of his wife, says, " she took cold with the slightest thing." Now what is " catching cold ?" How do we do it ? This way: There is some weakness or depression of the nervous system, and a relatively small amount of cold comes in contact with an exposed surface of skin. TM • sends too much blood to the throat, nose, and bronchial tubes, produces an irritation which causes a cough. and a congestion which stops the sense of smell and sets the mucous matters running .from the eyes and nose. Nar- cotics and cough mixtures won't do you a bit of good. If your doctor *ere as honest as your watchmaker, he would say of your blood,!' Dirty, wants cleaning." The letter we quote from continues: Twenty years ago my wife had rheumatic fever which left her low, weak, and nervous. After wards she had frequent attacks of faintness, with nausea, flatulence, and pain at the heart. She took cold with the slightest thing, and was constantly under the doctor, who patched her up from time to time. She went on in this way from year tc year. able to get about but always nervous and debili- tated. No medicine or treatment made any real differ ence for the better.

"Finally I heard of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, which was reported to possess remarkable medicinal properties. My wife began taking it and is now thank- ful that she did so ; it has done her a wonderful deal of good. For the past three years she has been; in better health than for twenty years previously. Indeed I may say that both my wife and mrself are maintained in health by this medicine. A dose or two soon braces us up and dispels any feelings of languor or weakness. _ . _

• "Several friends to whom I have recommended the Syrup have been benefited by it. If by the publibation of my letter other poor suff-mers may come to hear of this medicine you have my permission to make such use of it. Yours truly (signed) Wtia.mat Nawm., Prospect- terrace, Oxford-road, Reading, October, 28th, 1892." What are we to learn thee from the facts stated by this gentleman? We are to learn that the disposition or tendency to catch cold signifies that the blood is filled with impurities, which weaken and disorder the system and take away its powers to resist exposure, changes of weather, and also any sort of contagious influences. Where do the impurities come from? They come from the stagnant, undigested food in the stomach, which turns sour, ferments and fills the blood with poisonous acids. It is these, and not the cold, which cause those " shivery " sensations that make people I think they are going to be taken ill—and really do make them ill. Drive out all this stuff, and start the stomach, bowels, liver, and kidneys into natural action, and you are weather-proof. It may sound queer to say so, but nobody is ever takten ill unless he is ill before he is taken. That was Mother Seigel'a idea, and experience proves her quite right. ' •

RUGBY% WARRINGTON v. BARROW.

As was the first match of the season so was the last played in warm summer weather. This, however, was about the onle ooint of resemblance for the result was altogether different. The subjoined list of players ' shows that Warrington were far from being representa- tive, whilst Barrew out on the field the fifteen who have worked together all the season through almost un- changed. The match was played on• Saturday at Cavendish Park, Barrow, belore an attendance of about 2,000. Tbe ground did not look inviting, for it was bare in mane places and patchy in others. Warring- ton had the sun and a slight breeze behind them when Jack Bowker set the ball in motion. Houghton made the initial move for the visitors but he did not get the leather away and the Barrow quartette were at. once in possession and gave a sequence of passing which was a foretaste of much that was to follow. Jeffrey made a bo:d bid for a drop goal. From the kick out Thorniley, Barber, Berry. Callaghan, and Bate took play to Barrow lines wrtere Barber made his mark. Although Lawless ' made a plucky attempt to gat through it did not come off as the home defence proved equal to this turn, and also the next which Barber caused by again making his mark. Indeed, Barrow looked like profiting by this latter move, for the forwards came away with a rattling rush, and were gaining ground when Barber interrupted and robbed them by neatly getting in the kick. This was spoiled by offside play of Houghton, and the ball was ordered back again. Lawless receiving from Bates' pass by a smart low shot regained the ground thus lost and several line outs at Barrow quarter flag kept up the pressure, Boscow slsvays accounting for the flying I kicks which. came his way. Berry at this point had particularly hard lines,for after a:fine bit of combination between him and Bate he was grounded when within a yard of the line. The game quickly underwent a change. After Barrow had reached the half-way line, more by line outs than by enything else, they came away in a heap and working well in consort Dickinson was able to score under the bar. Parkinson easily placing a goal. Pi was really another bit of off-side play by Hough- ton that started the movement which cost Warrington so dear for he off-sided the players who caught one of Boscow's big kicki, and that too when there was no occasion for him to touch the man at all. Passing by Heesom, Lawless and Barton was the next item on the programme. Lawless did :a smart bit of dodging in eluding Fluehes, and font this it seemed a ten .to one chance that Warrington would draw level for three scaMmages took place in front' of OM Barrow sticks T. Bowker intercepted a pass which Bate intended for Bar- ber. Jeffery and Tom Dickinson took up the running with Bowker, and as Boscow slipped another goal was imminent when Barber did the same for Bell that Bowker ha,d doite for him for he took the ball from Bell's toes. It was an exciting moment. Heesom staved off a second attempt to score, and then B)scoer and T. Revoker ex- changed a few kicks together which resulted in cor.- siderable advantage .to Warrington so far as ground -gas concerned. Scrimmages in Barrow territory yielded nothing. Although Thorniley and Burton made strong efforts to get over all efforts were in vain, and half-time arrived with the score Barrow one goal, Warrington nil. With the sun in their eyes Warringten had a difficult task before them, but from the manner in which they followed Dakin's restart it wag evident they had plenty of go left in them. The opening movements of the second half were all in their favour, hut a forward pass by fleesum to Burton who had only a few yards to uo and nobody to ston him put the damper on th-ir early hopes. Warrington hid then to put in all they were worth to keep Barrow out, and it was mainly owing to Berton and Boacow that they suc- ceeded in doing so. Bate greatly advanced Warrington's progress over by an individual effort with nobody near enough him to put in the fiiiishinir touch, and again by a dodging move behind the pack when he found himself • floored an arm's length from the line. Tots was all the cnnsolation that was to. he had, for Bowker was again the means of affording another of these sudden changes

whieh came over the earlier part of the gime. Barber and Lawless made strong efforts to prevent what was coming (the latter actually struck the crossbar with his hurriedly-taken flying kick). .They succeeded in robbing Bowker, but from the ensuing scrimmage Bell scored. Another bit of luck fell to Barrow, for a minute or so later C. Sharp picked up from some loose play. Bosoow gave chase, but Sharp had that much of a start of him, that when he did succeed in overtaking and tackling him, Sharp fell halfway across the line and of course scored. • This was the first try Sharp had scored for seven years and his companions almost shook his hand off in their congratulations whilst the crowd cheered lustily. It was certainly an immensely popular if a lucky try. The game was essen- tially one of sudden changes. Bate was the means of causing play to be taken to Barrow line whereafter more scrimmaging the line was crossed at last, and Burrows scored. Towards the close of the game, when between half-way flag and quarter flag Burton and others were appealing to T. Barnes for flag, having gone in touch, to which appeal Barnes was apparently justified in not listening, the Barrow man kept on his way and no one seeking to stop him he seored behind the cross-bar for Parkinson to land a second goal. And so the season 1894-1895 , closed with as silly a won try as was ever obtained against Warrington or any other club: Final result, Barrow, 2 goals, 2 tries ; Warrington, 1 try. Barrow : C. Jeffery, T. Dickinson, It. Bell, R. Messin- ger, S. Northmore' Morgar, Thomas McGerry, John Bowker,Creorge Woodhouse,W. C.Sharpe,E.Dickinson,R. Parkinson. _ .
Warrington: Boscow, Heesom, Burton, Lawless, Barber, James Bate, Houghton, Berry. Burrows, Thornily, Swift, Bailey, Callaghan, Barrett, Dakin. RUNCORN v. WIGAN.

These teams met at Runzorn on Saturday afternoon. The match was robbed of a great deal of interest owing to the heity fall of rain and the late arrival of the visi- tors. The home team was only of moderate strength whilst the colliery tewn was strongly represented. The following players composed the Runcorn team : Hough- ton, back; Warder, W. Faulkner, Myers and Dunba- vand, three-quarters ; Abrams and Itobinson.half-backs; Farmer,Gayter,Williams,Taylor,llrmson,Stubbs, Walker and Johnson forwards. The ground was in a bad state, making accurate play impossible. The game was for some time of a scrambling nature,both sides of forwards showing strong play. Houghton made a clever save on the line, stopping Flowers from scoring. With the aid of a clever punt by Faulkner, Runcorn gained a little ground. A succession of scrimmages took place in the home quarter. Warder brought relief, by a smart dribble, which Wigan strongly checked. ,Uninteresting play followed up to half time, neither side scoring. On restarting,the home team made tracks for the %tip= lines, and Winstanley saved d aringly. Wigan put i some good footwork, but Houghton's defence was ad- mirable. Following an attack on Wigan lines, Flowers got hold from a kick by Gayter, and running strongly along the wing, he outraced Warder and W. Faulkner, but was safely tackled by Houghton. He however suc- ceeded in passing to Macnama, who in turn passed to Halliwell, and this player romped over under the posts. Webster took the kick and was successful in placing a fine goal. The home team now played up with vigour, but aided by some lucky flying kicks by Winstanley, the visitor's lines were kvt intact. W. Faulkner on one occasion had a fine opening, but injudiciously kicked. The game ended. Wigan one. goal, Runcorn nil. Wanninewon EXCELSIORS V. Anosarox.—This match was playedbn,the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, the kick off being at 515 instead of 3.30 as announced. lln consequence of the late start the "gatewas exceedingly small and the game began with Atherton playing 12 men the other three appearing shortly after. The Warrington team was composed as follows t—Full-back, Knight ; three-quarters Gleave, Raybold, Siddall and Carey; half backs, Mason and Woods; forwards, Fairhurst, Willcox, Thornton, Hammersley,Taylor, Sudlow, Hughes and A. N. Other. Throughout tile match the game was very pleasant and interesting, though the visitors were not equal to their opponents who ultimately won by 3 goals and a try to nil. The scorers were Siddall, Gleave and Mason, and a goal was notched from a penalty ck. ST. MARY'S V. LATCHFORD RANGERS.—This final tie of the Rugby Junior Football Competition, was played on the Warrington Football Ground on Monday night,before a fair number of spectators. St. Mary's were much the heavier team. The Rangers kicked off, and for about ten minutes play rested at midfield, Rutter was the means of St. Mary's pressing, but Ashurst pleated out the invaders finely. Hallam further improved the Rangers'position. Good kicking by the Stalary's backs reached Latchford lines, and Bennett passed to Ramp- son who handed on to O'Brien, and this player scored in a good position, but Roughley failed at goal. Play was very even from now to half-time, and at the interval St. Mary's were leading by a try to nil. On the restart St. Mary's pressed, but could not score,owing to the fine de- of the of the Latchford boys. Scott and Bramhall got in good defensive play, and Wilcocks and Fairhurst made several good rushes which gave St. Mary's a lot of trouble. Shortly before time was called a misunder- standing occurred between two of the Latchford players and Dakin scored,.P. Hill converting. Final result :St. Marys 1 goal 1 try, Latchford nil. As St. Mary's have TOW won the cup two successive years, it becomes their Property. The victors were naturally very jubilant over their victory, and on obtaining possession of the cup paraded the principal streets of the town, holding the cup aloft. They were followed by a large number of supgorters, and the cheering was loud and continued. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. MR. JOB BOSCOW'S TEAM.— BENEFIT Maron.—Tho above benefit match was played on Tuesday night an the Warrington Club ground,. Wiiderspool-road, on behalf of J. W. Plinston, and Es Eden. who were injured in the Junior Cup tie, Ranger v. Stockton Heath, on the 15th ult. The Rangers started, and were soon on their opponents, they pressing Boscow's line, where the ball rested For a while. The Rangers eventually by pressing hard scored a try. Boscow was awarded a free kick, and Burrows received and placed the ball over the line. The goal kick was a failure. The Rangers still pressed, but nothing further was scored up to the interval. rhe second half was more of an open game, the ball t.avelling front end to end. The Rangers, by means of good passing, again scored an unimproved try. Boscow's team became over- pow.ereri, and the Rangers again scored, this time the kick at goal being successful. Another try was added to the Rangers' list. Final result :—Rangers 1 goal, 3 tries, Boscow's team 1 try. ASSOCIATION.

BARNTON ROVERS V. PARR.—These two teams met on Saturday in the first tie of the cup competition, at the Arpley Cricket ground. Neither team reached the final last vear,Barnton Rovers being defeated in the semi-final by Warrington, who subsequently won the cup, while this was Parr's first entrance into the competition. There was a very large gate, and an excellent game was witnessed. Barnton were rather fortunate in scoring eight goals to one, as the game was not near so one- sided as the score wouh.. indicate. Three of the goals were obtained from free kicks. After the match the teams adjourned to the R.:chuck, where Mr. W. Gill presented the cup to the winners, expressing the opinion that now the cup had gone to Ilarnton it would be a difficult matter to get it away again. He also ex- pressed a high opinion of the play of the runners up. The captain of the Barnton Rovers team replied on be- half of the players,and a very pleasant meeting was held. This is the second year of the competition, War- rington being the winners last year,' but this year they were defeated hv their local rivals St. Elphins, after a drawn game. St. Elphins in their turn were beaten by the present winners.

SEFTON T. WARRINGTON.—The first of the season's fixtures between the above clubs took place on Saturday at Sefton Park, the wicket being on the soft side owing to the heavy rain. Sefton batted first, and closed their innines after scorinz 104 for six wickets. Warrington batted one man short. Score SEFTON. WARREMITON. Total 104 Total EARLESTOWN V. LEIGH.—The Earlestown Club opened their season en Stturday with a visit to Leigh. For several seasons past the initial game has been between these two clubs. The day was not of a promising character, hut with the exception of a slight shower cr two, tho game was not interfered with. The wicket was in a very wet state, giving the batters an advan- tage. Leigh won the toss, and elected to go to the wickets first. The bowling was not by any means dan- gerous, but with the score at 75, Leigh had lost six wickets. Turner and Hindley made a good stand, and changed the aspect of the game, and with the aid of some indifferent fielding on the part of Earlestown.they added another 75 runs, the home captain closing the in- nings at 157 for seven wickets. Bell attacked remark. ablv well, and secured four wickets for 29 runs. Earles- town had an hour and a half in which to rub off this score, and they made A splendid attempt to accomplish the task, Husband and Dennis adding 111 before they were parted, stumps being drawn on time with the score at 116 for the loss of one wicket. div.head: W YCLIFFE F.S.A.
div.p: W YCLIFFE F.S.A.
ANNUAL BUSINESS MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Wycliffe Congregational Church P.S.A. for the passing of reports and accounts was held on Monday evening in the church, Bewsey-st., Warrington, when the Rev. J. Yonge (president) occu- pied the chair. He was supported on the platform by Mr. T. Wallington (secretary), Mr. R. Atkinson (treasurer), and Mr. D. Prestwich (Stockport), secretary of the P.S.A Federation. GENERAL SECRETARY'S REPORT. After a brief address by the Chairman, Mr. T. W al- lington read his report of the business of the P.S'A. for the past year as fellows :—" In presenting this, the second annual report of the P.S.A. Society I do so with the greatest pleasure and thankfulness. Meeting as we do again to-night, to look back upon the events and circumstances connected with another year's work, I think we have every reason to do so with feelings of the deepest joy and gratitude for the bleving which has crowned our labours, and for the great success which has attended the- movement amongst us. The Society still maintains its high excellence as an organization accomplishing widespread good, and working untold blessings upon the lives, homes and characters of many who have been brought within the circle of its influ- ence. The steady progress made may he taken as an indication that although two pars have passed away since the Society was first inaugurated, its power and attractiveness is as great, if not greater to-day than in the earlier days of its career, establishing as it most certainly has the undeniable fact, of having had an unmistakable, elevating, and bene- ficial effect, not just simply upon those more closely connected with it in its working, but upon the whole town generally. And if the great principals upon which it is founded be only earefully watched, guarded, and diligently carried out, who can tell the great power it will be able to exercise in the near furture in helping to bring about the consumation of all our wishes, in the removal of many of the evils which surround us at the present time, and making our home life, our business life end social life, purer, brighter and happier. The first year of the Society closed with a sabscribing membership roll of 1,150, and my pleasure is to report, that at the end of the second year on February 24th last, the membership 'reached 1,203.—The attendances at the meetings have again been wonderfully large. The aver- age weekly attendance during tin first year of members and non-members was estimated at about 630, and that for the year j •st closed the weekly average has been about 829. In order that it may be seen that the regular attendance has been firm, strong and progressive, allow me to give a few figures as to the number of books gained as prizes.—At the end of the first half-year 399 were distributed. At the and of the second half 630, making a total for the first year of 1,029 books. At the end of the first half of the year just closed, 644 were given out, and at the end of the second half 681 making a total for the past year of 1,325 books, and a grand total for the two years of 2,354. Also that dur- ing the same period upwards of 480 certificates of merit have been gained for regular and punctual attendance. These figures speak for themselves, and show in unmis- takable and undeniable terms, that the society is still powerful, and diffusing help and influence among the people. During the year it is my pleasure to report that many of the members not connected with any Sunday school in the town, have, through the kind invitation given by the leader of the Young Mens' Bible Class con- nected with Wycliffe been led to throw in their let with them, and others have been influenced by the , movement to return to long-given up attendance at church and school in other parts of the constituency. , The finances of the society are in a very sound con- dition, for after paying all expenses, and contributing to the church maintenance fund there is a balance in hand to carry forward to the present year. The Benevo- lent Fund Committee have again done excellent work and have been the instruments in carrying cheer and comfort to many hearts and homes. The sick and absentee visitors have had a year of busy work and have very carefully and faithfully discharged their duties helping to maintain that touch of sympathy so essential in movements like ours. . . _ .

During the year all the members who signed the temperance pledge have been visited and hopes are en- tertained that shortly there will be better facilities for the carrying on ot this branch of the work. TREASURER'S REPORT.

Mr. R. ATKINSON. treasurer of the P.S.A. movement, in presenting big statement of accounts pointed out that the total income for the past year had been £195 16s. 40. and the total expenditure £lBB 185. 81 ~and the amount carried forward to next year's account was a 17s. Bd. The principal and most interesting of the items he enu- merated were £2O 17s. 2d. proceeds of collections at the four open meetings ; 2146 Hs. 2d., members' weekly contributions ; the money_ spent in prizes was at the first distribution in Auzu3r, 1894, £53 83. 51., in Febru. ary, 1895, £54 15s. 10i1., which made a total of £lOB 4s. 30. .

div.head: BENEVOLENT FUND ACCOUNTS.
div.p: THE BENEVOLENT FUND ACCOUNTS.

The statement for this fund was presented by Mr. A. Lang which read as follows :—" In presenting this our second annual report it gives the committee great pleasure to put it on record that your interest in this fund does not abate. The necessity for help has happily not been so great this year as last and therefore the call on you has been proportionately lighter. It is, however, the conviction of your committee that cases of need from time to time escape our notice. We be- lieve many of our members will rather bear the pinch of poverty than make their circumstances known. If every member would give us his co-operation and when any real case of distress is known to report it to Us, it would be attended to, and the objects of our fund be facilitated. We need scarcely say however that we cannot yet aspire to old age pensions or the support of the permaner.tly disabled nor vet give continuous relief in cases of chronic poverty. The total income this year —as the treasurer reports—has been 27 Bs. nd. made up as follows :—Ordinary collections £l3 4. Sid., special collections £9 73. 9d., donations £4 143. 61. The disbursements amounted to £23 4s. 4d. which included 45 ordinary cases of relief to whom £8 6s. 101. was dis- tributed, and four special cases which will be fresh in the minds of most of us. These four cases alone cost us £l4 17s. 6d., but your committee consider it was money well spent assistinv and " visiting the fatherless and widows in th6ir affliction." We began the year with a balance of £4 23. qd., and trust that it may be such a good year for all of us that the demands on our fund may be a diminishing quantity and prosperity rule in our midst."
• THE TEMPERANCE PLEDGE.

Mr. WALLINGTON read the report of Mr. C. H. Mills, secretary of the Temperance Society. In the report it was stated that 51 members of the P.S.A.had signed the pledge during the wear, and as far as was known only three had broken it.

div.head: ABSENTEE AND SICK VISITORS.
div.p: ABSENTEE AND SICK VISITORS.

Mr. R. Milms-in.Presenting his report on the work of the above committee, said they were sensible of the importanoe of the work they had in hand, and they had done the work cheerfully and in good heart, lie mentioned that in cases where absentees were out of work they had assisted them as far as lac? in their power. He was also glad to say that there had not been so many cases of sickness during the past year when they considered the great number of members upon the register. Mr. Mills also observed that when visiting any of the sick brethren they had always been received with the greatest respect, and the absentees had been glad to know that they had not altov.ether been forgot- ten. During the year there had been 714 persons visited. All these reports, after being read,were passed unani- mously.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The business for electing the various officers for the ensuing year was then proceeded' with and resulted in the appointment ef the following gentlemen :—President, the Rev. J. Yonge ; treasurer, Mr. R. Atkinson ; general secretary, Mr. T. Wallington ; registration secretary, Mr. A. Knowles ; absentee visitors' secretary, Mr. R. Mills ; benevolent fund secretary, Mr. A. Lang ; bene- volent fund treasurer, Mr. William Hickman ; markers secretary, Mr. W. Hayes, jun.; steward secretary, Mr. J. Knowles, jun. ; hymn book secretary, Mr. Ogden ; temperance pledge book secretary. Mr. C. H. Mills ; choir leader, Mr. W. H. Wallington ; besides these offi- cials the whole of the committee, with the exception of nine whose names had been crossed off owing to death and non-attendance, were re-elected and the fol- lowing gentlemen's names added :—Messrs. Crosskill, Lankford, G. Gough, Joseph Bavlev,A. Birch,'A. Healey, G. Bayley, Thopas Wood, Kelly, Pickton, T. Allen, and W. Slater.

div.head: VOTES OF THANES.
div.p: VOTES OF THANES.

On the motion of MT. -THOMAS HAWTHORN, seconded by Mr. Cnossitmr„ a vote of thanks was passed to all the officers for their past services.—There was a special vote of thanks accorded the choir-master, and the soloists who had so generously given their services during the year. Before the mPeting closed Mr. PRESTWICH gave an ad- dress on the " Works and Aims of a P.S.A." a subject which be expounded to his hearers with much capabi- lity.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

Lawt.r TENNIS Cturi BALL.—A ball in connection with the Lymm Lawn Tennis Club took place on Friday night at the Plough and Railway Hotel. Lymm. About 100 persons were present, and dancing was indulged in with much zest until two o'clock on Saturday morning. Mr. Johnson's band, of Warrington, supplied the music ; and the catering was in the hands of Miss Sumner, the pro- prietress of the Plough and Railway Hotel. ELECTION OF GUARDIAN.—We understand that Mr. John R. Smith, of Birch Brook Lodge, Heatley, a mem- ber of the Lymm Urban District Council, has been solicited by an influential deputation of Lymm gentlemen to allow himself to be nominated to fill this vacancy. The following ladies and gentlemen are his proposers and seconders, viz., Messrs. G. P. Dewhurst, James Gould, Thomas P. Norris, J.P., A. W. Callender, James Holt, Samuel Appleton, William Ogden, and John Wilkinson ; Mrs. Parkinson and Miss Dewhurst.
WA R RIN G TON RURAL bISTRICT COUN OIL.

The annual meeting of the above Council was held at the Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday. Mr. S. Sutton, the clerk, took the chair, pro tent, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. W. floughton,J. Houghton, J. Warburton, T. Mather, J. Dignum, J. Johnson,J. Ball ; Dr. Sephton (medical officer),W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector).

div.head: ELECTION OF MAILMAN AND VICE-CIIAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF MAILMAN AND VICE-CIIAIRMAN.

Mr. W. ROUGHTON proposed, and Mr. Knowles se- conded the rP-election of the Rev. G. F. Robertsas chair- man of the Board for the ensuing year. This was carried unanimously. Mr. Roberts then took the chair, and briefly thanked the members for their renewed confi. dence in him. Mr. W. Houghton was then elected vice- chairman, on the motion of the chairman seconded by Mr. Warburton.

div.head: DAY OF MEETING.
div.p: DAY OF MEETING.

The CLERIC said that it would be for the Board to con- sider whether the present time and place of meeting should be altered. lie suggested that the members meet at the Board room of the Workhouse as it would be much more convenient, as the present premises were rather circumscribed.—Mr. KNOWLES on the other hand thought that the premises were very convenient to the members as it was near the station and the market. He moved that the meeting be held at 1.45 p.m., on the Wednes- day of the special meeting of Warrington Board of Guardians.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON seconded.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON moved as an amendment that the Council meeting on the interim Wednesday of the meetings of the Board of Guardians at the Workhouse at 10 30.—Mr. DraNum seconded. Upon being put to the nseeting,Mr. KNOWLES' motion was carried, only the proposer and seconder voting for the amendment.

div.head: RIXTON CEMETERY.
div.p: THE RIXTON CEMETERY.

The CLERIC read a letter from the Rixton-with-Glaze- brook Parish Council in which the Council asked for the transfer of thl cemetery to themselves with all i+s liabi- lities at the earliest possible convenience of the Rural District Council. If the Council did not see its way to transfer the cemetery, the reason for not doing so was asked for.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON thought it would be well to transfer the cemetery to the Parish Council.—The CHAIRMAN, on the contrary, did not think it desirable.— Mr. KNOWLES said that the Rural District Council would be much more impartial in dealing with the matter as there must be factions in the village.—Mr. W. flouonToN said that the experience of the last few years certainly went to show that the cemetery would be better looked after if it w, s in the hands of the Rural District Council, The CLERK a -Weed the Council not to consent to the request of the Parish Council.—Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON thereupon moved that the Council did not at present see any reason for traiasfering the charge of the cemetery to the Parish Council.—Mr. KNOWLES seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: ALLEGED NUISANCE AT LITTLE SANKEY.
div.p: THE ALLEGED NUISANCE AT LITTLE SANKEY.

A letter was read from Mr. T. Tunstall,--t-h—e--cierk of the Little Sankey Parish Council, in .ahich he asked the Rural District Council to cause an abatement of the nuisance caused by Mr. Burton depositing manure upon land near to the township.—Mr. KERFOOT said that the manure was discharged at a point which was 400 yards from the nearest dwelling-house. Mr. Burton had seen him on the matter, and had promised to do all in his power to abate the nuisance.—Mr. KNOWLES : The smell only occurs during the discharge of the manure. The farmers must have some place to discharge it.—Mr. BALL: My wharf is only 50 yards from Win wick Hall, and I have no complaints.—After further discussion a resolution was passed to the effect that there was no unnecessary nuisance caused by the discharge of the maoure. Later in the meeting, Mr. Burton attended, and he promised that he would cause no more nuisance than he could not possibly help. He said that there was no smell except when the manure was taken out of the boat.

div.head: TREATMENT OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES.
div.p: TREATMENT OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES.

A letter was read from the Town Clerk of Warrington in reply to a communication from the Rural District Council, offering to receive cases of infectious disease which might occur in the district, and at an inclu.ive charge of £2 10s, per head per week. The Clerk said that this was a very reasonable offer. The charge was formerly £l3O per year, and two guineas per head per week, and even then the Corporation did not guarantee accommodation.—The offer was unanimously accepted.

div.head: DUST AND NIGHTSOIL CONTRACTS.'
div.p: DUST AND NIGHTSOIL CONTRACTS.'
Mr. B. Grimshaw was re-appointed contractor for Little Sankey for dust and nightsoil at £l2 per month, and Mr. Pownall for Penketh. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that for three weeks ended April 24th,there had been 40 births and 16 deaths. The death rate was equal to 13 6 per 1,000. There were no deaths from zvmotic diseases. During the month there had been eight eases a scarlet fever, and one case of erysipelas reported. —The report was adopted.

div.head: SURVEYOR'S RRYORT.
div.p: SURVEYOR'S RRYORT.

The SURVEYOR reported that during the month, inspec- tions have been made of Mr. Hindley's houses, Mr. Eztrd's houses, and Mr. J. Mason's house, Padgate, and a certificate of habitation had been issued to Mr. Mason. The following plans were approval : Mr. David Garnett, for additions of two houses at Peniteth. Messrs. Berkett and Co., the contractors for Burtonwood drainage, were proceeding satisfactorily with the work, and he had issued a certificate for a further payment on account of £2OO. Owing to an alteration which he had ventured to make in the arrangement of the road running from the highroad into the land purchased for purification of the sewage, the additional cost would be £l7 65. 7d., kit this would not be an extra charge on ths scheme, as the outlay was below the estimates submitted to the Local Government Board. Mr. John Thompson, the surveyor to the. Warrington Highway Board had expressed his willingness to take over at once, Dale-street and Owen- street, and after Friday, he expected to obtain his acceptance of all the remaining streets for adoption by that Board.—The report was adopted, and the meeting then terminated.

div.head: ' • -6„.._._ OHMY'S CIRCUS, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ' • -6„.._._ OHMY'S CIRCUS, WARRINGTON.

This, now most popular place of amusement has been again well filled during the put week when the pro- gramme submitted was of interest to all. For a greater part of the evening, Mr. Davies acted as ring-master, in the absence of Mr. Ohmy who usually oncupies that position, and it can only be said that he performed his duties in that capacity with creditable facility. The following are the individual items :—overture by the hand under the leadership of Captain Metcalfe ;Miss Minnie in a skilful exposition of horsemanship ; the clowns in an act of fun ; the three Keiths, dancers and posturists ; Nelson, the performing horse ; Miss Ariella, tight rope and firework act ; brothers Dianta in a won- derfully clever cap-throwing performance : Claud Ohmy as a horseback trick rider, with Clown Walker as humorist ; the same clown also proves him- self an agil" stilt wallvr ; the marvellous perform- ing dog troupe : Whimsical and his fighting bantam ; Douglas and Douglas, acrobats ; the Zula War scene; the Brothers Dianta in their entertaining perform- ance as musical clowns is—instrumentalism in almost all positions ; double act on two horses by Claud Ohmy and Tomasso, who both perform daring feats to the accom- paniment of numerous jokes by Clown Cartland ; the handsomest lady rider in the world ; Zesto,the gymnast; a laughable sack race by members of the audience was the final selection. Those of special mention for this week are the three Keiths, all small girls, who possess a large amount of grace and skill in dancing. Miss Ariella is an adept at the art of balancing and tight rope walking, both of which she does with large baskets fastened on her feet. To top all she concludes her exhibition by whirling round her head a huge fire-work which throw- ing out a shower of coloured stars 1144 a very pretty effect. Douglas and Douglas, father and son, the latter a small boy, are acrobats of the first water, and give a display which must be seen to be appreciated. A special feature this week is the Zulu war scene, which depicts Mr. Ohmy as a last resort leaving his command and setting imt to deliver the despatches himself. In the attempt he has an ex- citing struggle with some admirably got-up Zulus, and atter being wounded is saved in the nick of time by a faithful retainer appearing upon the scene. The hand- somest (?) lady rider is Clown Cartland in a ridiculous and laughable costume, which wins him a cabbage bouquet. Another item to which deserved prominence is given is Zesto's trapeze perfoxmance. This gymnast performs all his feats in mid air without any safeguard such as a net, and relies, therefore, on his own ability and skill. To crown all he springs from one trapese the full length of the building, through a paper drum and at the other side catches with alarming dexterity another trapeze. All these entertaining displays will be given at the two o'clock performance this afternoon, and the opportunity of seeing them should certainly not be lost.

It is stated that the ex-Speaker, on his elevation to the peeras‘e. has chosen the title of Viscount Peel. General Booth is not in such good health as might be desired. He has never quite shaken off the effects of the influenza from which he suffered during, his visit to America.

div.head: WARRING-TON TEMPERANCE
div.p: WARRING-TON TEMPERANCE
FEDERATION.
PRESENTATION TO THE REV. D. W. ROBERTB

A meeting of the Committee of the Warrington ,Tem- perance Federation was held at the British Workman Cocoa Rooms last Friday afternoon, for the purpose of presenting a purse to the Rev. D. W. Roberts who is leaving the town, owing to ill health. The chair was occupied by the President, the Rev. J. Youge,And there were also present the Revs. D. W. Roberts, E. T. Read, J. Kirtlan and J. E. Jones, Councillor Roberts, J.P., Messrs. W. Roberts, J. Drury, J. C. Dalton E. Boreland (district superintendent of the United Kingdom Alli- ance), J. Mounfield, H. Thornton, R. Storey, and Miss B. Dutton.

Mr. W. ROBERTS said that Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., Mr. E J. Guest, J.P., and Mr. Titchett had expressed to him their regret that it would be impossible for them to be present at the meeting that afternoon. The CHAIRMAN said that Friday afternoon was an inconvenient time for men ot business and also be men like himself, otherwise there would no doubt have been. a much larger attendance at that meeting. They met that afternoon in consequence of the decision of the Federation to meet their friend and fellow-worker, the Rev.D.W.Roberts,who for two and a half years had been the minister at Golborne-st. Chapel, but was now leav- ing the town. It was felt that he stihuld not be allowed to leave Warrington without some token being given to him of the personal esteem with which they regarded him, especially for the stand he had taken while he had been in the town in the cause of temperance. (Hear, hear.) They knew perfectly well that anyone who took a pronounced stand in a town like Warrington on the side of temperance, became the mark and the butt of a great deal of criticism and of not a little abuse, and the more pronounced he was and the more emphatic he was, Me more he would become the victim of vitupera- tion and reproach. But all those who had the cause of temperance at heart, were careless about that sort of thing. (Hear, hear.) He always thought that they ought to be glad when they produced in their friend,the enemy, anything like emphatic observation and harsh criticism. Mr. Roberts had taken a stand for temperance in the town that no one had ever done before. (Applause.) There was a feeling in the town that something must be done to bring about a very large measure of temperance reform. Their friend with the ardour of youth, and with the.eourage of strong con- viction, became a leader of them at that time and occu- pied a very conspicuous place, and held it with heroic fortitude which WOD a large amount of genuine admira- tion. He did not think that the work which he did last year, would be soon forgotten. Be only hoped that they would have the courage and fortitude which would enable them to carry to a still more successtui issue the campaign in which they were engaged. He was sure that they would all feel that after the stand their friend made. it *was only simple justice to themselves that they should meet that afternoon not only to make a gmall presentation but to assure him o their personal regard, and to wish him God speed. He hoped that other young men would come among them who would dash ahead regardless of consequences in the faith and hope that they would come out victorious at last. (Applause.) Mr. Wreetem ROBERTS said it would hardly be neces- sary for him to say much after the very lucid explanation of their president.' They would be aware that the committee of the federa- tion unanimously decided that they should make some presentation to Mr. Roberts before he left the town, and he would like to say, and Mr. Roberts would be glad to know, that there had been no personal can- vassing for subscriptions for the presentation, but that the subscriptions were all voluntary contributions. He, as the secretary of the Federation, simply addressed I letters to the more active Members of the organisation. I and the result as they would see was the voluntary con- tribution frem those connected with the organisation. I Mr. Roberts here read the names of the contributors. Continuing,he said that he wished to say personally how deeply he regretted that they were about to lose the services of Mr. Roberts in Warrington. He considered his departure from the town was a distinct loss to the movement, and he felt that every member of the tem- perance party was under an obligation to Mr. Roberts for the stand he had taken. He was an example to the men connected with the temperance party and was worthy of their emulation. He (the speaker) hoped that it would be an incentive to others to follow up similar work in the' future. They had so many temperance friends in War- rington who did not take any active part in the move- ment, and did not even subscribe to the funds of the organisation. He thought that those friends should consider their own position, and the responsibility, of their inaction. If their friends would only be united and put aside their little sectarian differences, the temperance party wolld present e much stronger front than it did at the present time. He only hoped that Mr. Roberts would before very long be completely restored te health, and that although, he was leaving Warrington, his position in the future would he materially improved in every respect. (Applause.) All of them would be glad from dine to time to hear of his success, and that wherever he might go his labours would be abundantly blessed. (Applause.) Councillor ROBERTS then rose to make the present- ation. He said that he had come at some inconvenience because he did not think that it was the thing to be away upon an occasion of that kind, when a man who had devoted so much time and energy, and shown such a strength or will and determination in the cause of what he believed to be right, was leaving them perhaps for the remainder of his natural life. He thought that it would have been bettelifor a member of the Federa- tion to have made the presentation. He had not been a member for two or three years, simply because as a magistrate it might be that his action might be called into question upon licensing matters if he were in any sense a member of the Temperance Federation. But his sentiments upon that question had not altered one jot ; if anything they were stronger than ever. That was because he had other means of seeing the value of the work which Mr. Roberts had done. Many people had said to him, and people from whom he had been surprised to hear it, that they had no sym- pathy with the manner in which the work was done,and that they ought not to put on any disguise of any kind. His answer to that was that it was a much greater pity that the condition of things in Warrington made such a system necessary. (Applause.) The evidence in the Police Court at Warrington, which was afterwards pro- duced in tho court of Quarter Sessions at Liverpool showed that a condition of things existed in thetown which demanded exposure (hear, hear),and showed that the visits were quite justifiable. To a man holding the position which Mr. Roberts did, with his cultyre, the work must have been very painful, and it must have been &strong sense of duty which made him enter upon work so humiliating and so degrading to his finer feel- ings. It was nothing but a stern sense of conviction of duty to the town, he was quite positive, what induced him to take work of the chraracterlwhich he had done. It was a pity that there were not more who were willing to undertake at any rate some amount of espion- age of the.condition of things in the town. He did not want to say anything against the police, and he was not going to say a single word which could in any sense reflect upon the police. He believed that there was amongst the members of the force a very different spirit from what there was some years ago, and he would like to see them supported more than they were by the public sentiment of the town. (Hear, hear.) If those present only knew what some of them knew of the difficulties which were put in the way of the police, and the sort of indirect kind of hints given to them that they might just AP well let things alone, they would not be surprised that they were not acting as strongly as they might do. Howiever, he believed that they had turned over a new leaf in the town, and this was a direct result of Mr. Roberts' action at the licensing sessions. The manner in which the general licensing busihess was conducted was better than it was a short time ago. There was no doubt that the houses were better looked after, and that thee was a general improvement both in the character of the managers and the way in which the heuses were con- ducted, upon what had been the case tor a number of years past. He was satisfied in his own mind that if the police knew of any breach of the law they would do all that was'possible to expose and punish it. .That condition of things was owing to the single action of Mr. Robert's more than any other cause. (Applause.) Addressing the Rev. D. W. Roberts, Councillor Roberts said that he was leaving them, and certainly they would miss him in more ways than one. They would miss one who was a Nonconformist—one of themselves. They would miss him still more as a temperance man, a man who they knew would not shrink from any cause which he con- sciously believed to be the right canse.The Master whom he tried to serve would be with him wherever he went, and he Would have the satisfaction of knowing that in Warrington he had tried to do something for his fellow. men. He had very great pleasure in handing him the puree. (Applause.) The Rev. D. W. ROBERTS , in accepting the purse thanked the donors fot their gifts. He said that it was a source of pleasure to him to know that he had done something which had been well thought of by his tem- perance friends. It had caused him a great deal of labour and a great deal of anxiety to do the little he had done in Warrington, but he could assure them that he really did it from conscientious reasods. He had been a total abstainer from birth, never having tasted intoxicating drink in any form whatever, and in furthering the temper- ance caus^, he was willing to take any risk whatever. He was prepared to do his duty to assist in freeing his fellnweenintrymen.f rem the thraldom of str.- ng drink —(apphuse)--and if they did not do it as ministers of relilion who would do it? Since the Brewster Sessions he had watched carefully, although he had not done what he had done previously, and he still said that things in this town were not as they should be by a very long way. There were still houses in the town which were not conducted as they ought to be, and at which the same things were carried on as was brought before the last Brewster Sessions. He thanked them all present for the kindness fflnd sympathy they had shown to him at that time. It was a heavy blow' to him to give up his pastorate at Golborne-st., but he had been told by two medical men that it was absolutely necessary that he

should have complete rest for three months at least. He had made a great number of friends in Warrington, sad he deeply regretted having to leave them. He thanked Mr. Yonge and the other ministers for the valued ser- vices and good counsel they had always given him, and also Mr. William Roberts for the trouble he had taken in getting the presentation up. He hoped that in a few months be would be a new man, and that he would be able to do good work for his fellow-men. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Rumex said that he could not allow that occasion to pass without saying one or two words. After what Mr. Roberts had done, he deserved the utmost sympathy of every right-minded man in the town. The temperance cause in Warrington had been advanced very much by theaction of Mr. Roberts. (Applause.) It was a cause of great gratification, and he was thankful to God that in His providence, Mr. Roberts had been brought to Warrington. If Mr. Roberts had done nothing else in Warrington than what ,pe had done in connection with the temperance cause and in exposing the drink traffic it was worth the three years he had spent in the town. He hoped that when he was restored to health he would continue his work with still greater usefulness. It was a source of great pleasure to him that he was present at that meeting. (Hear, hear) Mr. J. C. DALToie said that as a Catholic total abstainer he thanked Mr. Roberts on behalf of some of the poor people, for • the energy he had displayed in the removal of certain temptations from public houses. He must say that the dissenting body was notorious for loyalty to the temperance cause, and he felt certain that whatever differences there were be- tween the Catholics, Protestants,church people,and Non- conformists, there was one plank upon which they could stand and that was upon the temperance platform, This was the plank upon which all religions could join to re- claim men and women from drunkenness. He hoped Mr. Roberts would speedily be restored to health and strength and thus be able to continue the good work he had been doing. (Hear, hear,) The Rev. E. T. REED said that he had been associated very closely with the Rev. D. 1)V. Roberts in connection with the Christian Endeavour, an l he ceuld bear testi- mony to the energy with whicfl he worked for that society, as well as for the temperance cause. It was his desire to wish him God speed, and he trusted that in God's good providence he would soon he restored. He would no doubt be the better for his present suffering. He had no doubt that he would be able to do even more useful work than he had done at Warrington. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. R. STOREY said that from many sources he had heard expressions of regard for Mr. Roberts, men whose judgement was worth having. There was no doubt that the worry and the storm that he raised at the last Brewster sessions had a great deal to do with his present ill-health. He had acted with great heroism,and he deserved ttanks of every right thinking Man. Mr. BORELAND wished as a friendly stranger to say a few words. He was present during the examination and chief crass-examination of Mr. Roberts at the Brewster Qusrter Sessions, and it was the apinion nf the counsel and of everybody at the court that Mr. Roberts had borne himself nobly and in a highly 'satisfactory man- ner. (Applause.) Miss DUTTON said that she was glad to be able to say how she admired the moral courage of Mr. Roberts. She was sorry that she had not been present the whole of the meeting, as she had been unexpectedly detained. She was however glad that she could be present a short time. (Hear, hear). The Rev. Join. YONGE said that he would like to call attention to certain members of the Bench. It was their duty to be present when licensing cases were brought forward. He did not consider that they had done their duty in a certain application which had been recently made to re-build a public-house. He thought they had a right to know where they were on that occa- sion. Be would, however, like to say that those re- marks did not apply to the magistrate present. That gentleman had upheld his principles nobly, and he wished that all the others were like him. (Hear, hear). This concluded the special business, and a private meeting of the committee was afterwards held.

div.head: IS THE STEA.M ItAILWAYDOOMED ?
div.p: IS THE STEA.M ItAILWAYDOOMED ?

There are comparatively few people now living who can remember the time before steam railways were, and in fi few years it may safely be predicted that there will not be a human being alive who has never seen or trav- elled by the iron road. The nineteenth century will doubtless be known to posterity as the Railway Age. The year 1830 saw the first practical attempt at the modern railway system when the Liverpool and Man- chester Railway was inaugurated and entered upon its advanturous career. Since then, railways have sprung up on all sides till the metal lines now lie like gridirons over all civilised countries.

But steam railways are not immortal. Dike all human vanities they endure but for a season. Already there are signs of a change for some safer and quicker means of transportation, and prophets have arisen who warn us that steam power has nearly reached its culmination, and that the steam locomotive will soon be a thing of the past. Electric locomotives are already in practical use and the electric trolley system is gaining ground where- ever it has been tried. We are asiured that the Ameri- can Railway Companies are experiencing severe compe- tition from this quarter, and their diminishing profits testify to the popularity of the new rival. So great has been the success of " the blithe little trolley" in America that in many of the larger cities it has completely captured the cheap transportation field, and that, too, within a very brief period. That it is mere economical than tramways, the following state- ment of the working expenses for a month of tho two systems over The as me track seems to prove. The tram ways employed 450 horses, wihch consumed 94tons of cut hay, about B,ooolbs. feed, and two tons of straw. This, with shoeing cost the company about 4,500 dots. Against this the coal consumed in the same period for electrical maintenance cost 285 dollars, or a clear saving by the trolley of 3,915 dollars. On an average 80 men were employed around the stables and in the car sheds for looking after these 450 horses. For these the com- pany substitutes two or three electrical operatives, and saves about 5,000 dollars a month in expenses, besides anticipating a large augmentation of business. The machinery is so purely automatic and so easily manipulated that the material out of which drivers and conductors are made was worked over in a day into ' electric motor-men, who, instead of a wilder, found a far more tractable and manageable horse—one that went without whip, reins, or word of command; one that needed not to be put in or out, or changed for shorter or longer routes. Furthermore, the new steed not only guided but regulated itself, thus dispensing with a switchman ; and a horse that not only hauls, but obligingly lights and heats the cars as well.—" Science Siftings."

div.head: SUCKING EGGS.
div.p: SUCKING EGGS.

• 'You see, grandma," said a. hot-bed specimen of juvenile precocity, "that when I suck this egg, or,more properly speaking, when I extract the nutritive matter by a sudden and peculiar action of the muscles of the throat, I first made an incision in the apex, and theu a corresponding aperture in the base." "Mercy on me how things do change !" exclaimed the old lady, in such surprise that her old spectacles dropped off at the flish- ine of her almost sightless eyes ; " when I was a gal, all we did was to make a hole in each end and down it went. My stars ! this 'ere child hairat got long to live, I know."

--- THE ARMENIAN ATROCITIES.—POWERFUL SERMON BY THE REV. JOHN YONGE. Sir,—l own lam not much of a believer in the pro- ductions of the modern pulpit, delivered, as they generally are, by the help of notes on scraps of paper and manuscripts. The prominent way, however, in which you invited attention to the one in question induced me to read your report of it. I dare not, of course, question your editorial wisdom in describing it as a "poweiful sermon,"but I must humbly confess thatl it appeared to my uninipated mind more like a politica disquisition than a sermon. This, however, would be due to my infirmity in such matters. The sermon was admirably adapted to the introduction of the memorial which the good people of Wycliffe and their pastor were about to forward to the Foreign Secre- tary anent the atrocities in Armenia. I must, however, qualify my praise by saying that I had an uncomf )rtable suspicion that both the sermon and the memorial were tainted, to some extent, by the bellicose spirit of the destroyer of the works of God. I thought I detected in both documents phrases that might be construed to mean that, peaceful measures failing, the good pastor of Wycliffe and his followers would be prepared to sanction and encourage the application of the machine gun and the bayonet to drive the Turks," bag and baggage,"out ' of Europe.lf such a spirit as this occupies a corner in the Christianity of Wycliffe chapel I am sorry ; such a spirit has absolutely no place in the Christianity of Christ. That meek and lowly One enjoined his disciples to love their enemies. to do good to them that hated them, and to pray tor those who persecuted them ; and his whole life was a practical carrying out ef this blessed teaching. When he was reviled he reviled not again, and the awful atrocity of his cruel death by the Roman soldiers and his own countrymen only brought from his dying lips the touching prayer, brimful of love and tenderness for his enemies." Father, forgive them for they know not what

they do." Armenia is a long way off, and it is not in human nature to feel very keenly for wrongs we cannot see. But are there not many wrongs and mach suffering at home that call loudly for the prayers and efforts of all who love their fellow men. At the present moment many thousands, if not millions, of our fellow countrymen and their families are trembling on the verge of starvation through circumstances over which they have no control. As I have not seen any big posters or press reports of their alms-doing for the oppressed and suffering people I suppose I may infer that the pastor of Wycliffe and his people have not felt called upon to interest them- selves in the matter. Mr. Yonge's reference toMr. Gladstone was rather an unfortunate one. That distinguished Liberal patriot during his long tenure of office involved this country in an enormousless of blood and treasure, and even his admirers will hardly venture to say that his wars were always waged on behalf of the oppressed. The last cam- paign in Egypt, may, I think, be taken as a not unfair ' sample of the commercial and aggressive spirit which distinguished some of them at least. The wholesale slaughter of brave men badly armed and without dis- cipline by the deadly weapons of well-trained Christian soldiers, was not inflicted because they had committed atrocities upon other people. No,Alesandria was burned by English shells, and thousands of the Egyptian peo- ple murdered in that campaign because Mr. Gladstone and his Cabinet would have it so in the intereAs of British and F6rfitig,nl money lenders !—Yeurs truly, PEaCE AT ANY PRICE.

SOCIALISM. AND REPUDIATION. Sir,—l see we have " a fresh hand at the bellows " and, as a conseqaence, more wind. Your corres,Dond- ent, 3. Tungate, poses as an historian with the air of one having sole possession of the key to Rnglish his- tory ; with quite unusual powers for its interpretation. "We can trace historically," says this gentleman, "that in early times when agriculture was the chief industry of this country, those willing to work had the opportu- nity to work." Then we are told in mournful numbers that "the willing worker to-day is denied that privi- lege." Well,and who denies this privilege to the willing worker of to-day? Other willing workers who snap up every job that opens at starvation prices ! And how came these starvation prices to rule ? By the "willing worker" being also a far ton willing re-producer of his species! The " willing worker "has not yet learned to follow Nature's plan of regulating the population to the food supply. No scheme of public polity is worth a rap unless it has this principle as a basis. The wide adop- tion of it would go far towards removing the deep us- gradation of our present social arrangement. But this "limiting the output" demands a certain amount of personal self-saerifice ; and the "willing wcrker " pre- fers to seek the cause, and impute the blame elsewhere than in himself. Then we have much talk about" the neople" who were robbed of the land, Sze. Then let us "who are the people" ? Socialistically " the people', are the great family of Lacklands. while the robbers are the few !hut inuq Indlords and land- holders! Now, the Lacklands never had the land, and it is proverbially difficult to rob allighlandman of his breeches. Socialists seem to be mad on the land qur lion. They appear to entertain the pleasing delusion that if you turn a man, with a spade, loose mum an acre of ground he can support himself ! Well ! if the Socialistic leaders were compelled to " spade" thus instead of spouting thus we Should have less froth and more useful members of society, and an instance of how soon their Socialism would evaporate under the test of the practical application of their own principles. Then we have the proposed repudiation of the National Debt. Now this great debt was incurred to defend the lives and liberties of Britain. It is plainly upon the hocks that, had not this money been so borrowed and so applied, these frothy orators and inconsiderate scribblers would not have had the chance of uttering their socialistic audi- ties. If they wish to learn from practical experience how much they are indebted to this debt for the safe exercise of this much abused privilege of aeditious utter- ance—let them step ever to Germany or France and try the game on there. I imagine their shrift would be a short one, " They manage these things better in France." I have seen it asserted somewhere that confusion of languages is indicative of confusion of thought. What then must be the state of the mind which elaborated this precious fif ntPnce?"When the workers begin to think for themselves and get rid of the superstition and cant. then there willbe an need of keeping an army of hired assassins. to butcher those who demand their rights." This reminds one of the Judge's exhortation to the dunk- stealer. " God has given you a good measure of ability, instead of avii,ch you go about the country stealing &VW ! Our J. Tungate does not tell us how being free from " the " superstition and cant (of Social- ise) ?) would render a standing army unnecessary. and how it Would mitigate the greed for terri- torial acquisition in foreign nations and turn their minds to thoughts of peace. The " army of hired agslassins " have other duties to perform besides that of keeping the Socialist from insist- ing too forcibly upon their" right " to that which doesn't belong to them. "The land for the people "! Be aH means, let them have it—at lowest market price. And, when " they" have got it, let them he bound to work it—Socialistically—without capital. I precdict that these theoretical agrculturalists, if they grew nothing else, would themselves quickly develop into individualists and be disgusted with Socialism. I am not an extensive land owner myself ; hut have about as much as will serve for decent interment ; and I am sure risme of my Socialist frienas would begrudge ale this much ! Nay, rather would some of them wish me a speedy entrance into mine inheritance ! If we are to have reform of the many evils of our present social arrangement, by all means let them be honest ones—something we can look hack upon unre- grettfully and with a clear conscience.—Yours. Aen.. TONY LUMBKIN.

Mr. W. Saunders, the Liberal member for the Wal- worth division of Newington, died on Wednesday, after a prolonged illness. At the election in 1892 Mr. Saunders won the seat from the former Conservative member, Major Isaacs, by 2,514 votes to 2,218.
