div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

EARLESTOWN 'WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. From an advertisement in another column, it will be seen that the anniversary services in connection with the above school will be held in the chapel on Sunday the 12th inst. There will be special sermons morning and evening, and in the afternoon the choir and children will give a sacred cantata" Two Seasons." 'the band of the Earlestown Orchestral Society will be present throughout the day, and accompanying the various hymns, and also the cantata. The services are in aid of the Sunday schools, which are well worthy of support. EARLESTOWN DISTRICT SCHOOL. A meeting of the managers of the above school was held on Thursday afternoon for the purpose of electing two managers to fill vacancies caused by the retirement of Messrs. T. Latimer and T. A. rimblett. who, however, offered themselves for re-election. After the votes had been counted it was found that Mr. John Robinson, mine manager, Market-street, Earlestown, and Mr. George Clarke, surveyor, Newton, had been elected by a large majority. The election caused some excitement amongst those more intimately connected with the school, but the result was received with satis- faction. MINSTREL ENTERTAINMENT AT HAYDOCK

On Monday evening an entertainment was given in the Llaydock National Schools, by the St. James' Amateur Minstrels, in aid of the funds of the St. James' Church. Mr. W. S. Barrett, J.P., presided, and the room was packed with a most appreciative audience. In addition to one or two selections, well played by the band, the programme consisted of the usual type of nigger songs and choruses, in- cluding a stump speech by Mr. J. Clare,who dilated on' The Ship Canal." Mr. J. W. Puller officiated as interlocutor,and Mr. A.Bradshaw,as accompanist. The entertainment was brought to a close by a farce, entitled "The rival dummies," in which the troupe took part. GOOD TEMPLARS. The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earlestown on Monday evening. Bro. J. Miller C.T. presided, and there was a large attend- ance of members. One candidate was initiated and one was proposed for membership. An invitation to entertain the Hope of Vulcan lodge on Thursday was accepted. It was also decided to invite the' Pembroke Lodge, Liverpool to visit the Hope of Earlestown lodge during the quarter. Bro. E. New- man read circulars from the District lodge in which : it was stated that the next session of the Grand Lodge wouid be held in this district. It was re- solved by standing vote to tender a yore of con- dolence, to Bro. Barker, the secretary of the lodge, in his recent bereavement. A committee was ap- pointed to draw up the programme for the ensuing quarter,after which the officers were elected for the quarter,and will be duly installed next week. THE WHITSUNTIDE DEMONSTRATIONS. The first meeting in connection with the annual Sunday school demonstration was held in the Baptist Schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. P. Parr presided, and delegates were present from the Wesleyans, Baptists, Primitive Methodists and Salvation Army. Mr. John Taylor was appointed secretary. It was decided to hold a demonstration of Sunday schools on Whit Monday, as in previous years. The route was fixed to be that followed last year. Mr. T. Clare was chosen to conduct the singing. Messrs. Clare, Dickens and Harvey were I selected to take in hand the training of the children for singing. It was decided that the ministers of the different denominations should head the pro- cession, instead of each heading their own school, as formerly. Two bands are to be employed, and tenders have been sent out. The next meeting is for the purpose of balloting for positions, and will be held on Friday next, in the Primitive Methodist Infant Schoolroom. EMMANUEL CHURCH, WARGRAVE. The annual services on behalf of the Wargrave Vulcan schools were held on Sunday in the above church. There were very fair congregations at the morning and evening services, the morning service being conducted by the Rev. J. M. Courtenav, BA., I vicar of Parr Mounz, and the evening by the Rev. M. F. B. Binney, M.A., vicar of Sutton, both gentlemen- I preaching appropriate sermons. The school chil- dren were arranged in the body of the church, and I sang the hymns which were of an appropriate char- acter, their training having been undertaken by Mr. ft. Chandley. In the afternoon, an organ recital and musical service was given by the organist, Mr. E. Leyland and choir, before a large audience, the following programme being exceptionally well sub- mitted :--Urgan," Romance Saris Paroles;" duet and chorus," I waited for the Lord," Misses Roberts and Corlett ; recitation, " Behold," air, "The trumpet shall sound," Mr. George Wright; organ "Fanfare:" solo," The city beautiful," Miss A. Molyneux; recita- tion "And God created man,"air," In native worth," Mr. James Nichols ; solo " Calvary," Miss K. C. Corlett ; organ, a, " Minuet" (Samson), b," The ' pilgrim's song of hope:" recitation "I go on my way," air " For the mountains," Mr. W. H. Kay; I organ," Triumphal March," air "Honour and Arnie," Mr. C. H. Lea ; Chorus "Worthy is the Lamb," The collections throughout the day amounted to £l6 6s. 7d.. EIRLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODISTS. The annual services in aid of the Sunday Schools attached to the Earlestown Primitive Methodist chapel, were held on Sunday in the schoolroom. The morning and evening services were conducted by the Rev. T. Richards, of Crewe, who preached appropriate and instructive sermons to large con- gregations. The school children sang suitable hymns under the conductorship of Mr E. Dickens. In the afternoon the choir and scholars rendered in an excellent manner, the sacred cantata, "Tee Ruler's' Daughter." The connective readings were given by Mr. T. °rewind, Mr. W. Austin, accompanied, and the choir was conducted by Mr. E. Dickens. The various choruses, quartettes, &c., were very effec- tively sung, the time being exceptionally well kept. The principal singers were Messrs. R. S;eroston, F. Tomtits, C. Dickens, P. Tomlinson and Joseph Aus- tin, Mesdames Rawlins and orraand, Misses. B. L. and A. Dickens, Baxter, Stronach and Tombs. Oa Monday evening a lectur was given in the schoel- room by the Rev. T. Richards nn " Portraits and characters." Mr. E. J. George presided, and there was a very large audience, The lecture was of a most interesting and ineflueLiVe character, and at the close a vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer. The collections during the whole of the services in ' aid of the Sunday school funds, amounted to £36 16s, 1.0.G.T. (EBENEZER, LODGE). 1 The usual session of the Earlestown Ebenezer lodge was held in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday night. The session was presided over by Bro. W.J. Taylor, C.T., and there was a good attendance of members and friends. Bro. W. J. Taylor, L.D.. read the digest of the South West Lancashire district lodge to be held in the Wesley Hall, Soho-street, on ; Saturday May 4th. Bro. A. Morris proposed the Ifollowing resolution :—" That this society, the ' Earlestown Ebenezer lodge records its thanks to her Majesty's Government for introducing into the House of Commons the Intoxicating Liquor Traffic Local Control Bill, a measure deeply affecting the well-being of the country and calculated if put in operation to secure a great diminution of the evils resulting from intemperance, and this meeting urges the Government to put forth its full power to I ensure the passing of the Bill into law ; and that copies be forwarded to the Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequor, and also to the mem- ber for the Newton division, urging them to sup- port and secure its passage into la 77 during the present session of Parliament." the resolution was unanimously adopted. Afrer this the programme was gone through,Broe.J.Willis,and I.Dickson being responsible, and it was a financial success. Inter- esting songs and recitations were also given by various brothers and sisters. OLD FOLK'S TREAT AT HAYDOCK. The annual treat to the old people of Haydock was held in the National Schoolroom, Ifaydock, on Wednesday evening. Invitations were issued to all old people of 00 years of age and upwards, and a large number put in an appearance at the appointed time, wagonettes and other vehicles being used to convey those unable to walk, and those residing at a distance, to the schoolroom. An excellent sub- stantial meat tea was provided, the wants of the old people being ministered to by a number of young ladies. The arrangements were well carried out by a committee consisting of Messrs. A. H. L Evans (chairman), G Weldon (secretary), R. Brad- shaw. J. Turton, C. Derbyshire, .1. Jackson, E. Jack- son, J. Taylor, W. Cawley, S. Aspinall, E. Leyland, Revs. C. E. Bowdon, J. Andrews, J. 11. Ridette and Father Moore. After tea the subsequent proceed- ings were presided over by Mr. A. H. L. Evans,sup- Iported by the Revs. C. E. Bowdon and J. Andrews, Messrs. W. S. Barrett and J. Fairhurst, by whom short addresses were given. An entertainment was also given by St. James' Amateur Ministrels, the programme Consisting of the usual nigger songs and sketches, and a farce entitled "The rival dummies." Several recitations were also given by Mr. Schofield. Before leaving the old people were presented with tea, tobacco and fruit.
THE EXAMINER. 'SATURDAY, MAY 4, 1895

div.head: WESLEYAN lIETHDIST HOME MISSION
div.p: WESLEYAN lIETHDIST HOME MISSION
ANNIVERSA.TLY.

The annual home missionary sermons were held at the Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday, when the pul- pit was occupied by the Rev. J. W. Silcox of Widnes. On Wednesday evening the annual public meeting was held in the chapel, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., and there were also present, the Revs. J. Kirtlan, G. D. Mason, and D. L. Pawson, Miss B. Dutton, and Sister Daisy (Manchester Mission). The Rev. J. KIRTIAN read the home missionary report for the past year which was of a very encouraging char- acter. He stated that the total contribution: for the Warrington circuit amounted to £74 153. sd. which was an increase upon the previous year. The yearly collec- tions from the classes equalled £l6, and the congrega- tional collections realised £26 is. The collections at the public meetings amounted to £7 2s. 9d., and one-third lof the juvenile association offerings equalled £2l 81. 9d. The CHAIRMAN said that he thought it was important to have meetings of that sort, as information was given to those who would perhaps not otherwise know much about these matters. To his mind, he thought that the home missions had a very much stronger claim than the foreign missions. He had learned early that charity began at home, and he did not think that they could shut their eyes to the fact that there was a vast amount of squalor, misery, and wretchedness in their midst,even in small places like Warrington. Tf is was very • depressing, and he was quite sure that their brethren and sisters who worked the various missions often had their hearts pained, very deeply pained, with sights they saw. They wanted to upraise the world, and one of the great- est fulcrums of to-day was the gospel. There was no doubt Watt f they were to have the world better, it was not by the nostrums they saw in the newspapers, but it was the gospel of the blessed God which would upraise the world. The world was full of so-called socialism and he heartily endorsed certain points, as it showed that there was a great feeling in the midst of the public to get to a better position in life, but he maintained that the disposition and social position of the people would be elevated by their accepting the simple truth of the gospel. Sister DAISY then addressed the meeting, and gave a very interesting account of her work in connection with the Manchester Mission. She said that the people among whom she worked were very poor, and the work she did was real home work, as she visited the poor people aom house to house. The sisters could do work which their br )thers could not do,as they could sit in the houses with the mothers and show them the simple gospel,and a great amount of good work was done in this manner. There were six sisters in connec- tion with the mission, and it would therefore be seen , that they had plenty of work to do. Besides the sisters, 1 there was a noble band of women who during their spare time did work for their Master. She gave numerous anecdotes in connection with the mission, and her account was listened to with great interest.. The Rev. D. L. PawsoN said that there was a home in connection with the Manchester mission to shelter 50 men, and there was also a labour yard where they could earn an honest penny. They were trying to maintain and renew the manhood in them by allowing them to earn enough for their board and lodging. Mr. Pawson then proceeded to give the history of the formation of the Central Mission in Manchester. He said that the usual congregation on a Sunday night at the old Oldham- street Chapel was 80 or 90,but 1,500 was now considered a very ordinary number at the Cential Hall on Sunday night. The membership of Oldham-street Chapel at the last quarter before it was changed into the Central Hall was only 46, and two on trial. Now there were no fewer than 700 full members and 250 on trial. This was exclusive of a large number in connec- tion with the Free Trade Hall services. He contended that this wonderful change was owing to the bright ser- vices, and having a free hand. He did not see why the some result should not happen in Bold-street. He then gave an interesting episode in connection with the Central Hall meetings. During the evening Mr. Levi Richardson sang "The valley of shadows," and Miss Bessie Dutton recited " The song of the shirt," by Tom flood. A vote of thanks proposed by the Rev. J. Kirtlan, seconded by the Rev. G. D. Mason, was accorded to the Chairman and deputation for their presence that night, and the meeting was closed by the pronouhcing of the benediction. -

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE
ASSOCIATION.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the Newton Division Conserva- tive Association was held on Saturday after- noon in the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. H. Pearson, chairman of the council, and amongst those present were the Hon T. W. Legh, M.P., Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton, Colonel Richard Pilkington, Mr. F. Stapleton-Bretherton, M. C. B. F. Borron, Mr. RobertStone,Mr. William Richardson, Mr. R. W. Francomb,Mr. T. H. Sutton, Mr. T. J. Gilles- pie, Mr. James Smith, Mr. W. Valiant, Mr. W. Holland (hon. sec.). Mr. T. Crompton, Mr. Wyntham Smith and Canon Penhryn. The Chairman moved " That this meeting begs to thank the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., for his past services as representative of the Newton Division in Parliament, and sincerely assures him of continued confidence and support.' (Applause.)—Mr. F.Stepleton-Bretherton seconded the reselution,which was carried with acclama- tion. The Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., in replying said politics in the Newton Division had been enlivened by the pre- sence of a possible opponent to himself. This gentleman he understood, had not yet made up his mind whether he was going to fight or not. At present he was occu- pied in being trotted round the political ring under the guidance and tuition of an experienced master, to the edification of the local Liberate. (Laughter.) As they did not know whether lie would have the courage to contest the seat, or whether he would adopt a more prudent course and take warning by the sad fate which had befallen not only previous Radical candidates in that divisicn, but most of the Government candidates at the recent by—sleetions, they might leave him in peace. (Laughter and applause.) When he (the speaker) ad- dressed the association last year he pointed out that the present Government had only passed one measure of any importence—the Parish Councils Bill. On the spur of the inoment he could not recollect any important measure they had passed since, or seen very much pros- pect of their pagsing anythine, of any importance during the present session, with the exceptien, possibly, of the Factories arid Workshops Bi!l, to one porti...n of which there was strong and united oppositien from both masters and men in the Newton division. (Hear, hear). After all, what chance was there of the Government , passing any measure of importance when they had , announced that 'their policy consisted in " plough- ing the sands" and " filling up the cup "—a cup which decidedly looked as if it posses- sed no bottom at all. (" Hear, hear," and laughter). With their ridiculous majority, it was preposterous, almost an outrage, for the Government to attempt to pass Such a measure as the Welsh C'ntrch Disestablish- ment Bill. (Rear, hear.) That TheaSefe Might be objected to on many grounds, but what he particularly objected to was the nauseous and hypocritical declaration that it was brought in for the good of the church—as if the enemies of the Church were better able to judge of what was good for the Church than churchmen them- selves. The contention that the endowments of the Church were unnecessary, and did harm, and ought to be taken away, and that Nonconfermist endowments I ought to be left, was gross hyprocrisy, and only on a par with the statement that people who left money to the Church hundreds of years ago would be perfectly content if they were living now to see it devoted to baths and wash houses. (Hear, hear.) Nobody expected, either, that the Local Veto Bill would team Sir William Harcourt and his friends might talk very big and say they intended to get it through the second rrading before Whit Sunday, but the vast majority of the House of Commons were absolutely con- vinced that it would not pass, and was not meant to pas., and many Radicals would be exceedingly sorry if, by any accident, it was passed. (Hear, hear ) Speak- ing of the Indian cotton duties, Mr. Legh said be voted against the imposition of the duties because he non,idered it very unfair that the trade of Lancashire should alone bear the burden of , making UP the deficiencies in the Indian finances. (Hear, hear.) After a reference to foreign questions,Mr.Legh, in concluding, repudiated the assertion that serious differences had arisen between the Conservative and Liberal Unionist parties, and said so long as justice and honesty prevailed in polities those parties would stand shoulder to shoulder in protection of their Church, their constitution, and their empire. (Applause.) The Chairman then read letters apologising for ab- sence, from a number of gentlemen, after which he said he was sorry to say that during the last few months they had lost good friends, Mr. Ansom, who had for many years been chairman of the polling district, and Mr. Joseph D.lvies, of Warrington. They would all keow the services rendered by those gentlemen and he (the chairman) wished to propose a vote of condolence to the families, Mr. Holland Owen read the report, claiming a gain of 130 for the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists, on the registration court. The streasurer'a report was sub- mitted and passed. Votes of thanks having been passed. Messrs. Voisey and Worthington and Mr. Barton were elected auditors. Colonel Richard Pilkington (St. Helens) proposed a vote condemning the policy of the question. Ile said that the Unionist alliance was as strong as ever, though there might have been local splits. Il.ferring to Irish members and the Welsh members, Mr. Pilkington said the Home Rule Bill for Ireland and the cliseuablishinent of the four dioceses of the English Church in Wales were but the price of the votes of the Irish and Welsh mem- bers to suPport the Government. Mr. Grimke Drayton secereied the resolution. Canon Penrhyn, and Alderman Prem./mai, LP., of Warrington, supporting, and it was carried. This concluded the public

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
(BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR.)

I am pleased to find that, the Liberals of this division are at last stirring themselves. The can- didate, Mr. Moon, addressed an enthusiastic gather- ing at Elaydock, and laid his views before that portion of his constituents. The result was that he was unanimously accepted, and the meeting then set about electing a working committee. They are now fairly on the way, and with their organization in good working order, they will pro- bably be able to put that portion of the division, in good fighting condition.

I see the Conservatives had their annual day out last Saturday at Newton, when the rank and file of the party gathered from all parts of the division to listen to an address from the member, Mr. Legh. The hon. gentleman prefaced his remarks by an allusion to the introduction into the division of a Liberal candidates. Mr. Legh waxed witty over ' the matter, and his remarks would tend to convey to the uninitiated the idea that the division was impregnable,and it was utterly useless for anybody to attempt to oust him from the seat. He also tried to be contemptuous by saying that he would leave the benighted candidate in peace. That is all that is required. A peaceful but not a passive istrugele is what the Liberals must see to, and if the efforts of the Government are successful with the one man one vote question, I am inclined to think that Mr. Legh and his supporters will sing an altogether different time at the next election. In- dependent of that the case is not an hopeless one by any means, and with perfect organisation a difficult aspect-can be put on the result of the next contest.

The local festival in connection with the corona- tion of the May Queen is fast approaching, in fact it will take place next week,aud great preparations are being made for ensuring its success. The great- est factor towards this end, however, is a fine day, for without this all the efforts of the workers will

have gone for naught. The idea with which the affair was first started was the raising of funds to- wards the erection of public swimming baths. That was before the introduction of the Parish Council Act. Under this Act our representatives on the District Council can adopt the Public Baths and Wash houses Act, and erect swimming baths if re- quired. I have never heard the question men- tioned on the Council, but I supposed when they they have got over their internal squabbles,we shall probably hear of something being done for the pub- lic good. Public baths would do a sight more good than ornamental lamps.

div.head: INDUCTION OF CHURCHWARDENS AT WARRINUTON.
div.p: INDUCTION OF CHURCHWARDENS AT WARRINUTON.

• AN ARCHDEA2ON ON CHURCH FINANCES. The Ven. Archdeacon Taylor attended at the Warring- ton Parish Church on Wednesday for the purpose of admitting into office the churchwardens who were elected at the recent vestry meetings in the Rural Deanery of Winwick. In addition to the wardens,there were present several of the local clergy, including the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, H. V. Pigot, G. B. Thurston, A. A. Markham, H. M. R. Hutt, J. Davies, J. Carson,W. Tewnsend H. R. Wilde, Sze. Addressing the wardens, the Archdeacon thanked them for filling up and sending to him the usual returns. From the answers given to the question whether any Easter offertory was given to the clergy, he found that there was a growing tendency to revive the ancient custom of giving Easter offerings to the clergy. Be very much sympathised with that and had done so for many years, and especially of late years, because of the diminished incomes of the clergy resulting from various causes. These causes in- cluded a diminution in the value of the tithes, and the practical abolition or at all events the steady diminution of seat rents and the subetitution of weekly offertories. The incomes of the clergy had in consequence very considerably diminished and an Easter offertory presented to the minister was a very nice, simple, inexpensive, unostentatious, un- obstrusive, and may be effectual way of to some extent repairing the deficiency. It came from the whole con- gregation, there was no personal canvas, but in a quiet way the humble widow could give her mite and the mil- lionaire could give his large donation if he liked, and it presented a nice orderly reverent and religious way of making up:the ministers' income. He was glad to find the practice was largely on the increase,and he should be glai to see it adopted all through the diocese. He did not suppose that at present more than 50 out of the 102 churches in his archdeaeonry followed the custom, and where the practice had not been adopted lie would like to respectfully press upon the wardens the consideration of the matter. Another question to which replies :had been obtained was as to the source of the funds for maintaining the Church, and the answer generally was from the weekly offertory. The weekly offertory was a new thing. When he began his ministry there was no such thing as a weekly offertory for church expenses. It began in part owing to the aholitipn of the church rate and had gone on owing to the practical abolition of seat rents. His experience was that these weekly offertories had a good effect one way, but they had an injurious effect another. They did not always tend to increase the funds of the church. What- ever advantages a free church might have—and it had great advantages—financially it was not generally a success. Numerically it was a success, but financially a failure or rather not a great success. The Yen. Arch- deacon reminded the wardens that they represented the people, were the guardians of the church, and the officers of the Bishop. As regarded the services of the church, they had no authority to interfere at all. They must look on, and if they found occasion, make a complaint by presentment. There were, however, no complaints. He would like to press upon the attention ot the wardens a sug- gestion which originated with the Rev. Canon Venables, that they slaould have a collection on some Sunday after Trinity -for the increase of the permanent endowment of the church. In twenty years' time, the endowment of the Church would have largely increased, and with very little effort indeed. He suggested that a 3 a simple means of increasing the permanent endowment of the church, unless it was already well endowed, and then they might give the collection to some poorer church. They might say that disestablishment and disendowment might come on. Well, let them wait till they came. Even if they did come, recent endowments would not be touched. Even the most advanced Radical proposal did not refer to recent endowments. In conclusion the Archdeacon wished the wardens health, haleph3ess, and comfort in the discharge of their duties for the next yeer.

, THE RECONSTITUTION OF THE TRUST. The two Bills dealing with the constitution of the Weaver Navigation Trust were again before the Com- mittee of the House of Commons on Monday. Mr. J. Stuart presided. Before the adjournment for the Easter holidays the Committee determined the constitution of : the Trast by putting its total number of members at 38, apportioned as follows :—Ten to the old trustees, twelve to the Cheshire County Council,fourteen to the tollpayers and one each to Northwich and Winsford, with the con- dition that as the representatives of the old trustees died out their places should be filled by members chosen by but nit necessarily belonging to the County Council. The Committee also expressed the opinion that not more than six members should be allowed to any one trading interest. The Committee at the same time decided as the surplus that a reserve fund of £25,000 should be created before any surplus went to the county, that until the fund reached £50,000 the surplus was to go—one-half to the fund and one-hall to the county, and that after that amount was reached the surplus should be allocated in the proportions of two-thirds to the county and one-third to the reserve fund. The Committee further decided that the reserve fund might he applied for improvements of the naviga- tion. They also resolved to consolidate the two Hills, and subsequently got from the House the necessary par- mission to do this. Mr. CriPPs, Q.C. (for the Salt Union), on the Commit- tee reassembling, said he was glad to say that counsel had consolidated these Bills as had been suggested by the Committee, and there was really ns,thin,g now to be done but to paaa the preamble of the Bill. The Chairman took itthat the preamble of the Amal- gamated Bill accommodated itself to the changed eir- enmstances, an#l that it had been approved by all the parties concern-d. Mr. Grippe said that was so. Tile Committee then passed the preamble of the Bill, ' and proceeded to go through the various clauses. On Clause 15 Mr. Cripps pointed out that there was some difference in the provision regarding representa- tion and the decision of the committee. The committee expressed the opinion that note more than six members should be allowed to any one trading interest, but when they Came to work out that they found that in making the representation in proportion to the contribution of toils it was difficult to reduce the representation of the Salt Union. They paid 63 per cent. of the tolls, and, therefore, thought they were desirous of carrying, oat as far as they couli the suggestions of the Committee, all the parties had agreed that the provision, as it now -,toncl. should be inserted in the Bill. The provision really worked out in this way. There were seven re- presentatives as regarded the Salt Union, 115 as re- garded other salt traders, 2.75 :as regarded chemicals, I'so as regarded pottery, and 1 as regarded the general traders. Mr. POTP, Q.C., for the Cheshire County Council, said that after discu•sion they had come to the conclusien that the proposed alteration from six to seven was not unreasonable, and they acquiesced in it. The altelation was agreed to. The rest of the Bill !IA Ving ',Pell gone through,it was ordered to be reported I to the House as amended.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

A RUNAWAY HORSE.—On Monday, the son of Mr. Hugh Darbyshire, Ship Croft, was driving a milk cart past the quarry near Appleton Hall, when the back-bone broke and the horse bolted. The youth stopped in the cart for some little time and at last jumped out unhurt, but the horse continued its wild career and knocked down a lamp-post near London Bridge. Near the Twenty-step Bridge, one of the shafts caught the para- pet and the horse was thrown down and captured close to the Post Office where it was released from the cart. The animal was badly cut, and three of the milk tankards were burst and the milk spilled. Fortunately no one was hurt,

log af the above was held in the Church !Zoom on M I day evening, the president (the Rev. H. C.R. Vernon),in the chair. The minutes of the previous meeting having been read and confirmed the Rev. H. The accountl(which had been audited gratuit- ously by Mr. Edwin Bradshaw, chartered accountant, Warrington),were presented and passed,there appearing a balance against the Institute of £9 odd, this being due to the fact that many of the honorary ;members and sub- scribers had during the past year given their donations towards the building fund of the Chub Rooms. HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL.-At the close of the usual week night service on Tuesday evening, an in- teresting addition was made by the presentation of a purse of money to Mr. and Mrs. J. Grounds, Chapel House, as a small token of esteem and an expression of good wishes on the part of the members of the church and congregation, on the occasion of their marriage. The presentation was made by the Pastor, the Rev. J. S. Hughes, in a few choice and humorous words, and Mr. Grounds suitably acknowledged the gift.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.—A most successful con- cert in concection with the above society was given in the Vi'eslevan School, making the second concert of the season. The room was comfortably filled, the audience evidently knowing a good thing, as most of them have attended the previous concerts. The concert opened with a chorus " How lovely are the messengers," which was rendered with good effect. Mr. A. Cavanagh next followed with the song " Nazareth," for which he was well applauded. Another chorus was followed by a clarionet solo by Mr. Horst, of Liverpool, which quite took the fancy of the audience, aud was deservedly encored. A quartette, "God is a Spirit," was sung by Mrs. Clarke, Miss E. Boardman, and Messrs. Seed and Ellison. Miss A. Richardson sang " Cleansing Fires " in a very taking manner and was wellreceived. Another chorus brought the first part of the concert to a close. The second part was more open and consisted of songs, clarionet solos,part songs. " Sweet and low " was first sung by the members ,and was very pretty, the parts being very nicely arranged. Mr. Horst again was en- cored for his clarionet solo, "Ernani." A most amusing trio "The three old maids of Lee," was given by Miss Kate Booth, Miss E. Pollit, and Miss M. Foster. By a very effective make-up, the backs of the young ladies were arranged so that with a grotesque mask attached to the back of the head,a very doleful looking trio faced the audience when the singers turned round. The rendi- tion of this piece was excellent and received an uproarious encore. Mr. A. Cavanagh next gave " Father O'Flynn " in a masterly style, and received a well merited encore. A feature of the programme was a choral fantasia by the Society, several old ballads being introduced in a very clever and taking manner, which pleased the audi- ence immensely. Mr. W. Ireland was in very good voice and his rendering of "Jack's Wedding," was re- warded by a hearty encore. Another amusing part song by the members, "The Tickling Trio," was sung with great gusto, and was demanded again. Miss Richard- son favoured the audience with a grand rendering of " Her lad across the sea." Mr. Cavanagh sang " Will 0' the Wisp "and a part song by the members" who will win " brought the programme to a close. Mr. John Newcombe, who conducted, is to be congratulated upon the manner in which he has brought the class out. Miss Mary Standish accompanied on the pianoforte. This concert will close the season, but •Secretary W. L. Wilkinson hopes to have a still stronger company together at the next re-union. I HAND OF HOPE Tee MEETINQ.—On Monday evening a , tea was given to the members of the St. Mary's Church I of England Temperance Society. Tea was held in the Infants' schoolroom and was well attended by the children and friends. A short meeting was afterwards I held, the evening throughout being much enjoyed. GREAT Settxxv SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the above Board was held in the Boardroom at the Schools, Great Sankey, on Tuesday afternoon, when there were present—Messrs. W. P. Skelton (chairman). Henry Bate, Joseph Wright, J. Fairclough, and Samuel Sutton (clerk).—The Clerk reported that there was h balance standing in the Treasurer's book to the favour of the Board of £43 12s. 9d. After the cheques had been paid very little money would be left in hand.—Mr. G. Clarke, the headmaster, reported as follows for the week ending April 27th :—On books 351, present 317, average 284-0, fees 15s. The fees for the past three weeks amounted to £2 3s. 2d. There was, Mr. Clarke added, much broken attendance, the average being lower than at that time last year. There were nine children absent through fever in their houses. Mr. Shearer had visited the schools, and had taken a list of the worst attenders. —On the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. Fair- dough, the Rev. E. S. Jackson was unanimously elected vice-chairman of the Board.—The Clerk said that the next business was the consideration of the question of the clerkship. He desired to make a short explanation with regard to his resignation. At the last meeting he spoke under, as they were aware, censiderable heat at what he fancied to be an insult. As they heard from the minutes he had just read,he referred to the fact that he hal applied for an increase of salary some years ago, which was not granted.At the last meeting he was asked to send ia a written resignation, but he had not done so for a simplereason, that influential friends had endea- voured to persuade him if possible to retain tine office. Of course it rested with them entirely. That was all he wished to say except that they should re-instate him in the office he honestly thought that considering he had served the Board for 11 years, and that in the earlier years following the Board's formation there was extra work to be done for which he never received an extra penny, he was entitled to some consideration. That was all he wished to say on the subject.—After a short diacussion it was decided to accept Mr. Sutton's resignation of the office of clerk.—This was all the business,

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
SERVICES FOR THE PEOPLE.

The last of the present series of People's Services was held on Sunday afternoon in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church, and WRS conducted by Mr. W. Hickman. There was a large attendance and the address was given by Mr. James Evans, who said he wished to speak to them about the words "Fear the Lord and serve Him." After referring to the circumstances in which thee words were uttered he proceeded to speak of " Character." Just as Samuel had from the earliest days of his child- hood been weaving character, so they in the loom of life were weaving their characters. They were needed to- day both in the church and in the world those who were endeavouring to live the life of Jesus Christ, which was the ideal life. There were some who would say the standard was too high to be reached, but the Saviour had bidden them to follow, and if they did they would gradually grow into it. He generally found that those who said the gospel was a failure had never experienced it and to such he would say "Try it," and if they did, he ventured to say they would find they had been ereatly mistaken. The great mistake made by the Israelites was in chonsing a king in preference to the leadership of God. As then, so to-day, when men threw over the Divine for the human, they made a great mistake. He then proceeded to speak of " Service " remarking that service could not be given acceptably to liod unless the servant were right with God. If they were anxious to do work for God, let them find the sphere of labour for which they were fitted, let them get in harmony with the mind of God and in harness for the work and they would find that him who honoured God, God would honour. Mr. W. Hickman then gave a short review of the work done, and announced that the People's Services would be discontinued until about the Ist Sunday in October, when be hoped that all who had helped to make the services successful and to whom they were greatly indebted, would recommence the work with renewed vigour,determined to achieve even greater success than they had done in the past. Several selec- tion were rendered in an excellent marner by the orchestral band which has throughout the services been under the efficient conductorship of Mr. F. Pendlebury, i and the singing of a hymn and the pronouncing of the benediction brought to a close a series of services which have deservedly gained the reputation of being both pleasing and profitable.
WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.

On Sunday the anniversary of the Wycliffe Sunday School was celebrated. There were splendid congrega- tions both morning and evening, when the preacher on both occasions was the Rev. John Yonge (pastor), who delivered excellent discourses. In the morning the rev. gentleman preached specially for children and he took as his text Psalm 148, parts of the 12th and 13th verse., " And children,let them praise the name of the Lord." Upon these words Mr. Yonge spoke with great emphasis,

and made many earnest exhortations to the children to "be truthful in all things." The evening's service was no less interesting, the words of the text being " And He blessed Joseph, and said, God before whom my fathers Abraham and Jsaac did walk, the God which red me all my life long unto this day,.the Angel which redeemed me from all evil,bless the lads." Genesis, chapter 48, verses 15 and 16. The sermon on these words was characterised by great earnestness and feeling, and it can be said with all truthfulness that it was listened to with great intent- ness, both by young men, for whom it was intended,and also by their seniors. On the same day the previous year the collections an behalf of the school funds realized £43, while on Sunday £4O was received, but this is expected to be so augmented that the odd £3 will be reached and even surpassed. In the afternoon the church was completely crowded, when a cantata was given entitled" Under the Psalnastor the Jewish Flower Feast." This cantata is intended to illustrate the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles, or Harvest Festival, and to present a view of the teachings of the praphet Ezra. It is essentially a service of song consist- ing of solos, duets, quartettes and choruses, the whole forming a melodious piece. The characters were, Ezra, Mr. W. H. Wallington (bass) ; Joshus, Mr. Arthur Griffiths (tenor) ; Mixiam, Mrs. Pearson (soprano) ; Zillah, Miss F. Booth (contralto). Each took his :or her part with remarkable success and in the quartettes the four voices blended beautifully and were la great attraction. Mrs. Gleave also gave valuable• assistance in the quartettes and the efforts of every singer met with frequent ap- plause, Mrs. Pearson especially distlnouished herself in the solo " We remembered the graves of our fathers," and Miss Booth, in" 0 Lord, the harvest of the year," found a selection specially adapted to her voice, and she made an excellent use of her opportunity. Mr. Griffith's rich tenor voice was heard to great advantage in the opening solo, and there was no doubt as to its apprecia- tion by the audience. Mr. Wallington,as usual,acquitted in a satisfactory manner, though he had no special piece wherewith to display his vocal ability, but he certainly made an excellent Ezra. Notwithstanding that the cantata lasted an unusual time it was heartily enjoyed.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT, Cootioued from page 3.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT, Cootioued from page 3.
THURSDAY.-THE BUDGET.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evenirp, Sir E. GREY, replying to Mr. BYLES, said the Government had reason to hope that the*liicaraguan matter would shortly be settled. The hon. baronet informed Sir E. A. BARTLETT that he could not make any, statement at present on the sub ject of the Chino-Japanese treacly. Mr. W. JOHNSTON asked whether the Government, in deference to temperance opinion, would extend the Local Veto Bill to Ireland. Sir W. HARCOURT replied that he had already stated that it would be open to the House to gonsider whether or not Ireland should be in- cluded, and, answering a further question, he said it would be prematute for him to state what course the Governmont would take on the bill in committee. The Cuasicism.on of the EXCHEQUER introduced his Budget. He said that the revenue of the year just con- chided was estimated at £94,175,000. The amount realised was £94,684,000. The realised surplus of the year was £776,000, which would be appropriated to the liquidation of the permanent debt in the name of the old sinking fund. Customs receipts had been £440,000 more than in the previous year. There was, however, a decreased 'venue from wines of £66,000, and in spite of the extra sixpence there would have been little or no increase in the revenue from foreign spirits bit for the severity of the weather in Februarp. There was an increased consump- tion of non-dutiable articles, proving that the mass of the people in the past year and many years past had been able to obtain still larger quantities of the necessaries and comforts of life at lower prices. The net receipts on home made spirits had bsen £35,000 less than the estimate, the additional duty not having yielded half of what was expected. The amount re- ceived on beer was only £lB,OOO less than the estimate. The total yield of the Excise had been £25,875,000. The new probate and estate duties were estimated to yield £1,000,000, and they had in fact produced £973.000. The income tax had yielded an increase cf £70,000 upon the estimate. The national debt had been • reduced by £7,809,000. The gross liabilities of the State were now £660,000,000, a reduction of £100,000,000 in the last twenty years. There was no more satisfactory indication of the im- provement of the position of the people than was to be found in the returns of the savings banks and friendly societies. The excess of receipts over withdrawals in the Post-office was £958,000 in the year 1890-I—a prosperity year—and in 1894-5 it was over seven mil- lions. Turning to the prospects of the coming year,the right hon. gentleman said that the estimated expenditur was £95,982,000, an increase of £2,097,000 on the past year. The additional two millions was due to the navy (£1,400,000), Civil Service (£600,000), rates on Govern- ment property (£48,000), Sm. On the assumption that the additional duties on beer and spirits expired in July the estimated revenue was £95,662,000, and comparing this with the estimated expenditure there was an estimated deficit of £519,000. This de- ficit must be met by some form of taxation. The choice lay between the spirit duty :and the beer duty. Ile proposed to reimpose the additional sixpence on beer when the duty expired. The Qstimate of its yield for the nine months from July to the end of the financial year was £500,000, which would cover the estimated deficit and leave a small margin by way of surplus of £lBl,OOO. He did not think it necessary to prppose this additional duty beyond the presekt financial year. The spirit duty would expire in July,lind would not be re- imposed. In the course of his reply to various members Sir W. HARCOURT said he was not without hope that the Government might enter upon the question of teachers' mansions this session. After hinting that he might not have another opportunity of addressing the House in his present responsible capacity. _Sir WILLIAM warned hon. members and the country that the constant de- mands for increased expenditure might very soon pro- duce a crisis which the taxpayers would find very dis- agreeable. In his opinion the limit of taxation which would be found tolerable had very nearly been reached. The debate on the second reading of the Conciliation Bill was resumed and occupied members of the Opposi- tion until the hour for adjournment.
